GitLab CI/CD, Decoded#

Read, trace and fix any enterprise pipeline

Compiled bykodebot

GitLab 19.3 GitLab.com and self-managed Worked examples on AWS and Azure

Preface#

Your team's pipeline file is twenty lines long. The pipeline it produces is not, and keeping it working is now your job.

In a large organisation, a central team writes shared CI/CD templates, and each team writes its own pipeline file on top of them. Your file includes a template, which includes eight more. A job inherits from a job that inherits from another, in a repository you have never opened. Variables arrive from settings pages nobody on your team can see. When something breaks, the answer is often not in the file in front of you. And when your team needs a new job, a new rule or a deploy, you are the one who writes it.

GitLab's documentation explains each feature on its own. This book teaches you to do two things with a real pipeline. You learn to write and change your team's own file. You also learn to read everything the central team adds to it: to take any job and find where it came from, why it ran, what it was given and what it did. Everything is taught on MegaCorp, a fictional company whose GitLab is as tangled as the real ones, and on small practice projects that you build on your own GitLab.

Who it is for#

You are a developer who looks after your team's pipeline. Some of it comes from a central team's templates, and the rest your team writes. The book assumes that you know what CI/CD is, can use a terminal, and can create a project on a GitLab: GitLab.com's free tier, or your organisation's own. It assumes nothing more:

  • You don't need to have written a .gitlab-ci.yml, or any YAML.
  • You don't need to have used GitLab.
  • You don't need to have run a container.

Every term is explained where it first appears. The short chapter Before you start gives you the Git and GitLab words, enough YAML to read any pipeline file, and a first pipeline, in about ten minutes. Your first pipeline then has you run it on your own GitLab. Wherever an idea has parts, an order or a decision in it, a diagram shows it.

Conventions#

  • PremiumUltimate The lowest GitLab tier that has the feature. No tier badge means every tier has it.
  • Self-managedGitLab.com The feature exists only on that offering.
  • ExperimentalBetaDeprecated GitLab's own status for the feature.
  • Since 17.11 The release that introduced it. If your organisation runs its own GitLab, check which version it is on.

Examples come in a few shapes. A You wrote pane shows configuration as it sits in its file. A GitLab builds pane beside it shows what GitLab made of it, marked captured from GitLab when it is GitLab's own output. A symptom card goes from what you see to the cause, how to confirm it and the fix. A spot the bug exercise ends every chapter from Part III to Part IX. A lab is something to do on your own GitLab, with its steps and what you should see. A When you write it box gives the setting to choose, and the trap to avoid, when you write that mechanism in your team's file.

On accuracy#

GitLab releases every month, and search results do not sort by version. Every version-sensitive claim here was checked against GitLab's documentation. Every "GitLab builds" pane marked as captured is real output from a GitLab 19.3 instance, loaded with MegaCorp's projects exactly as this book shows them. Every lab was run end to end on that instance, and what each lab says you should see is what it printed. Where a behaviour needs a tier that instance doesn't have, the book says described, not captured.

It will still age. When this book and GitLab's documentation disagree, the documentation is right.

Before you start#

This book assumes you know what CI/CD is: code gets built, tested and shipped automatically whenever it changes. It assumes nothing else. This short chapter gives you the three things the rest of the book leans on:

  • the Git and GitLab words
  • enough YAML to read any pipeline file
  • a first pipeline, from a push to a result

If you already know all three, skip to chapter 1.

Git and GitLab words#

Git keeps the history of a project's files as a chain of saved changes. GitLab hosts that history and runs pipelines on it. Every word below appears on almost every page of this book:

WordWhat it isWhy a pipeline cares
commitone saved change to the files, with an ID like 4f2c9a1, called its SHAevery pipeline runs for exactly one commit
brancha named line of commits, such as feature/loginpushing to a branch starts a branch pipeline
default branchthe main line of the project, usually called maindeployments usually start from it
pushsending your new commits from your computer to GitLabthe most common way a pipeline starts
merge requesta request to merge one branch into another, with review and discussion; other tools call it a pull requestGitLab can run a pipeline for it, called a merge request pipeline
mergecombining a branch's commits into another branchmerging to main usually starts the pipeline that deploys
taga permanent name for one commit, usually a release number such as v1.4.0pushing a tag starts a tag pipeline, often the one that releases
protected branch or tagone that only chosen people may push tosecrets and deploy permissions are often limited to protected branches
projectGitLab's home for one repository, with its settings, pipelines and merge requestsa pipeline belongs to a project
groupa folder of projects, which can contain further groupssettings made on a group, such as CI/CD variables, reach every project inside it

YAML in five minutes#

A pipeline is described in a file called .gitlab-ci.yml, written in YAML. YAML is a way of writing data as indented text. Almost everything you will see is one of these few shapes:

# A comment: YAML ignores everything after #

name: payments-api        # a key and its value
retries: 2                # a number
enabled: true             # true or false

owner:                    # a map: the keys indented under "owner" belong to it
  team: payments
  email: payments@example.com

stages:                   # a list: one item per line, each starting with "-"
  - build
  - test

tags: [shared, linux]     # the same kind of list, written on one line

script: |                 # a block of text, kept line by line
  echo "first line"
  echo "second line"

Four rules explain nearly every YAML mistake you will meet:

  • Indentation is meaning. Keys indented under another key belong to it. Use spaces, never tabs; two spaces per level is the convention.
  • A dash starts a list item. - build is one item in a list. A key followed by a colon, such as stage:, starts a key in a map.
  • Numbers and true/false are not text. 21 is read as a number and true as a yes-or-no value. When you mean text, put it in quotes: JAVA_VERSION: "21". GitLab's variables are always text, which is why you will see so many quotes in pipeline files.
  • Some characters change the meaning. A value that starts with *, &, !, [ or {, or contains a colon followed by a space, means something special to YAML. Put such values in quotes when you mean plain text. Chapter 12 explains what the special ones do.

Numbers can even change as they are read. On the local GitLab 19.3, a variable written VERSION: 1.10 without quotes reached a rule as 1.1, so $VERSION == "1.10" never matched. Written as "1.10", it did.

In a .gitlab-ci.yml, every top-level key is one of two things. It is either a GitLab keyword that sets something for the whole pipeline, such as stages, or the name of a job. Here is the shape of the pipeline file you are about to read:

Your first pipeline file#

This is a complete .gitlab-ci.yml for a small Node.js project. It has two jobs: one builds the code, and one tests it.

practice · first-pipelinesteps/01-first.ymlpipeline
stages:
  - build
  - test

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test
LineWhat it means
stages:the stages of this pipeline, in the order they run: first build, then test
build-app:a job. Its name is up to you, as long as it isn't a GitLab keyword
stage: buildthis job belongs to the build stage
image: node:24.21.0-alpinethe job runs inside a container started from the node:24.21.0-alpine image, which has Node.js 24 installed
script:the commands the job runs, in order. If one fails, the job stops and fails
unit-tests:a second job, in the test stage, with the same image and its own commands

An image is a packaged set of tools and files. A container is a running copy of it, fresh for every job and thrown away afterwards. So nothing a job does on its own disk reaches the next job, unless the job saves it on purpose (chapter 30). That is why both jobs above run npm ci.

When you push a commit, GitLab turns this file into a pipeline. The pipeline graph shows each stage as a column and each job as a box:

Here is what happens between your push and the result:

A runner is a program, running somewhere your organisation chose, that asks GitLab for jobs and runs them. Chapter 2 takes each of these words further.

Every pipeline in this book is built from the same pieces: keywords, jobs, stages, images and scripts. The difficulty in a large organisation is not the pieces. It is that a real pipeline is assembled from many files, settings and teams you can't see from your own project. Finding those, and reading them, is what the rest of the book teaches.

Reading about a pipeline only goes so far. The next chapter, Your first pipeline, has you run this file on your own GitLab, break it three ways and fix it, in about a quarter of an hour.

Your first pipeline#

Before you start showed you a pipeline file. Now you run it on your own GitLab, then break it on purpose, three ways, so that you know what each kind of mistake looks like. You need about twenty minutes, a terminal with Git, and an account on a GitLab where you can create a project. GitLab.com's Free tier works, and so does your organisation's own GitLab.

The project#

The project is a tiny Node.js one. It has a function that builds a greeting, a test for it, and a build step that copies the source into dist/, the way a real build would bundle it. It has no dependencies, so npm ci has nothing to download. These are its files; each pane has a copy button.

practice · first-pipelinepackage.json
{
  "name": "first-pipeline",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "description": "The project of the first-pipeline lab: a greeting, built and tested.",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "node build.js",
    "test": "node --test"
  }
}
practice · first-pipelinepackage-lock.json
{
  "name": "first-pipeline",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "lockfileVersion": 3,
  "requires": true,
  "packages": {
    "": {
      "name": "first-pipeline",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  }
}
practice · first-pipelinebuild.js
// The build: copies src/ into dist/, the way a real build would bundle it.
import { cpSync, mkdirSync } from "node:fs";

mkdirSync("dist", { recursive: true });
cpSync("src", "dist", { recursive: true });
console.log("built dist/greet.js and dist/cli.js");
practice · first-pipelinesrc/greet.js
// The first-pipeline lab's one function.
export function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
practice · first-pipelinesrc/cli.js
// Prints a greeting: node src/cli.js <name>
import { greet } from "./greet.js";

console.log(greet(process.argv[2] ?? "world"));
practice · first-pipelinetest/greet.test.js
// The first-pipeline lab's test, run with node --test.
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { greet } from "../src/greet.js";

test("greet says hello", () => {
  assert.equal(greet("GitLab"), "Hello, GitLab!");
});
LabRun itabout 8 min#
You need

An account on a GitLab where you can create a project, a terminal with Git, and the six files above.

Steps
  1. In GitLab's upper-right corner, select Create new (the plus sign), then New project/repository, then Create blank project. Name it first-pipeline, leave everything else as it is, and select Create project.
  2. Clone the project with the address under its Code button. Copy the six files into the folder, keeping their paths.
  3. Add a file named .gitlab-ci.yml, with the pipeline from Before you start:
    practice · first-pipelinesteps/01-first.ymlpipeline
    stages:
  - build
  - test

build-app:
  stage: build
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run build

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test
  4. Commit and push: 
    git add .
git commit -m "Add the first pipeline"
git push
  5. In GitLab, open Build › Pipelines, then the newest pipeline, then its build-app job.
What you should see

The pipeline passes: build-app in the build stage, then unit-tests in the test stage. The job's log shows what the runner did, then each of your commands and what it printed. Here it is, cut to its main lines:

Note
On GitLab.com, a new account's first pipeline can stop with the message "Identity verification is required in order to run CI jobs". Select Verify my account in the banner, verify a phone number or add a payment method, then run the pipeline again. On your organisation's own GitLab, if the jobs just wait, ask your platform team: your project may have no runner it is allowed to use.

You need

The project from the previous lab, with its pipeline passing.

Steps

    practice · first-pipelinesteps/02-bad-indent.ymlbroken

  stage: build
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
 script:
    - npm ci

    practice · first-pipelinesteps/03-failing-command.ymlbroken

  stage: test

    practice · first-pipelinesteps/04-missing-file.ymlsmoke-test

  stage: build

What you should see

Bad indentation. The pipeline fails at once, with no jobs. Its badge says error, and its tooltip gives GitLab's reason: "The pipeline failed due to an error on the CI/CD configuration file." Paste the file into CI Lint (chapter 3) for the detail:

(<unknown>): did not find expected key while parsing a block mapping at line 1 column 1

Line 1 is where GitLab began the map it couldn't finish, not the line you changed. Look further down, where the indentation shifts.

A command that fails. unit-tests fails. npm says what went wrong, and the runner says why the job stopped:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ npm ci
⋯ lines omitted
$ npm run lint
npm error Missing script: "lint"
⋯ lines omitted
ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1

A file from an earlier job. smoke-test fails, because its fresh container has no dist/:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab

$ node dist/cli.js "smoke test"
⋯ lines omitted
Error: Cannot find module '/builds/practice/first-pipeline/dist/cli.js'
⋯ lines omitted

With the artifact, the job downloads build-app's files first, and passes:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
Downloading artifacts for build-app (192)...

$ node dist/cli.js "smoke test"
Hello, smoke test!

The third break is the one that surprises people most. Every job starts in a fresh container, so nothing a job leaves on its own disk reaches the next job unless the job keeps it on purpose. Chapter 30 covers artifacts, and their cousin, the cache.

LabA job with nowhere to runabout 4 min#
Steps
  1. Add a job that asks for a runner with a gpu tag, and push:
    practice · first-pipelinesteps/06-stuck.ymlstuck
    train-model:
  stage: test
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine
  tags: [gpu]
  script:
    - echo "no runner has the gpu tag, so this job waits"
  2. Open train-model's page from the pipeline.
  3. Cancel the pipeline, then delete the job from the file and push.
What you should see

The other jobs pass, but train-model stays pending. Its page says why, and lists the tag that no runner has:

On your organisation's GitLab, runners have tags that the platform team chooses. A job that asks for any other tag waits like this (stuck on tags).

That is the whole engine: a push, a file GitLab reads, jobs in stages, containers started from images, and runners that take the jobs whose tags they have. Chapter 2 takes each of these words further, and Part II grows this into a real service's pipeline.

The one-page map#

Part I · Orientation · Chapter 01· 5 min read

In a large organisation, a job is rarely written in one place. It is put together from layers:

  • your project's pipeline file
  • shared files written by a central team
  • settings that live in no file at all
  • the machine and the image the job runs on

GitLab combines these layers at four moments: when it reads each YAML file, when it joins the files together, when it creates the pipeline, and when a job runs. You can see the result of the first two in one place, Build › Pipeline editor › Full configuration. Everything after that you trace another way.

Nearly every question about a job is one of five. Where is it defined? When does it run? Where does it run? What does it execute? What goes in and out?

This chapter is the map you will keep coming back to. Read it for the shape, and don't try to learn every term on it yet: each one is explained properly in the chapter the map points to. Part II then has you write a pipeline of your own, before the rest of the book takes the layers apart one at a time.

Where a job comes from#

Picture a job as an onion. Your project's file is at the centre, and each layer around it can add to it or change it:

From the inside out:

  1. Your project's .gitlab-ci.yml. The file your team writes and changes. In a big organisation it is often only twenty lines.
  2. The central team's shared files. YAML files that your file pulls in with include. Most of your jobs are really defined there.
  3. Organisation settings. CI/CD variables, which are named values set on the settings pages of the project, of its groups, and of the whole GitLab installation, called the instance. They beat anything written in YAML.
  4. Run time. The runner's own configuration, and the image the job runs in. The real logic of a script often lives inside the image.

What the outer layers can hold#

Your own file usually has an include, a few settings, and perhaps one job adjusted. Sometimes there is no file at all, because the project's settings point to a file in another project.

The central team's files hold four kinds of thing:

  • hidden jobs: templates for jobs that never run themselves
  • real jobs that copy from a hidden job with extends
  • snippets pasted into jobs with !reference
  • a default: block that applies to every job

Part III explains each of these. On GitLab's top tier, Ultimate, security policies can also add jobs to every pipeline, from outside any file.

Four moments, and what you can see#

GitLab doesn't apply all the layers at once. It works in four phases: it reads each file, joins the files, creates the pipeline, and runs each job. The phase decides where you can see the result:

So if what you need to know happens in the first two phases, one page shows it: the Full configuration view. If it happens later, the table of tools at the end of this chapter says where to look instead.

The four phases in detail#

PhaseWhenWhat happensCan the merged view show it?
ParseGitLab reads each YAML file on its ownYAML's own copy-and-paste features are applied: anchors, aliases and merge keysyes
CompileGitLab joins the files togetherincluded files are copied in; extends and !reference copy settings from one job into anotheryes
CreateGitLab creates the pipelinerules decide which jobs exist; a job with parallel: matrix becomes several jobs; settings variables and policies applyno: look at the pipeline graph and the settings
Runa runner runs one jobthe image, the runner's configuration and any downloaded scripts do their partno: read the job log

Two details of the merged view surprise people:

  • A component's jobs appear with their inputs already filled in. Chapter 15 explains inputs.
  • The default: block appears on its own, not copied into each job. A job's final image or retry setting may therefore be in default:, not in the job.

Five questions for any job#

When a job surprises you, the question you are asking is almost always one of these:

QuestionWhere the answer usually isCovered in
Where is it defined?the Full configuration view, then the extends chain, then the included file; if it is in no file, a policyPart III
When does it run?workflow:rules, the job's rules, needs and stagesPart IV
Where does it run?the job's runner tags, the runner's executor and the job's imagePart VI
What does it execute?before_script and script, and whatever those call inside the imagereuse outside the YAML
What goes in and out?variables and secrets in; artifacts, caches, reports, images and deployments outPart V and Part VI

The same idea, as a pipeline#

Here is a merge request pipeline for payments-api, a service at MegaCorp. MegaCorp is the made-up company this book uses throughout. Each column is a stage and each box is a job. The project's own file defines none of these jobs:

Each job has a different origin, and each is traced a different way. Chapter 4 introduces the projects behind them.

Where each of these jobs comes from#

  • maven-build, maven-test and image-build are copied from the central team's hidden jobs, with extends.
  • sonar-scan comes from a component: a packaged, versioned piece of pipeline that a project includes.
  • container_scanning comes from a file GitLab itself ships for its scanners, adjusted by MegaCorp.
  • policy-sbom is in none of the project's files at all. A security policy adds it.

The tools that answer the questions#

Five places in GitLab answer most questions, and you will use each of them in this book:

ToolWhereWhat it answers
Full configurationBuild › Pipeline editor, then the Full configuration tabwhat GitLab assembled: included files, extends, !reference and anchors, all resolved
ValidateBuild › Pipeline editor, then the Validate tabwhich jobs a push would create, and problems with needs and rules
The pipeline graphthe pipeline's pagewhich jobs exist, in which stage, and which downstream pipelines were triggered
The job logthe job's pagewhat ran, in which image, on which runner, and what the script printed
CI/CD variablesthe CI/CD settings of the project, its groups and the instancevalues that no file shows

The rest of the book takes this map one layer and one phase at a time.

Next02The engine: pipelines, stages, jobs and runners6 min

The engine: pipelines, stages, jobs and runners#

Part I · Orientation · Chapter 02· 6 min read

A pipeline is one run of your CI/CD configuration, started by an event such as a push. It is made of jobs, grouped into stages. Stages run in order, and the jobs inside one stage run at the same time.

A job is a script plus what it needs to run: an image, variables, and files from earlier jobs. A runner takes the job from GitLab and runs it.

That is the whole engine. The rest of the book is about where its parts come from.

If you read Before you start, you have met these words already. This chapter makes them precise, and shows you how to read what GitLab shows you.

Six words#

TermWhat it isWhere you see it
Pipelineone run of the configuration, for one commit and one eventthe pipeline's page, with its graph
Stagea named group of jobs; stages run in the order they are listedthe columns of the pipeline graph
Joba script to run, with its settingsa box in the graph; the job's own page holds its log
Runnera program somewhere that takes jobs from GitLab and runs themthe job's page names it
Executorhow the runner runs a job: in a container, in a Kubernetes pod (a group of containers Kubernetes runs together), or directly in a shellthe first lines of the job log
Imagethe container image a job runs in, when the executor uses containersthe first lines of the job log

Stages#

If a configuration never lists its stages, GitLab uses five: .pre, build, test, deploy and .post. A job that doesn't name a stage lands in test. A project can declare its own list with stages:. MegaCorp's golden pipeline does: build, test, package, scan, deploy.

Stages run one after another, and the jobs within a stage run in parallel. When a job fails, the stages after it usually don't start. "Usually", because a job can be allowed to fail, and a job can use needs to start before its stage would (chapter 23).

.pre and .post never need listing. Every stage you list runs after .pre and before .post. A security policy can add two more stages outside even those (chapter 35).

Two stage mistakes stop GitLab from creating the pipeline at all. The first is a job whose stage isn't in the list. The local GitLab 19.3 reports it like this:

orphan job: chosen stage nowhere does not exist; available stages are .pre, build, .post

The second is easier to miss. A job with no stage goes into test. If a project's stages: list leaves test out, that job fails in the same way, with chosen stage test does not exist.

Reading the pipeline graph#

  • Columns are stages, in the order they run.
  • Within a stage, jobs are sorted alphabetically by name. They are not sorted by when they started, or by where they were defined. The graph tells you nothing about which file a job came from.
  • Numbered jobs are grouped. Names that differ only by a counter, such as build ruby 1/3 and build ruby 2/3, collapse into one box with a count.
  • Every job shows a status. A job usually moves through the same few, in order:
StatusWhat it means for you
createdthe job exists, but its turn hasn't come: an earlier stage is still running
pendingits turn has come, and it is waiting for a runner that can take it
preparinga runner has it and is getting the environment ready
runningthe script is running
successit finished, and every command succeeded
faileda command failed, or the runner gave up on the job
canceledsomeone or something stopped it
skippedit didn't run, usually because an earlier stage failed
manualit waits for someone to start it
scheduleda delayed job, counting down to its start
waiting_for_resourceit is ready, but another job holds the resource it needs

A job that sits in pending for ever is almost always a runner problem: no runner has the tags the job asks for (chapter 28). GitLab also has canceling and waiting_for_callback. You will rarely see either.

What can be a job#

Any top-level key in the configuration is a job, apart from GitLab's own keywords. That rule makes some mistakes quiet:

  • Keywords are never jobs. image, services, stages, before_script, after_script, variables, cache and include can't be job names. A top-level key called services: is read as the keyword, not as a job named "services".
  • A leading dot hides a job. .maven-base: never runs. It exists to be borrowed from (chapter 13).
  • Names are unique. Two definitions of the same name, one in your file and one in an included file, merge into one job. Two genuinely separate jobs can't share a name.
  • The limit is 255 characters. true, false and nil work as names only in quotes.

Runners, executors and images#

GitLab schedules jobs but doesn't run them. Runners do. A runner is registered with GitLab, keeps asking it for work, and runs each job it accepts with its executor:

  • With the Docker executor, each job runs in a fresh container started from the job's image.
  • With the Kubernetes executor, each job runs in a pod.
  • With the shell executor, jobs run directly on the runner's machine.

A runner has tags: labels such as linux or megacorp-shared. A job lists tags too. A runner takes a job only if it has every tag the job lists. If a job sets its own tags, they replace any default: tags completely rather than adding to them.

Gotcha
GitLab uses the word "tag" for two unrelated things. A Git tag, such as v1.4.0, names a commit and starts tag pipelines. A runner tag, set with the tags: keyword, chooses which runner takes a job. In .gitlab-ci.yml, tags: always means runner tags.

Runners belong to the whole instance, to a group, or to a single project. Their configuration is invisible from your project, which makes them one of the layers on the one-page map.

Reading a job log#

A job's log is written top to bottom, in a fixed order. The runner starts each part with a heading, and the job page lets you fold each part away. These are the headings as GitLab Runner 19.3 writes them:

HeadingWhat happens
Running with gitlab-runner 19.3.0, then the runner's namewhich runner took the job
Preparing the "shell" executorthe executor starts; the heading names the one in use
Preparing environmentwhere the job runs: Running on a host or a pod
Getting source from Git repositorythe fetch, its depth, and the commit checked out
Restoring cachecaches are fetched, if the job has any
Executing "step_script" stage of the job scriptbefore_script, then script: each line echoed after a $, then its output
Running after_scriptafter_script, in a separate shell
Saving cache for successful jobcaches are saved
Uploading artifacts for successful jobartifacts and reports are uploaded
Cleaning up project directory and file based variablesthe runner tidies up
Job succeeded, or ERROR: Job failed: …the result

To open a job, select it in its pipeline's graph, or find it under Build › Jobs. The log fills the page. On the right, Job details names the runner, the job's timeout and where that came from, and the tags:

When a job fails, read the log from the end backwards. The last command echoed is the one that failed, because a failing command stops the script. When a job does the wrong thing, read the log from the top, because the first lines tell you where it really ran.

One job's whole log#

Next03How GitLab builds a pipeline4 min

How GitLab builds a pipeline#

Part I · Orientation · Chapter 03· 4 min read

When you push, GitLab does a fixed sequence of things before any job runs:

  1. It finds the configuration: .gitlab-ci.yml, or the file the project's settings name.
  2. It fetches every included file and merges them all into one configuration.
  3. It resolves extends, !reference and anchors, and checks the result is valid.
  4. It decides whether a pipeline exists (workflow: rules) and which jobs are in it (each job's rules).
  5. It creates the jobs, and runners start taking them.

Two tools let you watch the first four steps without pushing anything: the pipeline editor and CI Lint.

From a push to a pipeline#

Every pipeline goes through the same checks, and each one can stop it. Knowing which check stopped it tells you where to look:

The first four steps are the compile and create phases from chapter 1. Part III takes the files and how they merge, and Part IV the rules.

Here is the whole assembly for one job. payments-api's file is short, and the job GitLab builds from it is not:

You wrotemegacorp/payments/payments-api · .gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - project: megacorp/devops/ci-templates
    ref: v4.2.0
    file: pipelines/java-service.yml
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/megacorp/devops/components/sonar-scan@2.1.0
    inputs:
      stage: test
      project_key: payments-api
You wrotemegacorp/devops/ci-templates · pipelines/java-service.yml
maven-build:
  extends: .maven-build

maven-test:
  extends: .maven-test

image-build:
  extends: .image-build
  needs: [maven-build]
→
GitLab buildsmerged configurationcaptured from GitLab
maven-build:
  variables:
    MC_TEAM: unknown
    JAVA_VERSION: '21'
    MAVEN_OPTS: "-Dmaven.repo.local=$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.m2/repository"
  artifacts:
    expire_in: 7 days
    paths:
    - target/*.jar
  rules:
  - - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
      when: never
  - - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
  - - if: "$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH"
  - - if: "$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\\d+\\.\\d+\\.\\d+$/"
  extends: ".maven-build"
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/maven:3.9-jdk${JAVA_VERSION}
  cache:
    key:
      files:
      - pom.xml
    paths:
    - ".m2/repository"
  before_script:
  - - source /opt/megacorp/lib/ci-lib.sh
  - - mkdir -p .m2
    - mc_maven_settings > .m2/settings.xml
  stage: build
  script:
  - mvn $MAVEN_CLI_OPTS -DskipTests package

Every line of the result came from a file payments-api never opens. The variables, the image, the cache, the rules and the before_script all arrived through the include and the extends chain, which chapter 13 walks one link at a time.

The pipeline editor#

The pipeline editor is at Build › Pipeline editor. It edits the project's .gitlab-ci.yml, and its tabs show what GitLab would do with it:

TabWhat it showsUse it to
Editthe file, checked against GitLab's schema as you type; the result appears at the top of the pagecatch syntax mistakes before you commit
Visualizeevery stage and job, with needs drawn as lines between jobssee the shape of the pipeline
Validatea simulated pipeline for a push to the branch you choose, under Pipeline run sourcefind problems with rules and needs before you push
Full configurationthe whole configuration as one file: includes copied in, extends merged, anchors and !reference replacedfind where a line of a job really comes from

A file-tree button in the upper-right corner lists every file the configuration includes, and opens each one. A commit form at the bottom of every tab saves your changes.

Three details matter when you rely on the Full configuration tab:

  • It shows one scenario. Anything conditional, such as an include with rules, is decided as if the pipeline were a push to the default branch. A file included only for merge requests won't appear.
  • Extra hyphens are harmless. Content pasted by !reference can appear as a list inside a list, with lines that start - -. GitLab documents this as expected, and it doesn't change what runs.
  • It can't show what happens later. Rules for each job, matrices, policies, settings variables and anything the runner does all come after this view (chapter 1).

If the project's configuration lives in another project, the editor can't open it. Chapter 19 shows how to see it anyway.

CI Lint: checking a snippet#

CI Lint checks configuration you paste in, so you can test a change without touching the project's file. It lives on the same Validate tab:

  1. Open Build › Pipeline editor, then the Validate tab.
  2. Select Lint CI/CD sample, and paste the configuration.
  3. To go further than syntax, select Simulate pipeline creation for the default branch.
  4. Select Validate.

A simulation evaluates the rules as a push to the default branch, so it finds the problems a real push would hit. Every error message quoted in this book came from the same check, run on the local GitLab 19.3. For example, a job whose stage isn't in stages: gets:

orphan job: chosen stage nowhere does not exist; available stages are .pre, build, .post

The same check is available outside the browser: from the GitLab CLI (glab ci lint), from the GitLab extension for VS Code, and from the API.

Which tool answers which question#

You want to knowUseIt can't tell you
what all the files add up toFull configurationanything decided when the pipeline is created
which jobs a push to a branch would createValidate, choosing the branchmerge request or scheduled pipelines
whether a snippet is valid, or what it would doCI Lint, with simulationanything about pipelines other than a default-branch push
how the jobs depend on each otherVisualizewhich of them a given pipeline will contain
which jobs a merge request or schedule getsa real pipeline of that kind, or a truth table (chapter 24)nothing: this is the ground truth

None of these tools shows variables set in settings, policies, or what the runner and the image do. For those, you need the pipeline graph, the settings pages and the job log, and the rest of Part I introduces them.

Next04Meet MegaCorp3 min

Meet MegaCorp#

Part I · Orientation · Chapter 04· 3 min read

MegaCorp is a made-up company, and so is everything in its GitLab. It is built the way large organisations build theirs:

  • A central DevOps team writes the shared pipeline files, the ready-made building blocks called components, and the container image most jobs run in.
  • The security team writes policies that add scans to every pipeline.
  • The platform team runs every deployment.
  • Each application team keeps a short file that pulls in everything else.

Every example in this book is a real file from MegaCorp's projects, labelled with its project and path. The same files are loaded into a real GitLab 19.3 instance, and every piece of GitLab output in the book comes from there.

The map#

Each box is a GitLab project, and the arrows show who uses whom:

The projects#

You don't need to follow every word in this table yet. The last column says where each project is explained.

ProjectOwned byHoldsYou'll meet it in
megacorp/devops/ci-templatescentral DevOpsthe shared pipeline files: job templates, script snippets, rules, and two complete pipelinesPart III
megacorp/devops/componentscentral DevOpscomponents, which are versioned building blocks with settings: sonar-scan, ecr-push and gitops-deploycomponents and inputs
megacorp/devops/ci-toolscentral DevOpsthe toolbox image most jobs run in, its shell functions, and MegaCorp's own mc commandreuse outside the YAML
megacorp/security/policiessecuritythe security policies that add scans and gates to other projects' pipelinespolicies and gates
megacorp/platform/deployerplatformthe deployment pipeline that every service startsGitOps repositories and promotion
megacorp/platform/chartsplatformthe Helm chart that every service is deployed withHelm
megacorp/platform/gitops-configplatformthe environment repository: what runs on eks-prod and aks-prod, and each environment's valuesGitOps repositories and promotion
megacorp/platform/infra-modules, infra-liveplatformthe OpenTofu that builds both clusters, their registries and their identitiesOpenTofu and Terraform
megacorp/payments/payments-apithe payments teama Java service: one include, one component, two adjustmentsthroughout
megacorp/web/web-portalthe web teama Node front end with no .gitlab-ci.yml at allorg-wide reuse
megacorp/data/monothe data teama monorepo, one repository holding many services, that generates its own child pipelinespipelines as building blocks
megacorp/legacy/billing-batchnobody, any morean old file from 2019, using older techniques: YAML anchors, a file included from a URL, and a trigger tokenYAML-level reuse

A service's whole pipeline file#

This is all the configuration the payments team maintains, apart from two small adjustments further down the same file:

megacorp/payments/payments-api.gitlab-ci.ymlinclude
include:
  - project: megacorp/devops/ci-templates
    ref: v4.2.0
    file: pipelines/java-service.yml
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/megacorp/devops/components/sonar-scan@2.1.0
    inputs:
      stage: test
      project_key: payments-api

include pulls another file's contents into this one, as if they had been typed here. The first include is MegaCorp's "golden pipeline" for Java services: a complete, ready-made pipeline that any Java project can take whole. This is what it pulls in:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatespipelines/java-service.ymlincludes
include:
  - project: megacorp/devops/ci-templates
    ref: v4.2.0
    file:
      - templates/base.yml
      - templates/snippets.yml
      - templates/rules.yml
      - templates/workflow.yml
      - templates/java-maven.yml
      - templates/container.yml
      - templates/security.yml
      - templates/deploy.yml

That is eight shared files, all pinned to the tag v4.2.0. Pinned means GitLab reads them as they were at that tag. A later change by the central team doesn't reach payments-api until someone moves the tag in this file.

Those files define hidden jobs. Their names start with a dot, and they never run by themselves. The golden pipeline turns three of them into real jobs:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatespipelines/java-service.ymljobs
maven-build:
  extends: .maven-build

maven-test:
  extends: .maven-test

image-build:
  extends: .image-build
  needs: [maven-build]

So there are four files between payments-api and the script its maven-test job runs. Chapter 13 walks that chain one link at a time.

What no file in the project shows#

Some of MegaCorp's configuration isn't in any repository the payments team can read:

  • Settings. Variables set on the instance and on the megacorp group, and web-portal's pointer to a pipeline file in another project. The book shows them in files called SETTINGS.yml, which GitLab never reads.
  • Policies. On GitLab Ultimate, the security team's policy project adds a secret-detection scan to every pipeline. It also adds a job that lists everything the build contains, known as an SBOM (software bill of materials).
  • The runners. Their configuration sets environment variables and cloud permissions for every job.

Here are the variables set on the megacorp group. Every project in the group receives them:

settingsgroup-megacorp.ymlgroup-variables
# Every project under megacorp/ receives these. A group variable takes precedence
# over any variable of the same name in a project's .gitlab-ci.yml.
group_variables:
  - key: MAVEN_CLI_OPTS
    value: "--batch-mode --errors --show-version -s .m2/settings.xml"
  - key: AWS_ACCOUNT_ID
    value: "123456789012"
  - key: MC_AZURE_TENANT_ID
    value: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
  - key: MC_ACR_REGISTRY
    value: megacorpprod.azurecr.io
  - key: MC_ACR_PUSH_CLIENT_ID
    value: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
    # the gitlab-acr-push application in Entra ID, which mc_acr_push signs in as
  - key: SONAR_HOST_URL
    value: https://sonar.example.com
  - key: SONAR_TOKEN
    value: "(set in the UI)"
    masked: true
    protected: true

Keep MAVEN_CLI_OPTS in mind. It matters in chapter 25.

Reading the specimen#

  • Every file opens with a comment saying what it is and which chapters use it.
  • Every quote is labelled with its project and path. When only part of a file is shown, the label also names the part, called a region.
  • Files named SETTINGS.yml describe settings made in GitLab's web pages. GitLab never reads them.
  • Every pipeline file in the specimen is valid. On the local GitLab, each one creates its pipelines. The deployer creates one only when a service passes it an image to deploy, by design. Like any real setup, the specimen also hides a few surprises, and the exercises find them.

The full, annotated listing is in the appendix.

Next · Part II05Build and test6 min

Build and test#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 05· 6 min read

Your team's pipeline starts with two jobs: one builds the service, and one tests it. Each job runs in a fresh container. So the build job keeps what it made as an artifact, which later jobs receive, and both jobs keep downloaded dependencies in a cache, which later pipelines reuse. The test job hands its results to GitLab as a report, so failing tests show on the pipeline and in merge requests.

This part grows one service's pipeline, a chapter at a time. The service is greeting-service, a small web service that answers GET /greet?name=Ada with a greeting. It comes in Node and in Java: pick yours with any Node or Java tab, and every tab in the book follows. Each chapter ends with a lab that you do on your own GitLab. Nothing here needs the rest of the book; where a chapter uses something that a later chapter explains fully, it links there.

Two jobs, two stages#

Here is the pipeline this chapter builds. Each column is a stage, and a stage starts only when the stage before it has passed:

practice · node-servicesteps/1-build-and-test.ymlpipeline
stages:
  - build
  - test

default:
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm run build
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - package-lock.json
    paths:
      - .npm/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm test -- --test-reporter=spec --test-reporter-destination=stdout --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=junit.xml
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - package-lock.json
    paths:
      - .npm/
    policy: pull
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
practice · java-servicesteps/1-build-and-test.ymlpipeline
stages:
  - build
  - test

default:
  image: maven:3.9.16-eclipse-temurin-25

variables:
  MAVEN_OPTS: "-Dmaven.repo.local=$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.m2/repository"
  MAVEN_CLI_OPTS: "--batch-mode --no-transfer-progress"

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - mvn $MAVEN_CLI_OPTS package -DskipTests
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - pom.xml
    paths:
      - .m2/repository/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - target/greeting-service.jar

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - mvn $MAVEN_CLI_OPTS test
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - pom.xml
    paths:
      - .m2/repository/
    policy: pull
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml

From the top:

  • stages lists the stages in order.
  • default: image gives every job the same image unless a job names its own: Node 24 for the Node service, Maven with Java 25 for the Java one. The version is pinned, so the job behaves the same next month.
  • build installs the dependencies and builds. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile lists. Maven's package compiles and makes the jar, and -DskipTests leaves the tests to the next job.
  • unit-tests installs the dependencies again, because it runs in a new container, and runs the tests.

Artifacts: what later jobs receive#

artifacts: paths tells GitLab which files to keep when the job ends. The Node build keeps dist/, and the Java build keeps target/greeting-service.jar. GitLab uploads them, and every job in a later stage downloads them before its script starts. That is how a later job, such as one that builds an image, gets the build's output without building again.

Without artifacts, the files vanish with the container, as the third break in your first pipeline showed. Chapter 30 covers artifacts in full.

Cache: what later pipelines reuse#

Every job downloads its dependencies again. A cache keeps them between pipelines, so that the next job starts from what the last one downloaded:

  • cache: key: files names the file whose content decides the cache: package-lock.json or pom.xml. Change the dependencies, and the key changes, so no job restores a stale cache.
  • cache: paths is what is kept: npm's download folder, .npm/, or Maven's local repository, .m2/repository/. The Node jobs point npm at it with --cache .npm. The Java jobs point Maven at it with the MAVEN_OPTS variable.
  • policy: pull on unit-tests means it reads the cache but never writes it back. Only build saves it.

A pipeline's first run finds no cache. The next one restores it, and its log says so. A cache can still miss at any time, for example on a different runner, so a job must work without it: a cache makes jobs faster, never correct. Chapter 30 explains why.

Test results GitLab can read#

artifacts: reports: junit hands GitLab a file of test results in the JUnit format. GitLab shows them on the pipeline's Tests tab, and in a merge request's test summary. The Node tests write one with the test runner's junit reporter; Maven's test plugin writes one per test class. when: always keeps the report even when tests fail, which is when you need it most.

When you write it

Key the dependency cache on the lockfile, key: files:, and give jobs that only read it policy: pull. The trap is one fixed key shared by every branch and job, which serves stale or half-written files (stale files).

An account on your GitLab, and the service's files for your stack. Copy them from the panes below, keeping their paths.

// Builds the greeting. zod checks the name before it is used.
import { z } from "zod";

const Name = z.string().trim().min(1).max(40);

export function greet(name) {

practice · node-servicesrc/server.js
// A tiny HTTP service: GET /greet?name=Ada answers {"message":"Hello, Ada!"}.
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { greet } from "./greet.js";

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8080);

createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, "http://localhost");
  if (url.pathname !== "/greet") {
    res.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }
  try {
    const body = JSON.stringify({ message: greet(url.searchParams.get("name") ?? "world") });
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" }).end(body);
  } catch {
    res.writeHead(400).end();
  }
}).listen(port, () => console.log(`listening on ${port}`));

practice · java-servicesrc/main/java/com/example/greeting/Greeter.java
package com.example.greeting;

/** Builds the greeting, after checking the name. */
public final class Greeter {
    private Greeter() {
    }

    public static String greet(String name) {
        String n = name == null ? "" : name.strip();
        if (n.isEmpty() || n.length() > 40) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("a name is 1 to 40 characters");
        }
        return "Hello, " + n + "!";
    }
}
practice · java-servicesrc/main/java/com/example/greeting/Server.java
package com.example.greeting;

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URLDecoder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

/** A tiny HTTP service: GET /greet?name=Ada answers {"message":"Hello, Ada!"}. */
public final class Server {
    private Server() {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        int port = Integer.parseInt(System.getenv().getOrDefault("PORT", "8080"));
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(port), 0);
        server.createContext("/greet", exchange -> {
            String query = exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery();
            String name = "world";
            if (query != null && query.startsWith("name=")) {
                name = URLDecoder.decode(query.substring(5), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            }
            int status = 200;
            String body;
            try {
                String message = Greeter.greet(name).replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"");
                body = "{\"message\":\"" + message + "\"}";
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
                status = 400;
                body = "";
            }
            byte[] bytes = body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("content-type", "application/json");
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(status, bytes.length == 0 ? -1 : bytes.length);
            try (OutputStream out = exchange.getResponseBody()) {
                out.write(bytes);
            }
        });
        server.start();
        System.out.println("listening on " + port);
    }
}

  • The key ends in -protected because main is a protected branch. GitLab keeps the caches of protected pipelines apart from the rest.
  • "No URL provided" means this runner keeps its cache on its own machine. GitLab.com's runners share a cache stored in Google Cloud Storage, so their log reads differently here.
  • unit-tests restores the same cache, and at the end says "Not uploading cache … due to policy". That is policy: pull.
  • The Tests tab counts the service's 2 tests, both passed.
Break it on purpose

In cache: key: files:, change the file's name to one that doesn't exist, and push. GitLab ignores a missing file, and when none of the named files exists the key is default. So the job looks for a different cache, and the one it saved before is no longer found. Put the name back.

Next06Merge request pipelines4 min

Merge request pipelines#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 06· 4 min read

So far, every push to any branch runs the whole pipeline. Once your team works in merge requests, you want one pipeline for each push to a merge request, with its result shown on the merge request, and no second pipeline for the same push. A workflow at the top of the file decides which kind of pipeline a push gets. Each job's rules then decide whether the job is in it. A rule on changed files lets a documentation change skip the build.

Two kinds of pipeline#

GitLab can run two kinds of pipeline for the same commit:

  • A branch pipeline runs when you push to a branch. Its $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE is push, and $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH holds the branch's name.
  • A merge request pipeline runs for a merge request, when it opens and on every push to its source branch. Its $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE is merge_request_event, and $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH is not set at all. Its result shows on the merge request.

A job with no rules runs only in branch pipelines. As soon as jobs have rules, they can run in merge request pipelines too, and one push can then create both kinds. Chapter 20 covers every kind of pipeline.

A workflow: one pipeline per push#

A workflow is checked before any job. GitLab tries its rules in order, and the first that matches decides. If none matches, there is no pipeline:

practice · node-servicesteps/2-merge-requests.ymlworkflow
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH
  1. A merge request pipeline: create it.
  2. A branch pipeline for a branch that has an open merge request: don't. The merge request pipeline covers that push.
  3. Any other branch pipeline: create it. That includes main.

The workflow is the same for both stacks. Chapter 21 explains workflows in full, including why the second rule matters (duplicate pipelines).

Skipping work when only the docs changed#

Each job now has rules of its own:

practice · node-servicesteps/2-merge-requests.ymlbuild
build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm run build
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - package-lock.json
    paths:
      - .npm/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - changes:
        - src/**/*
        - test/**/*
        - package.json
        - package-lock.json
practice · java-servicesteps/2-merge-requests.ymlbuild
build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - mvn $MAVEN_CLI_OPTS package -DskipTests
  cache:
    key:
      files:
        - pom.xml
    paths:
      - .m2/repository/
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - target/greeting-service.jar
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - changes:
        - src/**/*
        - pom.xml
  • On the default branch, main, the job always runs, so main always has a fresh build.
  • Anywhere else, changes decides. In a merge request pipeline, GitLab compares the merge request's changes with its target branch. The job runs only if a file matching one of the patterns changed.

So a merge request whose changes, taken together, touch only docs/README.md matches no rule in any job. A pipeline with no jobs isn't created, so that merge request gets no pipeline at all (no jobs, no pipeline). One surprise: on a branch pipeline, changes is always true for the first push of a new branch (runs on a new branch).

unit-tests carries the same rules, repeated word for word. Repeated rules drift apart, and Chapter 13 shows the usual way to write them once. Chapter 22 covers rules in full.

Break it on purpose

Delete the workflow's second rule and push a code change to the branch again. Two pipelines appear for the one push, one of each kind, and each job runs twice.

Next07Images, the registry and variables4 min

Images, the registry and variables#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 07· 4 min read

Production runs greeting-service as a container image, so the pipeline builds one and pushes it to the project's container registry, tagged with the commit it was built from. The values that jobs need come from variables: ordinary ones in the YAML, and secrets in the project's settings. A secret is masked, so logs never show it, and protected, so only protected branches such as main receive it.

The project's container registry#

Every GitLab project can hold container images in its container registry, under Deploy › Container Registry. On a self-managed GitLab, an administrator must turn the registry on first. A job reaches the registry through variables that GitLab sets for it:

VariableHolds
CI_REGISTRYthe registry's address
CI_REGISTRY_IMAGEthe registry's address followed by the project's path: this project's image name
CI_REGISTRY_USER, CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORDa user name and password that can push to this project's registry
CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHAthe first eight characters of the commit's SHA

Building an image in a job#

A new job builds the image from the service's Dockerfile and pushes it. It is the same for both stacks:

practice · node-servicesteps/3-image.ymlbuild-image
build-image:
  stage: package
  image: docker:29.8.0-cli
  services:
    - docker:29.8.0-dind
  variables:
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login "$CI_REGISTRY" --username "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin
    - docker build --provenance=false --tag "$IMAGE" .
    - docker push "$IMAGE"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  • The job runs in docker:29.8.0-cli, which has the Docker command but no Docker engine. The engine runs beside it as a service, a second container: docker:29.8.0-dind, short for Docker-in-Docker.
  • DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR makes the job and the engine talk over TLS.
  • The job logs in with the registry's variables, builds the image, and pushes it as $IMAGE. --provenance=false leaves out the build's provenance record, so the push is a single image rather than an index with an extra attestation manifest. On the local GitLab this book was checked on, the push failed without it.
  • The rule builds images only on main.

Docker-in-Docker needs a runner that allows privileged containers. GitLab.com's own Linux runners do. On your organisation's GitLab, ask your platform team: many allow it only on some runners, or offer another way to build images (chapter 29).

The Dockerfile starts from a pinned runtime image, and copies in what the build job kept as an artifact:

practice · node-serviceDockerfile
# The greeting service's image: its built files and its production dependencies.
FROM node:24.21.0-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY dist/ dist/
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
practice · java-serviceDockerfile
# The greeting service's image: the jar the build job made, on a Java runtime.
FROM eclipse-temurin:25.0.4_7-jre-alpine
COPY target/greeting-service.jar /app/greeting-service.jar
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app/greeting-service.jar"]

Variables in the YAML#

practice · node-servicesteps/3-image.ymlimage-variable
variables:
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

A top-level variables: block gives every job a value. Here IMAGE is built from two variables that GitLab sets: the project's image name, and the commit's short SHA. Tagging with the commit means that each image says exactly which code it holds, and a later deploy can name that one image. The Java pipeline has the same line beside its Maven settings. Values that aren't secret belong here, in the file, where reviewers see them (chapter 25).

Secrets in settings: masked and protected#

Secrets never go in the file. You add them under Settings › CI/CD › Variables, where two settings guard them:

  • Masked replaces the value with [MASKED] wherever a job prints it. GitLab can only mask a value it can find reliably, so the value must be a single line, with no spaces, at least 8 characters long. Masked is the default for a new variable.
  • Protect variable gives the value only to pipelines on protected branches and tags.

This chapter's pipeline has a job that exists only to show both, and that you would never keep:

practice · node-servicesteps/3-image.ymlsecret-check
secret-check:
  stage: test
  script:
    - echo "DEPLOY_TOKEN is '$DEPLOY_TOKEN'"

On main, which is protected, its log shows [MASKED]. On a feature branch the value is empty. That second fact is behind a common failure: a job that works on main and fails on every branch (fails only on branches). Chapter 26 covers secrets in full.

Next08Environments and deploys3 min

Environments and deploys#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 08· 3 min read

A deploy job names an environment, such as staging or production, and GitLab records each deployment: which commit went where, and when. greeting-service deploys to staging on every push to main, and to production only when a person starts the job. Until someone does, the pipeline shows as blocked.

A deploy job names its environment#

practice · node-servicesteps/4-deploy.ymldeploy
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.22
  script:
    - echo "Deploying $IMAGE to staging, with the token $DEPLOY_TOKEN"
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://staging.greeting.example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.22
  script:
    - echo "Deploying $IMAGE to production, with the token $DEPLOY_TOKEN"
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://greeting.example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual

environment: name makes a job a deployment job. GitLab lists every environment under Operate › Environments, each with its deployments, and url puts a link to the running service beside it.

These deploy scripts only print what they would do, with the token masked. A real deploy job runs whatever your organisation deploys with: a cloud's command-line tool, or a commit to a configuration repository that a tool in the cluster applies. Chapter 39 covers the rest.

Production waits for a person#

The production job's rule adds when: manual. The job appears in the pipeline with a play button, and runs only when someone selects it. A manual job added by a rule is not allowed to fail, so the pipeline waits for it and shows as blocked (a play button that waits).

Two more guards exist on paid tiers. A protected environment Premium lets only chosen people deploy to it, and deployment approvals Premium make a deploy wait for someone to approve it. Neither is needed for this lab.

Next09OpenTofu in your pipeline5 min

OpenTofu in your pipeline#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 09· 5 min read

Infrastructure that your team owns, such as a queue or a storage bucket, is often written as code with OpenTofu and changed through the pipeline. A merge request shows the plan, which is what would change, and merging to main applies it. GitLab can keep OpenTofu's state for you, so there is nothing else to set up.

OpenTofu in two minutes#

OpenTofu is an open-source tool that creates and changes infrastructure from files of code. It began as a copy of Terraform: its command is tofu where Terraform's is terraform, and it reads the same kind of files, written in a language called HCL. The words you need:

WordMeans
configurationthe .tf files: what should exist
providera plugin that talks to one kind of system, such as a cloud
planthe changes OpenTofu would make: what it would add, change and destroy
applymaking those changes
stateOpenTofu's record of what it has made, which the next plan compares with

This lab's configuration makes a random name for the team's queue. Its provider, random, needs no cloud account, so every plan and apply is real:

practice · team-inframain.tfsettings
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.12"
  backend "http" {}
  required_providers {
    random = {
      source  = "hashicorp/random"
      version = "3.9.1"
    }
  }
}
practice · team-inframain.tfresources
variable "team" {
  type    = string
  default = "payments"
}

resource "random_pet" "queue" {
  prefix = var.team
  length = 2
}

output "queue_name" {
  value = random_pet.queue.id
}

State that GitLab keeps#

The empty backend "http" {} block says the state lives on a web server, here GitLab. Variables tell OpenTofu where, and how to sign in:

practice · team-infra.gitlab-ci.ymlvariables
variables:
  TF_STATE_NAME: default
  TF_HTTP_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME
  TF_HTTP_LOCK_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME/lock
  TF_HTTP_UNLOCK_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME/lock
  TF_HTTP_LOCK_METHOD: POST
  TF_HTTP_UNLOCK_METHOD: DELETE
  TF_HTTP_USERNAME: gitlab-ci-token
  TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN

The state's address is under the project's API, and the job signs in with its own job token. GitLab lists the states under Operate › Terraform states. A Developer can plan against the state, but applying a change needs the Maintainer role, so merge requests can plan, and only the pipeline on main applies.

Plan in the merge request, apply on merge#

practice · team-infra.gitlab-ci.ymldefault
default:
  image:
    name: ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.12.6
    entrypoint: [""]
  before_script:
    - tofu init -input=false
practice · team-infra.gitlab-ci.ymlvalidate
validate:
  stage: validate
  script:
    - tofu fmt -check
    - tofu validate
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
practice · team-infra.gitlab-ci.ymlplan
plan:
  stage: plan
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache jq
    - tofu plan -input=false -out=plan.cache
    - tofu show -json plan.cache | jq -r '([.resource_changes[]?.change.actions?]|flatten)|{"create":(map(select(.=="create"))|length),"update":(map(select(.=="update"))|length),"delete":(map(select(.=="delete"))|length)}' > plan.json
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - plan.cache
    reports:
      terraform: plan.json
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
practice · team-infra.gitlab-ci.ymlapply
apply:
  stage: apply
  script:
    - tofu apply -input=false plan.cache
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  • default runs tofu init before every job, with the pinned ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.12.6 image. Its entrypoint is emptied, because the image would otherwise run tofu instead of your script (the script never runs).
  • validate checks the formatting and the configuration.
  • validate and plan carry rules for merge request pipelines and for main. A job without rules runs only in branch pipelines, and the workflow drops those while a merge request is open, so without the rules the merge request would get no pipeline at all.
  • plan saves the plan in plan.cache, then turns it into a summary with jq, GitLab's documented command. The summary is a report, so the merge request shows how many things the plan adds, changes and destroys.
  • apply runs only on main, and applies the plan saved by that pipeline's plan job.

Central teams often wrap these jobs in GitLab's OpenTofu component, gitlab.com/components/opentofu/validate-plan-apply, included at a version such as 4.8.1. You will recognise its jobs from these. On a self-managed GitLab, an administrator mirrors the component's project first.

LegacyGitLab's Terraform templates
Older pipelines include GitLab's Terraform CI/CD templates, and run their jobs in GitLab's terraform images. GitLab no longer distributes either. Use OpenTofu jobs like these, or the OpenTofu component.
LabOpenTofu: plan in a merge request, apply on mergeabout 15 min#
You need

An account on your GitLab.

Steps
  1. Create a blank project named team-infra. Add main.tf and .gitlab-ci.yml, both shown in full here:

# account, so every plan and apply is real.

  required_version = ">= 1.12"
  backend "http" {}
  required_providers {
    random = {
      source  = "hashicorp/random"
      version = "3.9.1"
    }
  }
}

variable "team" {
  type    = string
  default = "payments"
}

resource "random_pet" "queue" {

  length = 2
}

output "queue_name" {

# state, a merge request shows the plan, and merging to main applies it.
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

stages:
  - validate
  - plan
  - apply

variables:
  TF_STATE_NAME: default
  TF_HTTP_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME
  TF_HTTP_LOCK_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME/lock
  TF_HTTP_UNLOCK_ADDRESS: $CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/terraform/state/$TF_STATE_NAME/lock
  TF_HTTP_LOCK_METHOD: POST
  TF_HTTP_UNLOCK_METHOD: DELETE
  TF_HTTP_USERNAME: gitlab-ci-token
  TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN

default:
  image:
    name: ghcr.io/opentofu/opentofu:1.12.6
    entrypoint: [""]
  before_script:
    - tofu init -input=false

validate:
  stage: validate
  script:
    - tofu fmt -check
    - tofu validate
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

plan:
  stage: plan
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache jq
    - tofu plan -input=false -out=plan.cache
    - tofu show -json plan.cache | jq -r '([.resource_changes[]?.change.actions?]|flatten)|{"create":(map(select(.=="create"))|length),"update":(map(select(.=="update"))|length),"delete":(map(select(.=="delete"))|length)}' > plan.json
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - plan.cache
    reports:
      terraform: plan.json
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

apply:

    - tofu apply -input=false plan.cache
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  2. Push to main. When the pipeline finishes, open apply's log, then Operate › Terraform states.
  3. Create a branch. On it, change length = 2 to length = 3, and push. Then open a merge request from the branch into main.
  4. Look at the merge request once its pipeline finishes.
  5. Merge it, and open the apply log of the pipeline on main.
What you should see

The first pipeline on main creates the queue's name, and GitLab saves the state:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab

random_pet.queue: Creating...
random_pet.queue: Creation complete after 0s [id=payments-helped-sunfish]

Outputs:
queue_name = "payments-helped-sunfish"

Job succeeded

Operate › Terraform states lists one state, default. In the merge request, plan shows what the change would do. The length can't be changed in place, so OpenTofu would replace the resource:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ tofu plan -input=false -out=plan.cache
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
random_pet.queue: Refreshing state... [id=payments-helped-sunfish]
OpenTofu used the selected providers to generate the following execution
plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following symbols:
-/+ destroy and then create replacement
OpenTofu will perform the following actions:

The last lines upload plan.json as the terraform report, which is how the merge request shows the same counts. Merging runs the pipeline on main, and its apply destroys the old name and creates the new one:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ tofu apply -input=false plan.cache
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
random_pet.queue: Destroying... [id=payments-helped-sunfish]
random_pet.queue: Destruction complete after 0s
random_pet.queue: Creating...
random_pet.queue: Creation complete after 0s [id=payments-likely-careful-dane]

The state's serial, which goes up with each change, went from 1 to 2. Your names will differ, because random_pet picks them at random.

Next10The central team's templates5 min

The central team's templates#

Part II · Build your team's pipeline · Chapter 10· 5 min read

Your file doesn't have to hold every job. A central team can publish templates, which are files of hidden jobs that you extend, and components, which are packaged jobs with inputs. Your file includes them at a version you choose. You then change only what your team needs, and the pipeline editor's Full configuration shows the result.

Play the central team#

In this lab you are both teams. A second project, central-templates, holds the central team's files:

  • templates/node.yml and templates/java.yml, each with one hidden job: a job whose name starts with a dot, which never runs itself and exists to be copied.
  • templates/secret-scan/template.yml, a component: a job with typed inputs at the top, before a --- line. Its job has rules of its own, so it runs in merge request pipelines as well as branch pipelines.
practice · central-templatestemplates/node.ymlnode-test
.node-test:
  stage: test
  image: node:24.21.0-alpine

The central team tags the project 1.0.0. That tag is the version your file asks for.

Include at a version#

practice · node-servicesteps/5-central-templates.ymlinclude
include:
  - project: practice/central-templates
    ref: 1.0.0

    inputs:
      stage: test
  • project and file name a file in another project, and ref: 1.0.0 fixes which version of it.
  • component names the component by the instance, the project and its own name, then @1.0.0. $CI_SERVER_FQDN is your GitLab's address, so the line works on any instance. inputs fill in the component's inputs.

These files use the group practice. Change it to the group or user that owns your two projects. Chapter 14 and chapter 15 cover both kinds of include.

Extend, and change only what you must#

practice · node-servicesteps/5-central-templates.ymlunit-tests
unit-tests:
  extends: .node-test
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm test -- --test-reporter=spec --test-reporter-destination=stdout --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=junit.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always

        - src/**/*

        - src/**/*
        - pom.xml

extends copies the hidden job's settings into unit-tests, and then the job's own settings are laid on top. Lists are replaced whole, and maps are merged key by key. So the Node job's script replaces the template's, and keeps its image and cache. The Java job adds artifacts and keeps everything else.

To see what GitLab made of it, open Build › Pipeline editor, then Full configuration. Chapter 13 covers extends in full, including why changing a template job's rules is the classic trap (your rules replaced the template's).

GitLab writes the merged file its own way: list items sit level with their key, and a long line wraps onto the next. extends is still listed, but its settings are already copied in.

secret-scan came from the component, with its inputs filled in, and found no key:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ echo "Looking for private keys in ."
Looking for private keys in .
$ if grep -rl "BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY" .; then echo "A private key is committed"; exit 1; fi
⋯ lines omitted
Job succeeded

Read a new check's log once, to see that it really looked. In an Alpine image, grep is BusyBox's, which lacks some of GNU grep's options, such as --exclude-dir. Given one, it prints its usage and fails, and inside if that failure reads as "no key found": the job passes without looking.

Break it on purpose

Add a file to greeting-service containing the line -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----, and push. secret-scan fails and names the file. Delete the file again.

Next · Part III11Reuse at a glance6 min

Reuse at a glance#

Part III · Reuse · Chapter 11· 6 min read

Reuse means writing something once and using it in many places. In a large organisation, most of what your job does was written somewhere else. This book counts 37 ways that happens, in seven families. They run from YAML shortcuts inside one file to scripts built into an image.

Four questions sort them:

  • How far does it reach?
  • Is it pinned to a version?
  • Did your project choose it?
  • Can the merged view show it?

This chapter is the index to Part III. The first table lists every mechanism, and the second turns what you see into the mechanism responsible. The chapters that follow give each mechanism its own card.

You don't need to remember 37 of anything. You need to recognise which family a thing belongs to when you meet it, and know where that family is explained. This is how to use the chapter when a job surprises you:

Seven families#

The families are ordered by distance. The first lives inside your own file, and the last lives outside YAML altogether. The further away a mechanism is, the harder it is to see from your project:

FamilyMechanismsWhat they have in commonChapter
Inside one YAML file3plain YAML shortcuts that GitLab never sees as such12
Sharing between jobs5one job borrowing from another once the files are joined13
Pulling in files5the kinds of include, each fetching configuration from somewhere14
Parameters4values that change what shared configuration does15
Whole pipelines4one pipeline starting another16
Organisation-wide9settings and policies that reach projects without the project asking17
Outside the YAML7logic in images, scripts, build tools and runners18

Four questions for every mechanism#

For each mechanism, four answers tell you where to look, and whom to ask:

QuestionThe answersWhy it matters when something breaks
Scope: how far does it reach?one file · one project · cross-project · organisation-widetells you which repository or settings page to open
Binding: is it pinned?inline · copied once · pinned or floating · always livetells you whether a change somewhere else can break you without a commit of yours
Control: did you choose it?opt-in · inherited · enforcedtells you whether you can change it yourself, or have to ask someone
Visibility: does the merged view show it?shown · keyword only · not showntells you whether Full configuration answers the question, or you need another tool
