QuestionWhy does the scan run in one pipeline and not the other, and how could it run in the merge request pipeline instead?
Show the answer

GitLab's secret detection template runs its job in branch pipelines, and in merge request pipelines only when AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES is "true". Nobody set it, so the scan ran in the branch pipeline only.

Set AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES: "true", in the YAML or in settings. The job then runs in merge request pipelines, and is skipped in the branch pipeline while a merge request is open. Alternatively, redefine secret_detection with rules of your own, as MegaCorp did for container scanning. See the merge request gap.

Next34Third-party scanners2 min

Third-party scanners#

Part VII · Scanners and gates · Chapter 34· 2 min read

Many organisations also run tools that GitLab doesn't ship, such as SonarQube, Snyk or Trivy. They all follow one pattern: a job runs the tool, the tool's exit code decides whether the job fails, and a report file may carry the findings into GitLab. Find those three things, and the job's allow_failure and needs, and you know what the tool can really stop.

Tool, exit code, report, gate#

A report file lets GitLab show the tool's findings, instead of leaving them in the job log or on the tool's own website:

ReportForWhere GitLab shows it
codequalitylint and code-quality findings, in a simple JSON formatmerge requests, and the pipeline's Code Quality tab (Premium)
sarifsecurity findings from any tool that writes SARIF 2.1.0the Security tab and the vulnerability report (Ultimate, since 19.2)
junittest resultsthe pipeline's Tests tab, and the merge request's test summary

For code quality, GitLab's preferred route is exactly this: run your own linter and import its report. GitLab's built-in CodeClimate template is deprecated.

MegaCorp's SonarQube job#

MegaCorp's platform team ships SonarQube as a component (chapter 15):

megacorp/devops/componentstemplates/sonar-scan.ymljob
sonar-scan:
  stage: $[[ inputs.stage ]]
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/sonar-scanner:6
  variables:
    SONAR_PROJECT_KEY: $[[ inputs.project_key ]]
    SONAR_QUALITYGATE_WAIT: "$[[ inputs.quality_gate ]]"
  script:
    - sonar-scanner -Dsonar.projectKey="$SONAR_PROJECT_KEY" -Dsonar.host.url="$SONAR_HOST_URL"
  rules:
    - if: $SKIP_SONAR == "true"
      when: never
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  allow_failure: true

Read it with the pattern:

  • Tool: sonar-scanner, which sends the code to the Sonar server for analysis.
  • Exit code: the component's quality_gate input sets SONAR_QUALITYGATE_WAIT. It is meant to make the scanner wait for Sonar's quality gate, and fail the job when the gate fails.
  • Report: none. The findings stay on the Sonar server.
  • Gate: allow_failure: true, so even a failed gate is only a warning.

It also needs SONAR_TOKEN, which is protected, so in merge request pipelines from feature branches the scan can't sign in (chapter 26).

When you write it

A scanner job can only block a merge if it fails. Make the tool exit with an error on the findings you care about, and don't set allow_failure: true unless its result is advice. Keep its report as an artifact, so people can see why it failed (the gate didn't stop a deploy).

Spot the bugThe quality gate that couldn't stop a deploy#

A change that fails MegaCorp's Sonar quality gate is merged into payments-api's main. The pipeline goes green, and deploy-staging ships the change. sonar-scan shows an orange warning.

megacorp/devops/ci-templatespipelines/java-service.ymldeploys
deploy-staging:
  extends: .deploy
  needs: [image-build]
  variables:
    ENVIRONMENT: staging
  rules:
    - !reference [.rules, never-on-schedule]
    - !reference [.rules, default-branch]

deploy-prod:
  extends: .deploy
  needs: [image-build]
  variables:
    ENVIRONMENT: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/
      when: manual
QuestionName the two separate reasons the failed gate didn't stop the deploy.
Show the answer
  • sonar-scan has allow_failure: true, so its failure never fails the pipeline.
  • deploy-staging has needs: [image-build]. It starts as soon as the image is built, without waiting for jobs in the test stage, so it doesn't wait for sonar-scan at all (chapter 23).

To make the gate stop deploys, both would have to change: the scan must be allowed to fail the pipeline, and the deploy must wait for it. Whether the gate should block is a decision for the teams that own the pipeline. See the pattern.

Next35Policies and gates3 min

Policies and gates#

Part VII · Scanners and gates · Chapter 35· 3 min read

Security policies are rules the security team writes once for many projects. They need Ultimate, and come in three kinds:

  • scan execution policies add scanner jobs
  • pipeline execution policies add any jobs, or replace the pipeline
  • merge request approval policies demand approval when scans find problems

Policies win over anything a project writes. A toggle such as SAST_DISABLED skips a project's own scanner jobs, never a policy's. Turning a mandated scan off is a decision for the security team, not a change to the YAML.

Three kinds of policy#

PolicyWhat it doesHow you recognise it
Scan executionadds scanner jobs to pipelines, or runs scans on a schedulejobs such as secret-detection-1, in test, or in scan-policies when there is no test stage
Pipeline executionadds any jobs, or replaces the project's pipelinejobs in .pipeline-policy-pre, which runs first, and .pipeline-policy-post, which runs last
Merge request approvalrequires approval when scans find problemsan approval rule on the merge request, named after the policy

Pipeline execution policies have a scheduled variant Since 19.2. It creates pipelines of its own on a schedule, in every project it covers, and runs only the policy's jobs, never the project's.

All three live in one file, .gitlab/security-policies/policy.yml, in a separate security policy project linked to the group. A project can hold at most five policies of each kind. Chapter 17 shows MegaCorp's first two. This is the third:

megacorp/security/policies.gitlab/security-policies/policy.ymlapproval
approval_policy:
  - name: Block new critical vulnerabilities
    description: A merge into main that adds a critical finding needs security's approval.
    enabled: true
    rules:
      - type: scan_finding
        branches: [main]
        scanners: [sast, secret_detection, dependency_scanning, container_scanning]
        vulnerabilities_allowed: 0
        severity_levels: [critical]
        vulnerability_states: [new_needs_triage]
    actions:
      - type: require_approval
        approvals_required: 1
        group_approvers: [megacorp/security]

Toggles against policies#

GitLab's scanner templates switch off with variables: SAST_DISABLED, SECRET_DETECTION_DISABLED, CONTAINER_SCANNING_DISABLED and others. GitLab's documentation is exact about their limit: "Skipping jobs does not prevent any security jobs defined by scan execution policies from running." Two more rules follow:

  • A project can't override a policy's scanner jobs, even by using the same job name.
  • In a project under a scan execution policy, the scanners' exclude settings, such as SAST_EXCLUDED_PATHS, are preset, and only a policy can change them.

So when a team wants a mandated scan off, the answer isn't in their YAML. The security team decides, for example by narrowing the policy's scope.

When a merge request needs the security team#

MegaCorp's approval policy looks at merges into main. If a scan finds a new critical vulnerability, one member of megacorp/security must approve. The rule also applies when GitLab can't check it:

The second case surprises people. By default a policy fails closed: "Invalid or unenforceable rules of a policy require approval." So a scanner that was skipped or crashed doesn't let a merge request slip through. It blocks it until someone approves. The policy can say fallback_behavior: fail: open instead.

Finding the policies#

Anyone who can see a project can open its policies at Secure › Policies. The list shows each policy and whether it is enforced. Changes go through a merge request in the policy project:

Spot the bugThe toggle that only half worked#

payments-api's pipelines run two secret detection jobs, and the team wants to save time. They add this to their .gitlab-ci.yml:

variables:
  SECRET_DETECTION_DISABLED: "true"

secret_detection disappears from their pipelines, but secret-detection-1 still runs.

QuestionWhy did only one job go, and what should the team do if they want the other one gone too?
Show the answer

secret_detection comes from GitLab's template, included by MegaCorp's security.yml, and the template honours the toggle. secret-detection-1 comes from the scan execution policy "Secret detection everywhere". Toggles skip only a project's own jobs, never a policy's.

Removing the second job isn't the team's decision. They can ask the security team to change the policy's scope. Having the job twice is expected: GitLab runs both, because the two can use different settings. See toggles against policies.

Next · Part VIII36Building Java, Node and front ends4 min

Building Java, Node and front ends#

Part VIII · Delivery · Chapter 36· 4 min read

A build job is an ordinary job with the right image. What makes builds confusing in a big organisation is everything around the compiler:

  • where the dependencies come from: a company mirror, and a cache
  • what the build produces, and where it goes: an artifact, a package registry, an image or a bucket
  • which version number the result carries

Most "works on my machine" failures come from the first. Most "which version is running?" confusion comes from the last.

A Maven build at MegaCorp#

MegaCorp's Maven jobs start from one hidden job. It picks the JDK image, caches the local repository, and writes a Maven settings file before the script runs:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/java-maven.ymlmaven-base
.maven-base:
  extends: .megacorp-base
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/maven:3.9-jdk${JAVA_VERSION}
  variables:
    JAVA_VERSION: "21"
    MAVEN_OPTS: "-Dmaven.repo.local=$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.m2/repository"
  cache:
    key:
      files: [pom.xml]
    paths: [.m2/repository]
  before_script:
    # a job's own before_script replaces default:before_script, so re-add the functions
    - !reference [.snippets, functions]
    - !reference [.snippets, maven_settings]

The settings file comes from a function in the ci-tools image. It sends every download through MegaCorp's Nexus server, a company copy of the public repositories:

megacorp/devops/ci-toolslib/ci-lib.shmaven-settings
mc_maven_settings() {
  cat <<EOF
<settings><mirrors><mirror><id>nexus</id><mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf><url>${MC_NEXUS_URL:-https://nexus.example.com/repository/maven-public/}</url></mirror></mirrors></settings>
EOF
}

Three variables decide how Maven runs, and only one is in the YAML:

VariableSet inEffect
MAVEN_CLI_OPTSthe megacorp group's CI/CD settingsbatch mode, and the settings file above; it overrides any value a project writes in YAML (chapter 25)
MAVEN_OPTSthe templatekeeps Maven's local repository inside the project, so that it can be cached
MC_NEXUS_URLpayments-api's CI/CD settingswhich Nexus the mirror points at

maven-build packages the jar without running the tests, and keeps it as an artifact. maven-test runs the tests twice, on JDK 17 and 21, with parallel: matrix (chapter 13).

A Node front end at MegaCorp#

The Node templates install with npm ci, from a cache keyed on package-lock.json, and build into dist/ (chapter 30). web-portal's whole pipeline is three jobs:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatespipelines/web.ymljobs
node-build:
  extends: .node-build

node-test:
  extends: .node-test

deploy-site:
  extends: .publish-site
  needs: [node-build]
  rules:
    - !reference [.rules, never-on-schedule]
    - !reference [.rules, default-branch]

deploy-site copies dist/ to an S3 bucket and clears the CloudFront cache (chapter 37). web-portal has no .gitlab-ci.yml of its own: its settings point at this file (chapter 17).

Which version is it?#

Three numbers can describe one build, and they often disagree:

NumberComes frompayments-api's example
The version in the build filepom.xml or package.json, as committed1.8.0-SNAPSHOT
The Git tagthe release tag, in CI_COMMIT_TAG, which is set only in tag pipelinesv1.5.0
The image tagthe commit, in CI_COMMIT_SHAa 40-character commit hash

MegaCorp's mc tool can work out a version in any pipeline: the tag if there is one, otherwise 0.0.0- followed by the short commit hash.

megacorp/devops/ci-toolsbin/mcversion
version)
  echo "${CI_COMMIT_TAG:-0.0.0-${CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA}}"
  ;;

Nothing in the Maven templates uses it, though. The exercise shows the result.

Test results and coverage#

  • Test reports in JUnit XML, saved as artifacts: reports: junit, fill the pipeline's Tests tab and the merge request's test summary. The summary lists newly failed tests. A report never changes the job's status: the test command's exit code does.
  • A coverage percentage comes from the job log. The coverage keyword holds a regular expression, and GitLab shows the first number it matches in the merge request.
  • Line-by-line coverage comes from a Cobertura or JaCoCo file saved as artifacts: reports: coverage_report. GitLab marks the lines in the merge request's diff.

Publishing packages to GitLab's registries#

Some teams publish libraries to GitLab's own package registry, using the job token as the password.

Maven. A settings file sends the job token as a header:

<settings>
  <servers>
    <server>
      <id>gitlab-maven</id>
      <configuration>
        <httpHeaders>
          <property>
            <name>Job-Token</name>
            <value>${CI_JOB_TOKEN}</value>
          </property>
        </httpHeaders>
      </configuration>
    </server>
  </servers>
</settings>

The POM's distribution repository is ${CI_API_V4_URL}/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/maven, and a job runs mvn deploy. To refuse a version that is already published, a group Owner turns off Allow duplicates under Settings › Packages and registries.

npm. The job writes an .npmrc that points the package's scope at the project's registry, with the job token:

echo "@megacorp:registry=https://${CI_SERVER_HOST}/api/v4/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/npm/" > .npmrc
echo "//${CI_SERVER_HOST}/api/v4/projects/${CI_PROJECT_ID}/packages/npm/:_authToken=${CI_JOB_TOKEN}" >> .npmrc
npm publish

The scope is the top-level group of the project that hosts the package, in lower case: @megacorp. A package name can belong to only one project per top-level group. Publishing it from a second project fails, even with a new version.

When you write it

Build once, in one job, and pass the result on as an artifact; test and package that. Use npm ci rather than npm install, and Maven's --batch-mode, so that builds repeat exactly and logs stay readable. Publish test results with artifacts: reports: junit, so they show in the merge request.

Spot the bugThe release that called itself a snapshot#

After payments-api's v1.5.0 release, the support team checks the running service. Its version page, which reads the jar's version, says 1.8.0-SNAPSHOT. The image is the one that the v1.5.0 tag pipeline built.

megacorp/payments/payments-apipom.xmlversion
<artifactId>payments-api</artifactId>
<version>1.8.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/java-maven.ymlmaven-build
.maven-build:
  extends: .maven-base
  stage: build
  script:
    - mvn $MAVEN_CLI_OPTS -DskipTests package
  artifacts:
    paths: [target/*.jar]
QuestionWhere does 1.8.0-SNAPSHOT come from, and what would make the jar carry the release's version?
Show the answer

Maven takes the version from pom.xml, which says 1.8.0-SNAPSHOT. The build job runs mvn package without changing it, so every pipeline, the tag pipeline included, builds a jar with that version. The tag names the commit, but never reaches Maven.

Pass the version into the build in tag pipelines, for example from mc version, which returns CI_COMMIT_TAG there. Or make each release a commit that sets the POM's version, and tag that commit. See which version is it.

Next37GitLab, AWS and Azure15 min

GitLab, AWS and Azure#

Part VIII · Delivery · Chapter 37· 15 min read

Jobs that build and deploy to AWS or Azure need permissions there. The modern way, and MegaCorp's way, stores no password anywhere. Each job trades its ID token for short-lived access, as chapter 27 showed: temporary keys for an AWS role, or a sign-in as an application in Microsoft Entra ID, Azure's identity service.

This chapter covers:

  • what must match on each side, and who owns each part
  • which credentials each cloud's command-line tool really uses
  • working with several AWS accounts or Azure subscriptions
  • ECR and ACR, secrets from each cloud, and the usual deploy targets
  • what to check, in order, when AWS or Azure says no

Cloud words in two minutes#

If a cloud is new to you, these are the only words this chapter needs:

WordMeaning
Accounta separate AWS space with its own resources and bill, named by a 12-digit number such as 123456789012
Regiona location where resources live, such as eu-west-2 (London); jobs set it with AWS_REGION
IAMAWS's identity service: who may do what
Rolean identity with permissions and no password; a person or a system assumes it for a while
Trust policythe rules on a role that say who may assume it
Permission policythe rules on a role that say what it may do once assumed
ARNthe full name of anything in AWS, such as arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-ecr-push
STSthe Security Token Service, which hands out temporary keys for a role
ECRthe Elastic Container Registry, where images are stored
S3 and CloudFrontfile storage, and the network that serves those files quickly worldwide
ECS, EKS and Lambdathree places to run code: AWS's container service, Kubernetes clusters, and single functions
Secrets Manager and Parameter Storetwo AWS services that store secrets and settings
WordMeaning
Tenantan organisation's directory in Microsoft Entra ID, named by a GUID such as 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
Subscriptiona separate Azure space with its own resources and bill, also named by a GUID
Resource groupa named folder for resources inside a subscription, such as rg-delivery-prod
Microsoft Entra IDAzure's identity service: who may sign in, and as what; it used to be called Azure Active Directory
App registrationan identity for software, named by its client ID; its service principal is what receives permissions
Managed identityan identity that Azure creates and looks after for a resource, with no secret to store
Federated credentiala rule on an app registration or managed identity that says which outside tokens it accepts instead of a secret
Role assignmenta role, such as AcrPush, given to an identity at a scope: a subscription, a resource group or one resource
ACRAzure Container Registry, where images are stored
AKS and Container Appstwo places to run containers: Kubernetes clusters, and a service that runs containers without a cluster to manage
Key VaultAzure's store for secrets, keys and certificates

What must match#

A job gets into a cloud only when several pairs line up. Each pair has one half in GitLab and the other half in the cloud, and a different team often owns each half.

On AWS, five pairs must match:

At MegaCorp the GitLab halves live in the templates, which the platform team owns:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/container.ymlimage-build
.image-build:
  extends: .megacorp-base
  stage: package
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/buildah:1.37
  id_tokens:
    MC_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-ecr-push
    ECR_REGISTRY: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com
    IMAGE: $ECR_REGISTRY/$CI_PROJECT_NAME
  before_script:
    - !reference [.snippets, functions]
    - !reference [.snippets, aws_login]
  script:
    - mc_retry aws ecr get-login-password | buildah login --username AWS --password-stdin "$ECR_REGISTRY"
    - buildah bud -t "$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" .
    - buildah push "$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
    - !reference [.snippets, acr_push]
    - echo "IMAGE_REF=$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" >> build.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: build.env

The AWS halves are set in the AWS account itself. This file describes MegaCorp's:

awsiam.ymloidc-provider
# AWS accepts ID tokens signed by this GitLab, for this audience.
oidc_provider:
  arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/gitlab.example.com
  url: https://gitlab.example.com
  audiences: [https://gitlab.example.com]
awsiam.ymlecr-push-role
# Assumed by image-build, and by the ecr-push component, through mc_aws_login.
ecr_push_role:
  arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-ecr-push
  trust_policy:
    Effect: Allow
    Principal:
      Federated: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/gitlab.example.com
    Action: sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
    Condition:
      StringEquals:
        gitlab.example.com:aud: https://gitlab.example.com
      StringLike:
        gitlab.example.com:sub: project_path:megacorp/*:ref_type:branch:ref:*
  permissions: push and pull images in every ECR repository in the account

A mismatch in the first four pairs stops the login: STS refuses, and no keys come back. A mismatch in the fifth lets the login succeed, and a later command fails with an access-denied error. That difference tells you where to look.

On Azure, the pairs are much the same:

In GitLabIn Entra ID and AzureMatched how
the instance's URL, which becomes the token's issthe federated credential's issuer, https://gitlab.example.comexactly
aud in the job's id_tokens:the credential's single audienceexactly
the project, the kind of ref and the ref, which make the token's subthe credential's subjectexactly, with no wildcards
the client ID and tenant ID that az login namesthe app registrationexactly
what the job does once signed inrole assignments, such as AcrPush on the registryby scope

This file describes MegaCorp's application for image pushes, and what it may do:

azureentra.ymlapp-registration
# The identity that image jobs sign in as. Each federated credential names one kind of
# pipeline that may use it.
acr_push_app:
  display_name: gitlab-acr-push
  client_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  tenant_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  federated_credentials:
    - name: payments-api-main
      issuer: https://gitlab.example.com
      subject: project_path:megacorp/payments/payments-api:ref_type:branch:ref:main
      audiences: [https://gitlab.example.com]
azureentra.ymlrole-assignments
# What the app may do once signed in, on one registry only. AcrPush pushes and pulls
# images. az acr login also has to look the registry up in Azure Resource Manager, which
# AcrPush doesn't allow; Microsoft documents the second role for that, and it can also
# change or delete the registry, which is one more reason to trust main only.
role_assignments:
  - principal: gitlab-acr-push
    role: AcrPush
    scope: /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-delivery-prod/providers/Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/megacorpprod
  - principal: gitlab-acr-push
    role: Container Registry Contributor and Data Access Configuration Administrator
    scope: /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-delivery-prod/providers/Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/megacorpprod

The big difference from AWS is the subject. Entra ID matches it exactly, with no wildcards. So each project and branch that may sign in needs its own federated credential, and one application holds at most 20 of them. MegaCorp pushes images to Azure only from each service's main, which needs one credential per service. A wrong subject is saved without complaint: the error shows only when a job tries to sign in.

How a MegaCorp job logs in#

The template runs snippets that call functions from the ci-tools image:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/snippets.ymlsnippets
.snippets:
  functions:
    - source /opt/megacorp/lib/ci-lib.sh
  aws_login:
    - mc_aws_login "$AWS_ROLE_ARN"
  acr_push:
    - mc_acr_push "$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
  maven_settings:
    - mkdir -p .m2
    - mc_maven_settings > .m2/settings.xml
megacorp/devops/ci-toolslib/ci-lib.shaws-login
# Exchange the job's OIDC ID token for temporary AWS credentials.
mc_aws_login() {
  local role="${1:?role ARN required}"
  local creds
  creds=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \
    --role-arn "$role" \
    --role-session-name "gitlab-${CI_PROJECT_ID}-${CI_JOB_ID}" \
    --web-identity-token "$MC_ID_TOKEN" \
    --duration-seconds 3600 \
    --query 'Credentials.[AccessKeyId,SecretAccessKey,SessionToken]' \
    --output text) || { mc_log "AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity failed for $role"; return 1; }
  read -r AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN <<< "$creds"
  export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
  mc_log "assumed $role"
}

Step by step:

  1. aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity sends the role's ARN and the ID token to STS.
  2. STS checks the token and the trust policy. It returns three values: an access key, a secret key and a session token.
  3. The function exports them as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. Every later aws command in the job uses them.
  4. They expire after 3600 seconds, which is one hour.

To see which identity a job is really using, add this line. It needs no permissions, and it prints the ARN of the role in use:

aws sts get-caller-identity
megacorp/devops/ci-toolslib/ci-lib.shazure-login
# Sign in to Azure with the job's OIDC ID token, as the Entra application that trusts it.
mc_azure_login() {
  local client_id="${1:?application (client) ID required}"
  az login --service-principal -u "$client_id" -t "$MC_AZURE_TENANT_ID" \
    --federated-token "$MC_ID_TOKEN" --output none \
    || { mc_log "az login failed for $client_id"; return 1; }
  mc_log "signed in to Azure as $client_id"
}

# Push an image that is already built to Azure's registry as well. Only main's images go
# there: Entra matches a federated credential's subject exactly, and aks-prod deploys main.
mc_acr_push() {
  local image="${1:?image required}"
  if [ "${CI_COMMIT_BRANCH:-}" != "$CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH" ]; then
    mc_log "not on $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH, so not pushing to $MC_ACR_REGISTRY"
    return 0
  fi
  mc_azure_login "$MC_ACR_PUSH_CLIENT_ID"
  az acr login --name "${MC_ACR_REGISTRY%%.*}" --expose-token --query accessToken --output tsv \
    | buildah login --username 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --password-stdin "$MC_ACR_REGISTRY"
  buildah push "$image" "docker://$MC_ACR_REGISTRY/${image##*/}"
  mc_log "pushed $MC_ACR_REGISTRY/${image##*/}"
}

Step by step:

  1. On any branch but main, mc_acr_push stops at once. Merge request and tag pipelines never sign in to Azure.
  2. az login --service-principal --federated-token sends the ID token to Entra ID, with the application's client ID and the tenant ID. Both IDs come from the megacorp group's CI/CD variables.
  3. Entra ID compares the token's issuer, subject and audience with the application's federated credentials. If one matches, the CLI is signed in as the application.
  4. az acr login --expose-token trades that sign-in for a registry token, valid for 3 hours. Buildah logs in with it, under the all-zero user name that ACR expects, and pushes.

To see who a job is signed in as, add this line. It prints the subscription in use, and the identity that signed in:

az account show

Logging in to AWS without a script#

The AWS CLI can do the exchange by itself. Put the ID token in a file, and set two variables that name the role and the file:

publish:
  id_tokens:
    AWS_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-web-publish
    AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME: gitlab-$CI_JOB_ID
  script:
    - echo "$AWS_ID_TOKEN" > /tmp/web-identity-token
    - export AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE=/tmp/web-identity-token
    - aws sts get-caller-identity

Every aws command then assumes the role on its own. This works only when no access keys are set, because keys come first in the order below.

Which credentials each CLI uses#

A job can have credentials from several places at once:

  • credentials that a login step created
  • keys that someone stored in CI/CD settings long ago
  • an identity that belongs to the runner's machine

The two clouds' command-line tools deal with this differently.

The AWS CLI doesn't combine them. It takes the first it finds, in a fixed order:

Two failures follow from this order:

  • Old keys in settings win silently. A leftover AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in a group's CI/CD variables beats any role, until a login step overwrites it. A job that skips the login then acts as whoever owns those keys.
  • A skipped login falls through to the runner. A job that sets its own before_script replaces the template's, so the login never runs (chapter 13). The job then acts as the runner's role, which at MegaCorp can pull images but not push them.

The Azure CLI doesn't search in an order. It uses the sign-in that az login left in its local cache, under its configuration directory: $HOME/.azure, unless AZURE_CONFIG_DIR names another. Each command runs against the current subscription, which az account set --subscription changes. A machine's managed identity is used only after az login --identity.

Two failures follow:

  • A skipped sign-in usually fails loudly. In a fresh container the cache is empty, so the first az command stops and asks for a sign-in.
  • On a shell runner, the last sign-in lingers. The cache lives in the runner user's home directory, so it survives from one job to the next. A job that skips its own sign-in can act as whoever signed in before it. Give each job its own directory with AZURE_CONFIG_DIR, such as one inside the build folder.

Several accounts and subscriptions#

Large organisations split each cloud into several spaces, often one for shared tools and one for each environment.

A job can reach another AWS account in two ways:

  • Direct trust. Each account has a role whose trust policy accepts the ID token, and the job logs in to the account it needs. Each account checks the token's sub itself, so production can accept only release tags, for example.
  • Role chaining. The job logs in to one role, then uses it to assume a role in the other account. AWS limits a chained session to one hour, whatever the role allows, and asking for longer fails.

In Azure, one sign-in reaches every subscription in the tenant where the identity has a role assignment. az account list shows them, and az account set --subscription picks one. There's no chaining to worry about: what the identity may do in each subscription depends only on its role assignments there.

MegaCorp needs none of this. Its pipelines touch only the tooling account, 123456789012, where ECR and the website's bucket live, and one registry in Azure. Deploys go through the GitOps repository, and a controller inside each cluster pulls the new image (chapter 44). The pipeline never holds a production cluster's credentials at all.

Registries: pushing images, and pulling job images#

An ECR registry's address contains the account and the region: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com. To push, a job logs in to AWS first, then to the registry:

aws ecr get-login-password | buildah login --username AWS --password-stdin "$ECR_REGISTRY"

The user name is always AWS, and the password this prints is valid for 12 hours.

An ACR registry's address is its name followed by .azurecr.io: megacorpprod.azurecr.io. To push, a job signs in to Azure first, then asks for a registry token:

az acr login --name megacorpprod --expose-token --query accessToken --output tsv \
  | buildah login --username 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --password-stdin megacorpprod.azurecr.io

The user name is always the all-zero GUID, and the token is valid for 3 hours. Without --expose-token, az acr login hands the token to a Docker daemon itself, which a Buildah job doesn't have. The registry's admin user is off by default, and Microsoft advises leaving it off.

Tagging and promoting images is the subject of chapter 38.

Pulling a job's own image: from either registry is different. The runner pulls it before the job starts, so nothing in the job's script can help. The runner needs its own way in.

Job images from ECR or ACR#

For ECR, GitLab's documented way is the ECR credential helper. It is a small program that gets a registry password from AWS whenever the runner needs one. It must be installed on the runner, and the runner needs AWS credentials of its own. A DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG variable then tells the runner to use it:

{ "credHelpers": { "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com": "ecr-login" } }

GitLab's documentation notes that credential helpers aren't available on instance runners, or on any runner whose machine you can't configure.

For ACR, a common way is a registry token: a name and password that ACR creates, tied to a scope map that allows pulls from chosen repositories only. Tokens exist in every ACR tier, and work with an ordinary registry login, so they fit in DOCKER_AUTH_CONFIG like any other password.

MegaCorp avoids the question: its job images come from registry.example.com, not from either cloud.

Secrets from AWS and Azure#

A secret in a cloud's vault can reach software in three ways. The best one keeps it out of the pipeline completely:

RouteWho reads the secretWhat the job sees
The secrets: keyword, with aws_secrets_manager or azure_key_vault (Premium)the runner, as the job startsa file holding the value; for AWS, the value itself with file: false
The job's script calls the cloud's CLIthe jobthe value, which GitLab can't mask because it never saw it
The running service reads it: through an ECS task definition, or the External Secrets Operator on a clusterthe service, when it startsnothing at all

With the keyword, the runner does the fetching. It logs in with an ID token named AWS_ID_TOKEN and the role in AWS_ROLE_ARN. The region comes from AWS_REGION, which MegaCorp's base template sets for every job:

db-migrate:
  id_tokens:
    AWS_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/payments-db-migrate
  secrets:
    DB_PASSWORD:
      aws_secrets_manager:
        secret_id: payments/db
        field: password
  script:
    - ./migrate.sh --password-file "$DB_PASSWORD"

Without an ID token, the runner uses its own AWS role instead. On the Kubernetes executor, that role must be on the runner manager, the part that starts the job pods. If it is only on the pods, the job fails with no EC2 IMDS role found.

From a script, the commands look like this. Capture the value in a variable, and never print it:

DB_PASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id payments/db --query SecretString --output text)
DB_URL=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /payments/db-url --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text)

The third route is the cleanest. An ECS task definition can name the secret, and ECS reads it when the container starts, using the task's execution role:

"secrets": [
  { "name": "DB_PASSWORD",
    "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-2:123456789012:secret:payments/db-AbCdEf" }
]

The pipeline deploys a task definition that holds only the secret's name. The value never passes through GitLab.

With the keyword, the runner signs in as the application in AZURE_CLIENT_ID, with the ID token that token: names, and reads the vault at AZURE_KEY_VAULT_SERVER_URL:

db-migrate:
  id_tokens:
    AZURE_JWT:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AZURE_KEY_VAULT_SERVER_URL: https://megacorp-prod-kv.vault.azure.net
    AZURE_CLIENT_ID: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
    AZURE_TENANT_ID: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  secrets:
    DB_PASSWORD:
      token: $AZURE_JWT
      azure_key_vault:
        name: payments-db-password
        version: 00000000000000000000000000000000
  script:
    - ./migrate.sh --password-file "$DB_PASSWORD"

The runner writes the value to a temporary file, and DB_PASSWORD holds the file's path. version names one version of the secret: a GUID written without dashes.

From a script, after az login:

DB_PASSWORD=$(az keyvault secret show --vault-name megacorp-prod-kv --name payments-db-password --query value --output tsv)

The third route is the cleanest here too. On MegaCorp's clusters, the External Secrets Operator copies the secret from Key Vault into the service's namespace, with its own identity (the External Secrets Operator). The value never passes through GitLab.

The usual deploy targets#

Most deploys are one of these. Each is a few CLI commands, run with the short-lived access the job got:

TargetWhat the job runsWhere to look when it fails
Static site on S3 and CloudFrontaws s3 sync, then aws cloudfront create-invalidationif visitors still see old files, check that the invalidation ran
ECSa new task definition that names the new image, then aws ecs update-service and aws ecs wait services-stablethe wait checks every 15 seconds and gives up after 40 checks, with exit code 255; the service's events show why new tasks fail
EKSaws eks update-kubeconfig, then kubectl or helm, or a GitOps handoffbesides its AWS permissions, the role needs access inside the cluster, which the cluster's owners grant
Lambdaaws lambda update-function-code, with a new image or zip filethe role's permission on that function, then the function's own logs
Infrastructure as codeOpenTofu or Terraform, with state stored in GitLab; or CloudFormationthe role needs every permission the change needs, so guard it with protected branches and environments
TargetWhat the job runsWhere to look when it fails
AKSaz aks get-credentials, then kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli, then kubectl or helm; or a GitOps handoffbesides its Azure roles, the identity needs access inside the cluster, which the cluster's owners grant
Container Appsaz containerapp update --name … --resource-group … --image …, which starts a new revision of the appthe app's revisions, then the new revision's logs
Infrastructure as codeOpenTofu or Terraform with the azurerm provider, with state stored in GitLabthe identity needs every permission the change needs, so guard it with protected branches and environments

MegaCorp's website job is the first AWS kind:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/node.ymlpublish-site
.publish-site:
  extends: .megacorp-base
  stage: deploy
  id_tokens:
    MC_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-web-publish
  before_script:
    - !reference [.snippets, functions]
    - !reference [.snippets, aws_login]
  script:
    - aws s3 sync dist/ "s3://$SITE_BUCKET/" --delete
    - aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id "$CF_DISTRIBUTION_ID" --paths '/*'
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://www.example.com

GitLab's ready-made AWS templates#

GitLab ships templates for AWS, and some older pipelines use them:

  • AWS/Deploy-ECS.gitlab-ci.yml builds an image into GitLab's registry, creates a new task definition revision, and updates an ECS service. You set CI_AWS_ECS_CLUSTER, CI_AWS_ECS_SERVICE and a task definition variable. The deploy waits for the rollout unless CI_AWS_ECS_WAIT_FOR_ROLLOUT_COMPLETE_DISABLED is set.
  • AWS/CF-Provision-and-Deploy-EC2.gitlab-ci.yml creates a CloudFormation stack, pushes the build to S3, and deploys it to EC2.
  • Both expect access keys stored as the CI/CD variables AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION. GitLab's own page says ID tokens are more secure, but don't work with these templates.
  • GitLab's image registry.gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cloud-deploy/aws-base contains the AWS CLI. If its output fails on a non-ASCII character, set LANG: "UTF-8".

Small things that bite#

  • The amazon/aws-cli image. Its entrypoint is the aws command itself. On the Docker executor, which keeps an image's entrypoint, it can't run your script unless you set entrypoint: [""]. The Kubernetes executor ignores entrypoints by default, so the same job can work on one runner and fail on another (chapter 29).
  • The region. AWS commands without --region use AWS_REGION, which MegaCorp sets to eu-west-2. A resource in another region looks as if it doesn't exist.
  • AWS keys expire after an hour. MegaCorp asks for 3600 seconds. A job that runs longer after logging in gets expired-token errors part-way through.
  • The ID token can expire first. Log in at the start of the job, not after a long build.
  • The cloud must reach GitLab. AWS's STS and Microsoft Entra ID both download GitLab's signing keys from the instance. A self-managed GitLab that the internet can't reach gets InvalidIdentityToken from AWS. GitLab documents a workaround for AWS that publishes the keys elsewhere; for Azure, its page says the instance must be publicly accessible.
  • A new federated credential takes a few minutes. Until it has spread through Entra ID, sign-ins can fail with AADSTS70021, as if it didn't exist.

When AWS or Azure says no#

Read the error first, because it names the step that failed. Then ask these in order:

To compare sub with the trust policy or the federated credential, print the token's claims, not the token. A token has three parts separated by dots, and the middle part holds the claims. GitLab's documentation suggests this command:

echo "$MC_ID_TOKEN" | cut -d '.' -f2 | base64 -d | jq .

The claims include the email address of the person who started the pipeline, so remove the line when you have your answer. base64 may also print base64: invalid input and return an error, because a token leaves out the padding that base64 expects. It happened with two tokens in four on the local GitLab 19.3, and the claims still printed in full.

When you write it

For each AWS role, write the trust policy's subject condition for exactly the refs that need it, such as project_path:megacorp/payments/payments-api:ref_type:branch:ref:main. Test it from tag and merge request pipelines too (refused in some pipelines). In Entra ID, add one federated credential for each project and branch that must sign in, spelled exactly.

Spot the bugThe release that couldn't push#

payments-api tags v1.5.0. In the tag pipeline, image-build fails during the login:

An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity operation: Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity

The same job pushed an image from main an hour earlier, and from a merge request pipeline this morning. This is the push role:

awsiam.ymlecr-push-role
# Assumed by image-build, and by the ecr-push component, through mc_aws_login.
ecr_push_role:
  arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-ecr-push
  trust_policy:
    Effect: Allow
    Principal:
      Federated: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/gitlab.example.com
    Action: sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
    Condition:
      StringEquals:
        gitlab.example.com:aud: https://gitlab.example.com
      StringLike:
        gitlab.example.com:sub: project_path:megacorp/*:ref_type:branch:ref:*
  permissions: push and pull images in every ECR repository in the account
QuestionWhy is only the tag pipeline refused, and how would you change the role without opening it to every tag?
Show the answer

A tag pipeline's ID token has a subject that ends in ref_type:tag:ref:v1.5.0. The pattern accepts only ref_type:branch, so STS refuses. Pipelines on main, and merge request pipelines, match because both run on branches.

Add a second pattern for release tags, such as project_path:megacorp/*:ref_type:tag:ref:v*. IAM accepts a list of values for one condition, and any match is enough. payments-api protects tags matching v*, which limits who can create them. On self-managed GitLab, AWS can't check ref_protected, so the pattern is the only guard.

While you are there, notice that ref:* lets any branch push images, including unreviewed feature branches. See how AWS checks an ID token.

Spot the bugThe branch Azure didn't know#

The payments team starts releasing from branches such as release/2026-09. At its request, the platform team changes mc_acr_push so that release/* branches push to ACR too. The first pipeline on release/2026-09 fails in image-build:

AADSTS70021: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion.

Pushes from main still work, and nobody has touched Entra ID.

azureentra.ymlapp-registration
# The identity that image jobs sign in as. Each federated credential names one kind of
# pipeline that may use it.
acr_push_app:
  display_name: gitlab-acr-push
  client_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  tenant_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  federated_credentials:
    - name: payments-api-main
      issuer: https://gitlab.example.com
      subject: project_path:megacorp/payments/payments-api:ref_type:branch:ref:main
      audiences: [https://gitlab.example.com]
QuestionWhy is the release branch refused, and what are the choices?
Show the answer

The job's token has the subject project_path:megacorp/payments/payments-api:ref_type:branch:ref:release/2026-09. The application's only federated credential names ref:main. Entra ID compares subjects exactly, with no wildcards, so nothing matches and the sign-in fails.

A credential for release/2026-09 would work, but only for that branch, and each release would need another, up to 20 per application. The simpler choice is to keep pushing to Azure only from main, and release the image that main built (from build to deploy). See what must match.

See no matching federated credential.

Next38Images to ECR and ACR4 min

Images to ECR and ACR#

Part VIII · Delivery · Chapter 38· 4 min read

MegaCorp builds each service's image in the pipeline, tags it with the commit's SHA, and pushes it to Amazon ECR. On main, it pushes the same image to Azure Container Registry too, for aks-prod. The deploy jobs receive that exact reference. The goal is build once, promote many: the image that staging tested is the image that production runs.

The common way to break that goal is to build again later, for example in a tag pipeline. A rebuild is a new image, even from the same commit.

How an image is named#

An image reference has three parts: the registry, the repository and a tag. MegaCorp's look like this:

123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:3f9c1e2…
└──────────── registry ─────────────────────┘ └─ repository ─┘ └ tag ┘
megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api:3f9c1e2…
└───── registry ──────┘ └─ repository ─┘ └ tag ┘

A tag is only a label, and labels can move. A commit SHA as the tag ties the image to exactly one commit, which is why MegaCorp uses $CI_COMMIT_SHA. A tag such as latest says nothing about what is inside, and changes with every push.

From build to deploy#

image-build logs in to AWS and ECR, builds with Buildah, and pushes. On main, it pushes the same image to ACR as well, under the same repository and tag (chapter 37). Then it writes the ECR reference to a dotenv report as IMAGE_REF (chapter 30). The deploy jobs pass it on to the deployer:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/deploy.ymldeploy-trigger
.deploy:
  stage: deploy
  trigger:
    project: megacorp/platform/deployer
    branch: main
    strategy: depend
  variables:
    APP: $CI_PROJECT_NAME
    IMAGE_REF: $IMAGE_REF

The deployer writes only the tag into the environment repository. Each cluster's values name its own registry, so eks-prod pulls the image from ECR, and aks-prod pulls the same tag from ACR (from tag to pod).

payments-api's tag pipeline runs maven-build and image-build again before deploy-prod. The release tag usually points at a commit that main already built and staging already tested. The rebuild pushes a second image under the same SHA tag. Base images and libraries may have changed in the meantime, so it is not the image that was tested. What happens next depends on the ECR repository:

  • Mutable tags: the new image quietly replaces the tested one.
  • Immutable tags: the push fails with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException.

ACR never sees the rebuild. A tag pipeline isn't on main, so image-build skips the push to Azure, and aks-prod keeps the image that main built. With mutable tags in ECR, the two clusters would then run different images under the same tag.

Promoting without rebuilding#

To promote, deploy the reference that was already built and tested. To give the same image a friendly name as well, add a tag in ECR without pulling or pushing anything:

MANIFEST=$(aws ecr batch-get-image --repository-name payments-api \
  --image-ids imageTag="$CI_COMMIT_SHA" --query 'images[].imageManifest' --output text)
aws ecr put-image --repository-name payments-api \
  --image-tag "$CI_COMMIT_TAG" --image-manifest "$MANIFEST"

Now v1.5.0 and the commit's SHA name the same image. With immutable tags, ECR refuses any attempt to move either of them.

ACR's tags are mutable by default. Its owners can lock a released tag, so that nobody can overwrite or delete it:

az acr repository update --name megacorpprod --image payments-api:3f9c1e2… --write-enabled false
When you write it

Tag each image with the commit it was built from, such as $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA, and deploy that one tag everywhere, rather than rebuilding for each environment or each cloud. With immutable tags in ECR, a retried push of the same tag fails (the tag already exists). In ACR, ask for the tags you release to be locked.

Spot the bugTwo images, one tag#

Commit 3f9c1e2 was built on main, deployed to staging, and tested for a week. Then it was tagged v1.5.0. The tag pipeline built and pushed payments-api:3f9c1e2… again, and deploy-prod shipped it. In production, a bug appears that staging never showed. At the time, payments-api's ECR repository had mutable tags. The platform team has made them immutable since.

megacorp/devops/ci-templatespipelines/java-service.ymljobs
maven-build:
  extends: .maven-build

maven-test:
  extends: .maven-test

image-build:
  extends: .image-build
  needs: [maven-build]
QuestionHow can production run code that staging never tested, when both used the same tag?
Show the answer

image-build runs in tag pipelines too, so the release built the commit a second time. That rebuild picked up whatever base image and libraries were current, made a different image, and pushed it under the same tag. With mutable tags it replaced the tested image. Production then deployed the new one.

Build once: skip image-build in tag pipelines, and deploy the image that main built. Add the release tag with put-image. Turning on tag immutability in ECR makes a rebuild fail loudly instead of replacing the image. See from build to deploy.

Next39Environments and deployments3 min

Environments and deployments#

Part VIII · Delivery · Chapter 39· 3 min read

An environment is GitLab's record of a place you deploy to: a name, a URL, and a history of deployments. A job with environment: becomes a deployment job, and that unlocks five safeguards:

  • who may deploy there
  • approvals before a deploy runs
  • one deploy at a time
  • refusing outdated deploys
  • re-deploying an earlier version

At MegaCorp every environment lives in the deployer project, so that is where to look when a deploy won't start.

Environments and deployments#

MegaCorp's deployer names each environment after the target and the service:

megacorp/platform/deployer.gitlab-ci.ymldeploy
variables:
  ENVIRONMENT: $[[ inputs.environment ]]

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools:3.2
  resource_group: $APP-$ENVIRONMENT
  environment:
    name: $ENVIRONMENT/$APP
  script:
    - mc deploy "$ENVIRONMENT" "$IMAGE_REF"
  rules:
    - if: $IMAGE_REF == null
      when: never
    - if: $ENVIRONMENT == "production"
      when: manual
    - when: on_success

Each run of this job records a deployment of staging/payments-api or production/payments-api. Its history appears under Operate › Environments. The names come from variables, so one job serves every service. The resource_group lets only one deploy per service and environment run at a time (chapter 23).

An environment also scopes variables. A CI/CD variable limited to the production/* environments reaches only jobs deploying there (chapter 25).

A deployment here records the deploy job, not the running software. At MegaCorp the job succeeds once mc deploy has written the new tag into the environment repository. The cluster rolls it out afterwards, so a green deployment can still end in pods that never start. Chapter 40 follows the rest of the way, and chapter 51 shows how to tell whether it worked.

Who may deploy, and approvals Premium#

  • Protected environments. A Maintainer can protect an environment, and list who is Allowed to deploy: roles, users or groups. Anyone else's deploy job to it can't run.
  • Deployment approvals. A protected environment can require approvals. Its deployments are blocked until all of them are given, under Operate › Environments, on the deployment's status badge. Approving doesn't start the job: someone must still run it.
Note
A trigger job, such as MegaCorp's .deploy, can use deployment-only access to a protected environment only if it has an environment: of its own. Without one, GitLab treats it as an ordinary job, with ordinary permissions.

One at a time, newest wins#

Two pipelines can race. The newer one deploys first, and then the older one finishes and puts the old version back. The project setting Prevent outdated deployment jobs stops that. An older deployment job then fails with:

The deployment job is older than the latest deployment, and therefore failed.

GitLab judges a job's age by when it started, not by its commit. So running an old pipeline's manual deploy blocks a newer pipeline's manual deploy.

Rolling back#

Under Operate › Environments, each earlier successful deployment offers Rollback environment, and the latest offers Re-deploy to environment. Both simply run that deployment's job again. That works only if the job holds everything the deploy needs. At MegaCorp it does: re-running the job writes the old IMAGE_REF's tag into the environment repository, straight to main for staging, and as a merge request for production (promotion by merge request). Reverting the deploy's commit in that repository does the same, and leaves a clearer history (drift, and going back).

When you write it

Give every deploy job an environment, so that GitLab records what runs where, and make the production job when: manual; on Premium, also protect the environment. Add a resource_group, so that two deploys to one environment never run at once (a deploy waits).

Spot the bugApproved, but not deployed#

The production environment in megacorp/platform/deployer needs one approval. A release manager approves a payments-api deployment at 17:55 and goes home. At 09:00 the next day, production still runs the old version. The deployer pipeline shows the deploy job waiting.

megacorp/platform/deployer.gitlab-ci.ymldeploy
variables:
  ENVIRONMENT: $[[ inputs.environment ]]

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools:3.2
  resource_group: $APP-$ENVIRONMENT
  environment:
    name: $ENVIRONMENT/$APP
  script:
    - mc deploy "$ENVIRONMENT" "$IMAGE_REF"
  rules:
    - if: $IMAGE_REF == null
      when: never
    - if: $ENVIRONMENT == "production"
      when: manual
    - when: on_success
QuestionWhy didn't the deploy happen after the approval?
Show the answer

Production deploys are when: manual in the deployer's rules. A deployment approval unblocks the job, but never starts it. Someone allowed to deploy must still select Run. The approval was needed, but it wasn't enough.

Make running the job part of the release manager's routine. See who may deploy, and approvals.

Next · Part IX40The delivery map6 min

The delivery map#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 40· 6 min read

Your pipeline ends when the image is in the registry. Four more steps happen before anyone uses the new version, and GitLab sees only the first. The new tag is written into a GitOps repository. A controller in the cluster notices, renders the chart or overlay, and applies it. Kubernetes replaces the old pods with new ones. Then the running service sends back signals: logs, metrics and traces. This part follows those steps, one chapter each, and this chapter is the map. When a deploy is missing, walk the map from left to right.

From commit to cluster, and back#

StepWhat happensWho owns it
build and pushyour pipeline builds the image and pushes it, tagged, to a registryyour team
request the deploya job writes the new tag into a values file in the GitOps repositoryyour team, often through a central job
synca controller in the cluster sees the change, renders it, and applies the resultthe platform team runs the controller; the values are yours
roll outKubernetes starts pods from the new image, checks them, and stops the old onesthe cluster: the cloud and the platform team
run and reportthe service runs, and sends logs, metrics and traces to where people watchyour team

Your team owns the two ends: the service and its pipeline, and what the service reports. The platform team owns the middle: the clusters, the controllers, the add-ons they install, and the shape of the GitOps repository. The cloud provider runs the managed Kubernetes, the registry and the identities. So a failure in the middle is usually found by you and fixed with them. The chapters that follow give you enough to find it.

Push and pull#

A pipeline can deploy in two ways:

  • Push: a job changes the target itself, for example by running helm upgrade against a cluster, or updating a cloud service.
  • Pull, or GitOps: a job writes the new version into a Git repository, and a controller running inside the cluster notices and applies it.
PatternThe pipeline needsWhen the job finishes, you know
Pushcredentials for the cluster or the cloud servicethe change was applied, and ready, if the job waits for it
Pullwrite access to the GitOps repository onlyonly that the change was committed

Pull keeps production credentials out of the pipeline, since only the controller touches the cluster. It also means that Git holds the truth: to see what should be running, read the repository; to go back, revert a commit. The price is that the pipeline can't see the deploy happen. MegaCorp pulls.

MegaCorp's delivery side#

RepositoryOwned byHoldsReaches
megacorp/payments/payments-apithe payments teamthe service and its pipeline fileECR and ACR, with images; the deployer, with a trigger
megacorp/platform/deployerthe platform teamthe deploy pipeline, which runs mc deploygitops-config: a commit for staging, a merge request for production
megacorp/platform/gitops-configthe platform team; teams change their own valueseach cluster's Flux setup, the add-ons, the ApplicationSets, and each service's valueseks-prod and aks-prod, which pull from it
megacorp/platform/chartsthe platform teamthe shared service chartevery ApplicationSet, at a tagged version
megacorp/platform/infra-modulesthe platform teamOpenTofu modules for clusters, registries and identitiesthe AWS account and the Azure subscription

The last step that GitLab shows is the deployer's job. It runs mc deploy, which writes the new tag into the environment's values file in gitops-config: straight to main for staging, and in a merge request for production:

megacorp/devops/ci-toolsbin/mcdeploy
deploy)
  env="${1:?usage: mc deploy <environment> <image-ref>}"
  image="${2:?usage: mc deploy <environment> <image-ref>}"
  tag="${image##*:}"
  mc_log "promoting ${APP} ${tag} to ${env} through the GitOps repository"
  git clone --depth 1 \
    "https://gitops-bot:${GITOPS_TOKEN}@gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git" gitops
  yq -i ".image.tag = \"${tag}\"" "gitops/envs/${env}/${APP}.yaml"
  git -C gitops commit -am "deploy ${APP} ${tag} to ${env}"
  if [ "$env" = production ]; then
    # production changes wait in a merge request until someone merges them
    git -C gitops push origin "HEAD:deploy/${APP}-${tag}" \
      -o merge_request.create -o merge_request.target=main \
      -o merge_request.title="Deploy ${APP} ${tag} to production"
  else
    git -C gitops push origin HEAD:main
  fi
  ;;

Both clusters run the same way. The platform team's Flux installs the add-ons, including Argo CD, from gitops-config. The payments team's services are then deployed by Argo CD, one Application for each environment. The chapters on chapter 42 and chapter 43 take the files apart.

Five questions for a deployment#

The decoding method asks five questions of a job (chapter 54). They work for a deployment too, with different answers:

QuestionFor a jobFor a deployment
Where is it defined?the merged configurationthe chart, the values and the overlays, in the GitOps repository
When does it run?the pipeline's source and the job's rulesafter a merge, when the controller next syncs
Where does it run?a runner, with its tagsa cluster, a namespace, some nodes
What does it run?its image and scriptan image, named by tag and digest, with its command and config
What goes in and out?variables and artifactsin: config and secrets; out: logs, metrics and traces

When a merged change never reaches production, ask the first two in order. Read the GitOps repository, then the controller's sync status, then the pods' events. The rest of this part shows where each of those is.

Spot the bugGreen, then nothing#

payments-api's pipeline on main passed at 10:02, including the trigger to the deployer. At 10:20, staging still serves the old version.

QuestionWhich steps of the map could the deploy be stuck at, and which do you check first?
Show the answer

Any step after the pipeline: the deployer's commit to gitops-config, the controller's sync, or the rollout. Check them from left to right. First, does the staging values file in gitops-config name the new tag? If it does, has the controller synced since that commit? If it has, did the new pods start and stay up? The pipeline can't tell you any of this, because GitLab sees nothing after the commit.

See green pipeline, old version.

The lab kit: tools, runtimes, networks and tokens#

The labs in this part come in two kinds. Render-and-read labs need only the helm and kustomize commands, and no cluster. Cluster labs run a small Kubernetes cluster on your computer with kind, which runs each cluster node as a container. Every cluster lab also has a render-and-read path.

ToolThe labs useFor
helm4.3rendering charts
kustomize5.8, or kubectl 1.36, which has it built inbuilding overlays
kubectl1.36reading the cluster: within one minor version of the cluster
kind0.33, with the Kubernetes 1.36.4 node imagethe local cluster
flux2.9installing Flux, and reading its objects
argocd3.5reading Argo CD's applications
a container runtimesee belowrunning kind's node

A container runtime. kind uses Docker by default. Docker Desktop is free only for personal use, education, non-commercial open source, and businesses with fewer than 250 employees and less than US$10 million in revenue; everyone else needs a paid subscription. On Linux, Docker Engine is open source and free. Elsewhere, open-source runtimes such as Rancher Desktop and Podman Desktop are alternatives. kind's support for Podman is experimental, and needs extra setup.

Company networks. kind passes HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY into its nodes, so a proxy that works for Docker usually works for the cluster. A proxy that inspects HTTPS re-signs every certificate, so its certificate authority must be trusted inside the nodes too; ask your IT team for it. If a registry such as ghcr.io is blocked, pull the image wherever you can and load it with kind load docker-image <image>. The first run downloads several hundred megabytes of images. On a slow connection, a chart's install can run out of time while they download (a HelmRelease that timed out).

Tokens. The cluster labs use two deploy tokens. A project's deploy token works only in that project, and only for what its scopes allow. Flux and Argo CD read the environment repository with one that has the read_repository scope. The cluster pulls the image with one that has read_registry on the project that built it. A token on the environment repository can't pull another project's images, however it's scoped (pods that can't pull their image). Deploy tokens are free on every GitLab offering. Project access tokens need Premium or Ultimate on GitLab.com. Avoid personal access tokens: they act as you, in every project you can reach. A lab that needs more says why.

Next41Containers and Kubernetes, enough to read5 min

Containers and Kubernetes, enough to read#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 41· 5 min read

A container runs one image: a program packaged with everything it needs. Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster of machines, from objects that describe what should run. You'll read a handful of them. A Deployment keeps a number of pods running, each with the service's container, and replaces them when their template changes. A Service gives those pods one stable name, and an Ingress brings outside traffic to it. Secrets hold settings that must stay hidden, and a ServiceAccount gives pods an identity. You rarely write these objects: MegaCorp's chart writes them from your values. This chapter shows how to read what it writes.

Images and containers#

An image is a program packaged with everything it needs to run. It's stored in a registry, under a repository and a tag, such as payments-api:3f9c2e1a. A container is one running copy of an image. Chapter 29 covered how pipelines build images; here, they're what runs.

A tag names an image, but tags can move. A digest, sha256: followed by 64 hexadecimal characters, names exactly one image and never moves. When you need to know exactly what ran, the digest is the answer.

The objects you'll read#

Kubernetes objects are YAML, like pipelines, and each one names its apiVersion and kind. A controller in the cluster watches each kind, and makes the cluster match what the objects ask for. MegaCorp's chart makes these for each service:

ObjectWhat it isWhat you change, in the service's values
Deploymentkeeps a number of pods running from one pod template, and replaces them when the template changesreplicaCount, image.tag, env, probes and resources
ReplicaSetmade by the Deployment, one for each version of the pod template; it keeps that version's pods runningnothing: you read it, to see which versions exist
Podthe smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network and storagenothing directly: pods come and go
Serviceone stable name and address for a set of pods, which it finds by their labelsusually nothing
Ingressroutes outside HTTP and HTTPS traffic to a Service, by host and path; an ingress controller must be runningingress.host
ExternalSecret and Secretthe Secret holds the service's secrets, which the External Secrets Operator copies from the cloud's vaultsecrets.keys
ServiceAccountthe pods' identity inside the cluster and, through its annotations, in the cloudserviceAccount.annotations
Namespacethe named group that holds one service's objects in one environment, such as payments-stagingnothing: the platform decides

Reading a Deployment#

This is payments-api's Deployment in staging, as MegaCorp's chart renders it:

helm templateoutputcaptured at the baseline
---
# Source: service/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm
    helm.sh/chart: service-3.4.0
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: payments-api
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:3f9c2e1a"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: PAYMENTS_PROVIDER_URL
              value: "https://sandbox.pay.example.com"
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "staging"
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: payments-api
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 256Mi
  • replicas is how many pods run. Staging runs one; production runs three.
  • selector and the template's labels must agree. They're how the Deployment, and the Service, know which pods are theirs.
  • template is the pod template. Change anything under it, such as the image, and the Deployment makes a new ReplicaSet and moves the pods over to it (rolling, the default).
  • image is the full reference: registry, repository and tag. mc deploy changes only the tag.
  • env holds plain settings. envFrom adds every key of the payments-api Secret as a variable (the External Secrets Operator).
  • readinessProbe decides when a pod may receive traffic. livenessProbe restarts a container that stops answering.
  • resources.requests is what the pod is given, and what Kubernetes uses to choose a node. limits.memory is the most it may use; a container that goes over it can be killed.

None of it was typed into the Deployment. The port, the probe's path and the resources are the chart's defaults, which every service starts from:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/values.yamlcontainer
port: 8080
env: {}                   # plain settings, as NAME: value
probes:
  path: /actuator/health
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi

The image, the settings and the replica count come from staging's values file, which overrides those defaults for payments-api (values).

What you see with kubectl#

You read a running service with a few kubectl commands. Each one needs the namespace, such as -n payments-staging:

CommandShowsLook for
kubectl get podseach pod, whether it's ready, its status and its restarts1/1 ready and Running; restarts that keep growing
kubectl describe pod <pod>a pod's settings, with its events at the endwhy it can't pull its image, start, or become ready
kubectl logs <pod>what the container wrote to standard outputthe service's own errors; add --previous for a run that crashed
kubectl get deployment payments-apihow many pods are ready, up to date and availablea rollout that hasn't finished
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-apiwaits until a rollout finishes, or failssuccessfully rolled out, or a progress-deadline error

This is payments-api in staging, on the local cluster the book was checked on:

kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
payments-api-796d6777f9-stwjv   1/1     Running   0          14m
kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME           READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
payments-api   1/1     1            1           14m

And the parts of kubectl describe pod you'll read most: the pod's status, its image, its readiness check, and the events at the end. The image was already present because the local cluster can't pull from ECR, so a stand-in was loaded into it under the same name. On a real cluster, the kubelet pulls the image first, and says so.

kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
Name:             payments-api-796d6777f9-stwjv
Namespace:        payments-staging
⋯ lines omitted
Status:           Running
⋯ lines omitted
    Image:          123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:3f9c2e1a
⋯ lines omitted
    Ready:          True
⋯ lines omitted
    Readiness:  http-get http://:http/actuator/health delay=0s timeout=1s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
⋯ lines omitted
  Type                        Status
⋯ lines omitted
Events:
  Type    Reason     Age   From               Message
  ----    ------     ----  ----               -------
  Normal  Scheduled  14m   default-scheduler  Successfully assigned payments-staging/payments-api-796d6777f9-stwjv to delivery-lab-control-plane
  Normal  Pulled     14m   kubelet            spec.containers{app}: Container image "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:3f9c2e1a" already present on machine and can be accessed by the pod
  Normal  Created    14m   kubelet            spec.containers{app}: Container created
  Normal  Started    14m   kubelet            spec.containers{app}: Container started

Most of what you read about a pod comes from other objects. Its image comes from the Deployment, which comes from the chart and your values. Its secrets come from the ExternalSecret, and its traffic from the Service and the Ingress. When something is wrong, the object at fault is often not the pod.

When you write it

Change a service through its values, not its objects: the controller undoes a change made with kubectl. Point the readiness probe at something that shows the service can do its work. Give each pod the resources.requests it really needs, and a memory limit that it won't reach in normal use.

Spot the bugRead production on aks-prod#

This is payments-api's Deployment for production on aks-prod, rendered from the same chart:

helm templateoutputcaptured at the baseline
---
# Source: service/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm
    helm.sh/chart: service-3.4.0
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: payments-api
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api:1c7d4b09"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: PAYMENTS_PROVIDER_URL
              value: "https://pay.example.com"
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "production"
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: payments-api
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 256Mi
QuestionHow many pods run, from which image? Where does DB_PASSWORD come from, and when does a new pod start receiving traffic?
Show the answer

Three pods, from replicas: 3. The image is megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api:1c7d4b09: Azure's registry, with production's tag. DB_PASSWORD isn't in the Deployment at all. envFrom loads every key of the payments-api Secret, which the External Secrets Operator fills from Key Vault. A new pod receives traffic once its readiness probe on /actuator/health passes (0/1 ready).

Next42Helm8 min

Helm#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 42· 8 min read

Every service needs the same handful of Kubernetes objects, with different names, images and settings. Helm writes those objects once, as a chart: YAML templates with gaps, and a default for every gap. A values file fills the gaps for one service in one environment, and helm template prints the result. That is how a new image tag travels from a values file into the Deployment that runs the pods. MegaCorp has one chart for every service, and each service's values live in gitops-config.

One chart, many services#

A service on Kubernetes needs the same few objects. A Deployment runs its pods, a Service sits in front of them, and an Ingress brings in traffic from outside. A ServiceAccount carries its identity, and something brings in its secrets. Written by hand, that is about a hundred lines of YAML for each service in each environment, and the copies drift apart.

Helm writes the objects once, with gaps where services differ. MegaCorp's platform team keeps one chart, service, in megacorp/platform/charts. Teams don't edit it. They write values.

WordMeans
charta folder of templates and default values, versioned as one package
templatea YAML file with gaps, each written {{ … }}
valueswhat fills the gaps: the chart's defaults, then yours
renderfill every gap and print plain YAML, which is what helm template does
releaseone installation of a chart in a cluster, with a numbered revision for each change

What's in a chart#

A chart is a folder with three kinds of file. Chart.yaml names the chart and its version:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/Chart.yaml
# service/Chart.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: the shared Helm chart that every
# MegaCorp HTTP service deploys with. The charts repository tags each release, such as
# service-3.4.0, and the ApplicationSets name that tag.
# Used by the chapters "Helm" and "Argo CD".
apiVersion: v2
name: service
description: One MegaCorp HTTP service, with its Service, Ingress and secrets
type: application
version: 3.4.0

values.yaml holds a default for every gap. The image's repository and tag are empty, because only a service and an environment can answer them:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/values.yamlimage
image:
  repository: ""          # set for each service
  tag: ""                 # set for each environment; mc deploy writes it
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

The templates folder holds YAML with gaps: deployment.yaml, service.yaml (with the ServiceAccount and the Ingress) and externalsecret.yaml. A file whose name starts with an underscore, such as _helpers.tpl, makes no objects: it holds named pieces that the other templates reuse.

The charts repository tags each release, such as service-3.4.0, and each ApplicationSet names the tag it uses. A new chart version reaches a service only when someone changes that line.

Reading a template#

Here is the line that sets the image, in the Deployment template:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/deployment.yamlimage
image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ required "image.tag is set for each environment" .Values.image.tag }}"
imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}

Everything between {{ and }} is an action, which Helm replaces with text. Everything else is copied as it is. This book shades actions, so you can tell them from the YAML around them. The actions you will meet most:

You seeIt means
{{ .Values.image.tag }}the value at image.tag
{{ required "…" .Values.image.tag }}the same, but stop with that message if it's empty
{{ include "service.name" . }}the text of a named template from _helpers.tpl
