{{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}a whole block of values, indented 12 spaces. The - trims the spaces before the action
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} … {{- end }}the lines between, only when the value is true
{{- range .Values.secrets.keys }} … {{- end }}the lines between, once for each item in the list
{{- with .Values.podLabels }} … {{- end }}the lines between, only when the value is set, with . meaning that value
Where the name comes fromdeep dive

{{ include "service.name" . }} is the release name, cut to 63 characters: the first word after helm template or helm install. Argo CD sets it from releaseName in the ApplicationSet, so every object is called payments-api, whatever the environment. The namespace, not the name, keeps staging and production apart.

Values: the defaults, then yours#

Helm starts from the chart's values.yaml, then lays each values file over it, in order. Maps merge key by key, and anything else is replaced, lists included. So a values file only says what differs:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configenvs/staging/payments-api.yamlimage
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api
  tag: 3f9c2e1a

The staging file sets the repository and the tag, and keeps the chart's defaults for everything it doesn't mention, such as the probes and the resources.

Argo CD adds layers of its own. From weakest to strongest: the chart's values.yaml, value files, inline values, valuesObject, and single parameters, which beat everything. aks-prod uses that: its ApplicationSet adds inline values that switch the image to Azure's registry and give the pods their Azure identity:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configapps/aks-prod/applicationset.yamlazure-values
valuesObject:
  image:
    repository: megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      azure.workload.identity/client-id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  podLabels:
    azure.workload.identity/use: "true"

Render it yourself#

You never need a cluster to see what a chart makes. helm template takes a release name, the chart and your values, and prints the manifests. --show-only keeps one template's output:

helm template payments-api ./service -n payments-staging \
  -f envs/staging/payments-api.yaml --show-only templates/deployment.yaml
helm templateoutputcaptured at the baseline
---
# Source: service/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm
    helm.sh/chart: service-3.4.0
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: payments-api
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: payments-api
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:3f9c2e1a"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: PAYMENTS_PROVIDER_URL
              value: "https://sandbox.pay.example.com"
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "staging"
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: payments-api
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 256Mi

Read it from the top. The name comes from the release name, and the labels from _helpers.tpl. The replicas, the image and the settings come from the staging file. envFrom is there because the file lists a secret. Everything the cluster will run is on the page.

A required value that's missing stops the render, with the chart's own message:

helm templateoutputcaptured at the baseline
Error: execution error at (service/templates/deployment.yaml:28:52): image.tag is set for each environment

Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML

helm lint checks a chart's structure in the same way, also without a cluster.

From a tag to a pod#

When a deploy seems not to have happened, follow the tag through three places, in order:

The first two need no cluster: read the file, and render it. The third asks the cluster which image each pod was started from:

kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME                            IMAGE
payments-api-6c854bc48b-lzhss   123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1c7d4b09
payments-api-6c854bc48b-nsd64   123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1c7d4b09
payments-api-6c854bc48b-qpdqw   123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1c7d4b09

That is production on the local cluster: three pods, as replicaCount: 3 in production's values file asks, each started from the tag 1c7d4b09 that the same file names.

Releases, and who installs them#

helm install and helm upgrade render a chart and apply the result, and keep a release: a record in the cluster of what was applied, with a revision number for each change. helm list shows releases, helm history shows a release's revisions, and helm rollback goes back to one.

With GitOps, people rarely run these commands. What happens to a chart depends on the controller:

ControllerWhat it does with a chartIn helm list?
Flux, with a HelmReleaseinstalls and upgrades a real releaseyes
Argo CDrenders the chart with helm template, then applies and tracks the output itselfno

So on MegaCorp's clusters, helm list shows the add-ons that Flux installed, and none of the services that Argo CD deploys, even though their objects carry the label app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm.

helmoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME            	NAMESPACE       	REVISION	UPDATED                                	STATUS  	CHART                  	APP VERSION
argo-cd         	argocd          	2       	2026-09-14 06:40:20.289277196 +0000 UTC	deployed	argo-cd-10.9.0         	v3.5.2     
external-secrets	external-secrets	1       	2026-09-14 06:33:33.744648979 +0000 UTC	deployed	external-secrets-2.10.0	v2.10.0
⋯ lines omitted

On the local cluster, Flux installed both of these. payments-api runs in staging and production, yet it has no release: Argo CD deployed it. The line left out is the lab cluster's own ingress controller, installed with helm directly.

Note
The book targets Helm 4.3. Charts written for Helm 3 work unchanged. Two flags in older pipelines were renamed: --atomic is now --rollback-on-failure, and --force is now --force-replace. The old names still work, with a warning. New releases are applied with server-side apply.
When you write it

Put everything that differs by environment in that environment's values file, and nothing environment-specific in the chart. Never type an image tag into a chart or a template: the deploy writes tags into values files, and a required gap stops a render that has none.

Spot the bugWhich image runs on aks-prod?#

payments-api's production values file names the tag 1c7d4b09 and an ECR repository. aks-prod's ApplicationSet adds the inline values shown above.

QuestionWhich image do payments-api's production pods run on aks-prod, and why?
Show the answer

megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api:1c7d4b09. The tag comes from the production values file. The repository comes from the inline values, which beat value files. Rendered with the same values, the Deployment says so:

helm templateoutputcaptured at the baseline
⋯ lines omitted
kind: Deployment
⋯ lines omitted
  name: payments-api
⋯ lines omitted
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
⋯ lines omitted
          image: "megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api:1c7d4b09"
⋯ lines omitted

See a value that loses to another.

LabRender the shared chart with your valuesabout 10 min#
You need

Helm 4.3 on your computer, and the image you pushed in chapter 7. No cluster.

Steps
  1. In a new folder, save MegaCorp's chart as service, keeping these paths:
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/Chart.yaml
    # service/Chart.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: the shared Helm chart that every
# MegaCorp HTTP service deploys with. The charts repository tags each release, such as
# service-3.4.0, and the ApplicationSets name that tag.
# Used by the chapters "Helm" and "Argo CD".
apiVersion: v2
name: service
description: One MegaCorp HTTP service, with its Service, Ingress and secrets
type: application
version: 3.4.0
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/values.yaml
    # service/values.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: the defaults every service starts
# from. A service's file in gitops-config sets what differs.
# Used by the chapters "Helm" and "GitOps repositories and promotion".

image:
  repository: ""          # set for each service
  tag: ""                 # set for each environment; mc deploy writes it
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

replicaCount: 2

port: 8080
env: {}                   # plain settings, as NAME: value
probes:
  path: /actuator/health
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi

serviceAccount:
  annotations: {}         # the pod's cloud identity, where the cloud needs one
podLabels: {}

ingress:
  enabled: false
  className: nginx
  host: ""

secrets:
  store: ""               # the ClusterSecretStore to read from
  keys: []                # each one: {name: DB_PASSWORD, remote: payments-api/staging/db-password}
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/_helpers.tpl
    {{- /*
service/templates/_helpers.tpl in megacorp/platform/charts: named templates that the
other templates share, so every object gets the same name and labels.
Used by the chapter "Helm".
*/}}

{{- define "service.name" -}}
{{- .Release.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" -}}
{{- end -}}

{{- define "service.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
{{- end -}}

{{- define "service.labels" -}}
{{ include "service.selectorLabels" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}
{{- end -}}
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/deployment.yaml
    {{- /*
service/templates/deployment.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: the Deployment that runs a
service's pods. Used by the chapters "Containers and Kubernetes, enough to read" and "Helm".
*/}}
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "service.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "service.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
        {{- with .Values.podLabels }}
        {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
        {{- end }}
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: {{ include "service.name" . }}
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ required "image.tag is set for each environment" .Values.image.tag }}"
          imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: {{ .Values.port }}
          {{- with .Values.env }}
          env:
            {{- range $name, $value := . }}
            - name: {{ $name }}
              value: {{ $value | quote }}
            {{- end }}
          {{- end }}
          {{- if .Values.secrets.keys }}
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
          {{- end }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
              port: http
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/service.yaml
    {{- /*
service/templates/service.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: the service's ServiceAccount,
the Service in front of its pods, and the Ingress that brings outside traffic in.
Used by the chapters "Containers and Kubernetes, enough to read", "Helm" and "AWS and
Azure for delivery".
*/}}
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
  {{- with .Values.serviceAccount.annotations }}
  annotations:
    {{- toYaml . | nindent 4 }}
  {{- end }}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  selector:
    {{- include "service.selectorLabels" . | nindent 4 }}
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  ingressClassName: {{ .Values.ingress.className }}
  rules:
    - host: {{ required "ingress.host is needed when ingress.enabled is true" .Values.ingress.host }}
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
                port:
                  name: http
{{- end }}
    megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/externalsecret.yaml
    {{- /*
service/templates/externalsecret.yaml in megacorp/platform/charts: asks the External Secrets
Operator to copy a service's secrets from the cloud's vault into a Kubernetes Secret, which
the Deployment reads. Used by the chapters "Helm" and "Secrets and config after the pipeline".
*/}}
{{- if .Values.secrets.keys }}
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: {{ required "secrets.store names the ClusterSecretStore" .Values.secrets.store }}
  target:
    name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  data:
    {{- range .Values.secrets.keys }}
    - secretKey: {{ .name }}
      remoteRef:
        key: {{ .remote }}
    {{- end }}
{{- end }}
  2. Beside the service folder, save your values as greeting-values.yaml, with your own image's repository and tag:

Next43Kustomize5 min

Kustomize#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 43· 5 min read

Kustomize changes plain YAML without templates. A base is ordinary YAML that works on its own. An overlay names the base and lists only what differs for one environment: a namespace, an image tag, a patch. kustomize build prints the base with the overlay's changes applied, and kubectl and Flux have Kustomize built in. MegaCorp uses it to set up each cluster's add-ons, and many teams use it for their services. Always read the build's output: a change that matches nothing is skipped without a word.

Plain YAML, then changes#

Helm fills gaps in templates. Kustomize has no gaps: its input is the same YAML you would apply by hand. It edits that YAML with changes that you list in a file called kustomization.yaml.

WordMeans
basea folder of plain YAML, with a kustomization.yaml listing its files, that works on its own
overlaya folder whose kustomization.yaml names a base and lists changes
patchone change to one object: set a field, add one, or remove one
buildapply an overlay's changes to its base and print the result

A base and an overlay#

The lab at the end of this chapter uses greeting-service, the Node service from Part II. Its base is a Deployment and a Service, with the image tagged latest. Staging's overlay changes three things:

practice · deliverykustomize/overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml
# practice/delivery/kustomize/overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml: staging's overlay. It takes
# the base, puts it in its own namespace, pins the image's tag, and runs two replicas.
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: greeting-staging
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: gitlab.example.com:5050/practice/node-service
    newTag: 0648d3dd
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: greeting
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 2
  • resources names the base, as a path to its folder.
  • namespace puts every object in greeting-staging.
  • images finds each container whose image has the name given, and sets its tag. The name is the image without its tag, and it must match exactly.
  • patches changes one object. This patch is a list of operations, each with a path into the object: replace the value at /spec/replicas with 2.

kustomize build overlays/staging prints the result:

kustomize buildoutputcaptured at the baseline
⋯ lines omitted
kind: Service
⋯ lines omitted
  name: greeting
  namespace: greeting-staging
⋯ lines omitted
kind: Deployment
⋯ lines omitted
  name: greeting
  namespace: greeting-staging
⋯ lines omitted
  replicas: 2
⋯ lines omitted
      - image: gitlab.example.com:5050/practice/node-service:0648d3dd
⋯ lines omitted

Kustomize prints every map with its keys in alphabetical order, so image now comes before name. The meaning is the same.

A patch as part of an object#

A patch can also be written as a piece of the object, and Kustomize merges it in. aks-prod's add-ons overlay does that. It keeps MegaCorp's base of add-ons, and gives the External Secrets Operator the Azure identity it needs to read Key Vault:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/add-ons/aks/kustomization.yamloverlay
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../base
patches:
  - target:
      kind: HelmRelease
      name: external-secrets
    patch: |-
      apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
      kind: HelmRelease
      metadata:
        name: external-secrets
      spec:
        values:
          serviceAccount:
            annotations:
              azure.workload.identity/client-id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
          podLabels:
            azure.workload.identity/use: "true"

The patch names the object by kind and name, and gives only the fields to add. Maps merge key by key, so the values the base already set, such as the service account's name, stay:

kustomize buildoutputcaptured at the baseline
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: external-secrets
  namespace: external-secrets
spec:
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: external-secrets
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: external-secrets
        namespace: flux-system
      version: 2.10.0
  install:
    crds: CreateReplace
  interval: 30m
  upgrade:
    crds: CreateReplace
  values:
    podLabels:
      azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
    serviceAccount:
      annotations:
        azure.workload.identity/client-id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
      name: external-secrets

eks-prod needs none of this, because EKS Pod Identity is set up in AWS, not in the cluster. So eks-prod's Flux builds the base itself.

Where Kustomize runs#

WhereHow
your terminalkustomize build <folder>, or kubectl kustomize <folder>: kubectl 1.36 has Kustomize 5.8.1 built in
kubectl apply -k <folder>builds the folder and applies the result
Fluxeach Kustomization object names a path in a Git source, and Flux builds and applies it
Argo CDan Application whose path holds a kustomization.yaml is built with Kustomize

So the file you read in a GitOps repository is never what the cluster gets. The build's output is.

A change that matches nothing#

When an images entry names an image that isn't there, Kustomize doesn't complain. It builds as usual, and the tag stays as it was. Here is the same overlay with node-service misspelt as node-servce. The namespace and the replicas still change, which makes the miss easy to overlook:

kustomize buildoutputcaptured at the baseline
⋯ lines omitted
kind: Service
⋯ lines omitted
  namespace: greeting-staging
⋯ lines omitted
kind: Deployment
⋯ lines omitted
  namespace: greeting-staging
⋯ lines omitted
  replicas: 2
⋯ lines omitted
      - image: gitlab.example.com:5050/practice/node-service:latest
⋯ lines omitted

Before merging a change to an overlay, build it and read the line you meant to change.

LegacypatchesStrategicMerge and commonLabels
Kustomize 5 replaced several fields. patchesStrategicMerge and patchesJson6902 became patches, commonLabels became labels, and a base is listed under resources, not bases. Old files still build, with a warning at the top of the output:
kustomize buildoutputcaptured at the baseline
# Warning: 'commonLabels' is deprecated. Please use 'labels' instead. Run 'kustomize edit fix' to update your Kustomization automatically.
# Warning: 'patchesStrategicMerge' is deprecated. Please use 'patches' instead. Run 'kustomize edit fix' to update your Kustomization automatically.
⋯ lines omitted
kustomize edit fix rewrites the file for you.
When you write it

Keep the base valid on its own, and put each environment's differences in its overlay. Change image tags with images, not by editing the base. Build the overlay and read the output before you merge: a name that matches nothing changes nothing, without a warning.

Spot the bugWhat does aks-prod's overlay change?#

eks-prod's Flux builds infrastructure/add-ons/base. aks-prod's builds infrastructure/add-ons/aks, the overlay shown above.

QuestionWhich objects differ between the two clusters' add-ons, and how?
Show the answer

Only the External Secrets Operator's HelmRelease. On aks-prod its values gain the azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation for the service account, and the azure.workload.identity/use: "true" label for the pods. The namespaces, the Helm repositories and Argo CD's HelmRelease are the base's, unchanged, on both clusters.

Without that patch, the Operator's pods would have no Azure identity (a pod without its Azure identity).

Break it on purpose

In the overlay's images entry, misspell the image's name, and build again. The build succeeds, and the image is back to latest.

Next44GitOps repositories and promotion6 min

GitOps repositories and promotion#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 44· 6 min read

With GitOps, a deploy is a commit. A service's application repository holds its code and pipeline, and an environment repository says what runs where. The pipeline's last job writes the new image tag into the environment repository, and a controller in each cluster applies whatever that repository says. Promotion to production is a merge request in the environment repository, so merging it is the approval, and going back is a revert. A change made in the cluster by hand doesn't last: the controller puts back what the repository says.

Two kinds of repository#

RepositoryHoldsChanged by
application repositorythe service's code, its Dockerfile and its pipeline filethe team, in merge requests; its pipeline builds and pushes images
environment repositorywhat runs in each cluster and environment: which chart or overlay, which values, which image tagdeploy jobs, and people in merge requests

Keeping them apart makes the environment repository's history the history of deploys: one commit for each change to what runs. Its permissions can differ too: many people change code, and fewer may change production. MegaCorp's environment repository is gitops-config. Some teams keep their deployment files in the application repository instead, in a folder such as deploy/, and point the controller at that folder.

Inside an environment repository#

Folder in gitops-configHoldsOwned by
clusters/each cluster's Flux setup: where it syncs from, and what it runs, in orderthe platform team
infrastructure/the add-ons every cluster runs, and each cloud's changes to themthe platform team
apps/each cluster's ApplicationSets: which services it deploys, from which chartthe platform team, with the teams
envs/each service's values in each environmentthe teams, and the deploy job

A service's team mostly touches one file for each environment. This is payments-api's in production:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configenvs/production/payments-api.yamlimage
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api
  tag: 1c7d4b09

The job that bumps a tag#

MegaCorp's service pipelines don't write to gitops-config themselves. A service's deploy job triggers the platform team's deployer pipeline, whose job runs mc deploy:

megacorp/devops/ci-toolsbin/mcdeploy
deploy)
  env="${1:?usage: mc deploy <environment> <image-ref>}"
  image="${2:?usage: mc deploy <environment> <image-ref>}"
  tag="${image##*:}"
  mc_log "promoting ${APP} ${tag} to ${env} through the GitOps repository"
  git clone --depth 1 \
    "https://gitops-bot:${GITOPS_TOKEN}@gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git" gitops
  yq -i ".image.tag = \"${tag}\"" "gitops/envs/${env}/${APP}.yaml"
  git -C gitops commit -am "deploy ${APP} ${tag} to ${env}"
  if [ "$env" = production ]; then
    # production changes wait in a merge request until someone merges them
    git -C gitops push origin "HEAD:deploy/${APP}-${tag}" \
      -o merge_request.create -o merge_request.target=main \
      -o merge_request.title="Deploy ${APP} ${tag} to production"
  else
    git -C gitops push origin HEAD:main
  fi
  ;;
  • It clones gitops-config with the deployer's token, and changes one line: the tag, in the service's file for that environment.
  • For staging, it pushes the commit to main, and the controllers pick it up on their next sync.
  • For production, it pushes a branch, and asks GitLab to open a merge request. Nothing changes in production until someone merges it.

The trigger jobs use strategy: depend, so a service's pipeline turns red if the deployer's pipeline fails (chapter 16). But the deployer's pipeline is green as soon as the push succeeds. Anything that goes wrong after that never reaches GitLab: a controller that hasn't synced, or pods that crash.

Promotion by merge request#

To promote is to move a version that is already running in one environment into the next. In an environment repository, that is a change to the next environment's file, and a merge request is the safest way to make it:

  • it shows exactly what will change: one tag, from one value to another;
  • whoever may merge into main may deploy, so the branch's protection is the approval rule;
  • the merge is the record of who promoted what, and when.

With push options, the deploy job opens the merge request in the same push, and GitLab answers with its link:

git pushoutputcaptured at the baseline
remote: 
remote: View merge request for deploy/greeting-7d625fae:        
remote:   https://gitlab.example.com/practice/greeting-gitops/-/merge_requests/3        
remote:

Without the options, GitLab only offers a link to create one, and nobody is asked to review anything:

git pushoutputcaptured at the baseline
remote: 
remote: To create a merge request for deploy/greeting-7d625fae-plain, visit:        
remote:   https://gitlab.example.com/practice/greeting-gitops/-/merge_requests/new?merge_request%5Bsource_branch%5D=deploy%2Fgreeting-7d625fae-plain        
remote:

Drift, and going back#

Drift is any difference between the cluster and the repository. It usually comes from a change made by hand, such as kubectl edit or kubectl scale. Both controllers put the repository's version back:

ControllerA change made by hand
Fluxreverted at the Kustomization's next reconciliation; MegaCorp's reconcile every ten minutes
Argo CD, with selfHeal: truereverted automatically, a few seconds after Argo CD sees it
Argo CD, without selfHealshown as OutOfSync, until someone syncs

So the way to change a running service is always a commit, and that includes going back. kubectl rollout undo and helm rollback change the cluster, and the controller changes it straight back. Revert the deploy's commit in the environment repository instead:

git revert <the deploy's commit>

The revert is itself a commit, so it deploys like any other change, and the history shows it.

Automatic image updates#

Some setups have no deploy job. A controller watches the registry, picks new tags by a rule, and writes them into the environment repository itself. You can tell by what's in the repository:

You seeIt isIt writes
# {"$imagepolicy": "flux-system:greeting"} at the end of an image: line, and ImagePolicy and ImageUpdateAutomation objectsFlux's image automationcommits to the branch that its ImageUpdateAutomation names
an ImageUpdater object, or the annotation argocd-image-updater.argoproj.io/image-list on an ApplicationArgo CD Image Updatereither the Application's parameters, or commits to Git

If a tag changed and no pipeline ran, look for these. MegaCorp doesn't use them: it wants a pipeline, with its tests, to decide what gets deployed.

GitLab's agent for Kubernetes#

The agent for Kubernetes is a program installed in a cluster that keeps a connection open to GitLab. It is available in every tier, and does two jobs:

  • Push, through the agent. Projects and groups listed under ci_access in the agent's configuration get a kubeconfig file in every job, at $KUBECONFIG, with a context for each agent they may use. kubectl and helm then reach the cluster without any cluster credentials stored in GitLab.
  • Pull, with Flux. When the agent sees a push to a repository that a Flux GitRepository watches, it can tell Flux to sync at once. Otherwise Flux checks on its own interval.
Note
The agent can trigger an immediate sync only for its own configuration project and for public projects. For a private environment repository, such as gitops-config, Flux syncs on its interval, so a deploy can appear minutes after the pipeline goes green.
When you write it

When your pipeline hands off to GitOps, its job ends when the change is committed to the environment repository, not when it is running. Say so in the job's name, such as request-deploy, and give the environment the URL where the deploy can be watched (deploys appear minutes later).

Spot the bugGreen, but still the old version#

At 10:02 a payments-api pipeline on main goes green, including deploy-staging and the deployer pipeline it triggered. At 10:05, staging still serves the old version. MegaCorp's clusters run Flux, connected through GitLab's agent, and gitops-config is a private project. By 10:12 the new version is live, and nobody changed anything.

QuestionWhat happened between 10:02 and 10:12, and where would you have looked at 10:05?
Show the answer

The pipelines ended when mc deploy pushed the new tag to gitops-config. Because that repository is private, the agent couldn't trigger an immediate sync, so Flux picked the change up on its next scheduled check. The pods then rolled out. None of this shows in GitLab.

At 10:05, check the latest commit in gitops-config, then the controller's last sync, then the cluster's rollout. See the job that bumps a tag.

See deploys that appear minutes later.

LabPromote by merge requestabout 10 min#
You need

An account on your GitLab, git, and two tags of the image you pushed in chapter 7. No cluster.

Steps
  1. Create a blank project named greeting-gitops. Add envs/production/greeting.yaml: your values from the Helm lab (render the shared chart), with the older tag. Push to main.
  2. Change the tag to the newer one, and commit.
  3. Push the commit to a new branch, and ask for a merge request: 
    git push origin HEAD:deploy/greeting-<tag> -o merge_request.create \
  -o merge_request.target=main -o merge_request.title="Deploy greeting <tag> to production"
  4. Open the merge request, and read its changes.
What you should see

GitLab answers on the push with the merge request's link:

git pushoutputcaptured at the baseline
remote: 
remote: View merge request for deploy/greeting-7d625fae:        
remote:   https://gitlab.example.com/practice/greeting-gitops/-/merge_requests/3        
remote:

The merge request changes one line of envs/production/greeting.yaml: the tag. Merging it is the deploy's approval.

Break it on purpose

Push the same commit to another new branch, without the -o options. GitLab only offers a link to create a merge request, and nobody is asked:

git pushoutputcaptured at the baseline
remote: 
remote: To create a merge request for deploy/greeting-7d625fae-plain, visit:        
remote:   https://gitlab.example.com/practice/greeting-gitops/-/merge_requests/new?merge_request%5Bsource_branch%5D=deploy%2Fgreeting-7d625fae-plain        
remote:
Next45Flux6 min

Flux#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 45· 6 min read

Flux is a set of controllers that keep a cluster in step with Git. A GitRepository says what to fetch, and how often. A Kustomization says which folder to apply, how often, and what to do about drift. A HelmRelease installs a chart with its values. MegaCorp's platform team uses Flux to install each cluster's add-ons, in order, from gitops-config. GitLab's agent for Kubernetes can tell Flux about each push, so that it syncs at once instead of at its next check, but only for public projects and the agent's own project.

Flux's objects#

KindapiVersionWhat it does
GitRepositorysource.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1fetches a repository at a branch or tag, every interval
HelmRepositorysource.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1fetches a chart repository's index
Kustomizationkustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1builds one folder of a source with Kustomize, and applies the result, every interval
HelmReleasehelm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2installs or upgrades a chart, with values, as a Helm release
Receivernotification.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1a webhook that tells Flux to fetch now
Provider and Alertnotification.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta3send Flux's events elsewhere, such as to Grafana or a chat
ImagePolicy and ImageUpdateAutomationimage.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1pick new image tags, and commit them to Git (automation)

Two things share a name. Flux's Kustomization is an object in the cluster that applies a folder. Kustomize's kustomization.yaml is a file in that folder, which says how to build it (chapter 43). A folder without one still works: Flux generates it, for all the manifests in the folder.

How eks-prod's Flux starts#

flux bootstrap gitlab installs Flux in a cluster, and commits two objects that point Flux at the repository it came from:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configclusters/eks-prod/flux-system/gotk-sync.yamlsource
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: flux-system
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m0s
  ref:
    branch: main
  secretRef:
    name: flux-system
  url: https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git
megacorp/platform/gitops-configclusters/eks-prod/flux-system/gotk-sync.yamlsync
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: flux-system
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m0s
  path: ./clusters/eks-prod
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: flux-system

Flux fetches main every minute. At least every ten minutes, it applies ./clusters/eks-prod, and with prune: true it deletes whatever that folder no longer holds. Everything else on the cluster follows from that folder.

Add-ons, then settings, then applications#

eks-prod's folder holds three more Kustomizations. The first installs the add-ons:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configclusters/eks-prod/platform.yamladd-ons
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: add-ons
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  retryInterval: 1m
  path: ./infrastructure/add-ons/base
  prune: true
  wait: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: flux-system

With wait: true, the Kustomization is ready only once every object it applied is healthy. retryInterval retries a failure after a minute, instead of ten. The second waits for the first:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configclusters/eks-prod/platform.yamlconfig
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: config
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  dependsOn:
    - name: add-ons
  interval: 10m
  path: ./infrastructure/config/eks
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: flux-system

dependsOn applies config only after add-ons is ready. The order matters: the ClusterSecretStore in config is a kind that the External Secrets Operator's chart adds, so it can't be applied before that chart is installed. The third, apps, waits for config in the same way, and applies the ApplicationSets that Argo CD turns into applications (chapter 46).

While a dependency isn't ready, flux get kustomizations says so. This is the local cluster, where apps waits directly on add-ons, a minute after Flux started installing the add-ons:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME   	REVISION	SUSPENDED	READY  	MESSAGE                                       
add-ons	        	False    	Unknown	Reconciliation in progress                   	
apps   	        	False    	False  	dependency 'flux-system/add-ons' is not ready

Charts through Flux#

An add-on is a HelmRelease, which names a chart, its version, where to fetch it, and its values:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/add-ons/base/add-ons.yamlexternal-secrets
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: external-secrets
  namespace: external-secrets
spec:
  interval: 30m
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: external-secrets
      version: 2.10.0
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: external-secrets
        namespace: flux-system
  install:
    crds: CreateReplace
  upgrade:
    crds: CreateReplace
  values:
    serviceAccount:
      name: external-secrets

The HelmRepository it names is in the same file. crds: CreateReplace makes Flux create the chart's custom resource definitions, and replace them when a new chart version changes them. By default, Flux creates them on install and skips them on upgrade. Flux installs a real Helm release, so helm list shows it, unlike an Argo CD application (no release in helm list).

Each Helm action has five minutes by default, including the chart's hook Jobs. An install that runs out of time stays failed: Flux tries again only if install.remediation.retries says so, and the default is 0. On the local cluster, Argo CD's first install timed out while its image was still downloading:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAMESPACE       	NAME            	REVISION	SUSPENDED	READY	MESSAGE                                                                                                                                                                               
argocd          	argo-cd         	10.9.0  	False    	False	Helm install failed for release argocd/argo-cd with chart argo-cd@10.9.0: failed pre-install: timeout waiting for: [Job/argocd/argo-cd-argocd-redis-secret-init status: 'InProgress']	
external-secrets	external-secrets	2.10.0  	False    	True 	Helm install succeeded for release external-secrets/external-secrets.v1 with chart external-secrets@2.10.0

With the image in place, flux reconcile helmrelease argo-cd -n argocd --force installed it (a HelmRelease that timed out).

Drift and pruning#

  • Drift. Every ten minutes, a Kustomization compares the cluster with Git, and puts back what differs. The annotation kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/ssa changes that for one object: Override reverts every change, and is the default; Merge keeps fields that other tools added; IfNotPresent creates the object and then leaves it alone.
  • Pruning. With prune: true, objects that Flux applied earlier, but that the current revision no longer holds, are deleted from the cluster.

GitLab's agent, and when Flux syncs#

Left alone, Flux sees a new commit only at its next fetch. GitLab's agent for Kubernetes, in every tier, can shorten that. It finds the GitRepository objects that point at GitLab projects, sets up a Receiver for each, and calls it on every push, so Flux fetches at once. The cluster needs Flux's source and notification controllers as well as the agent.

There's a catch. The agent can reach only its own configuration project and public projects. A private environment repository, like gitops-config, is still synced on Flux's own schedule (deploys appear minutes later).

On the local cluster, once everything had synced, Flux showed this:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME   	REVISION          	SUSPENDED	READY	MESSAGE                              
add-ons	main@sha1:9f3c2960	False    	True 	Applied revision: main@sha1:9f3c2960	
apps   	main@sha1:9f3c2960	False    	True 	Applied revision: main@sha1:9f3c2960
fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAMESPACE       	NAME            	REVISION	SUSPENDED	READY	MESSAGE                                                                                                    
argocd          	argo-cd         	10.9.0  	False    	True 	Helm upgrade succeeded for release argocd/argo-cd.v2 with chart argo-cd@10.9.0                            	
external-secrets	external-secrets	2.10.0  	False    	True 	Helm install succeeded for release external-secrets/external-secrets.v1 with chart external-secrets@2.10.0

The local cluster applies add-ons and apps only: its secret store is a stand-in, so it has no config. Argo CD's release is at revision 2, because its first install timed out and was forced again.

LabLet Flux deploy greeting-serviceabout 20 min#
You need

A cluster from the lab kit, with Flux installed by flux install; the kustomize folder from the Kustomize lab; and the image you pushed in chapter 7. No cluster? Do the first step, then run kustomize build kustomize/overlays/staging: that is exactly what Flux applies, and the expected output shows what it did with it.

Steps
  1. On your GitLab, create a project called greeting-gitops, and push the kustomize folder to it.
  2. Add two deploy tokens, each under Settings › Repository, in Deploy tokens. In greeting-gitops, add one with the read_repository scope, for Flux. In the project that built your image, add one with the read_registry scope, for the cluster. Neither can reach any other project.
  3. Make the namespace, and let its pods pull your image with the second token: 
    kubectl create namespace greeting-staging
kubectl create secret docker-registry gitlab-registry -n greeting-staging \
  --docker-server=<your registry> --docker-username=<pull token's username> --docker-password=<pull token>
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n greeting-staging -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "gitlab-registry"}]}'
  4. Give Flux the first token, then point it at the repository and at staging's overlay: 
    flux create secret git greeting --url=https://<your GitLab>/<your group>/greeting-gitops.git \
  --username=<token's username> --password=<token>
flux create source git greeting --url=https://<your GitLab>/<your group>/greeting-gitops.git \
  --branch=main --secret-ref=greeting --interval=1m
flux create kustomization greeting --source=GitRepository/greeting \
  --path=./kustomize/overlays/staging --prune=true --interval=1m --wait=true
    If your GitLab's certificate comes from a private authority, add --ca-crt-file=<its certificate> to the first command.
  5. List the pods: kubectl get pods -n greeting-staging.
  6. In the overlay, change newTag to another tag of your image, then commit and push. Wait a minute or two, run flux get kustomizations greeting, and list the pods with their images.
What you should see

Flux applies the overlay, and waits until everything it applied is healthy:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
✚ generating Kustomization
► applying Kustomization
✔ Kustomization created
◎ waiting for Kustomization reconciliation
✔ Kustomization greeting is ready
✔ applied revision main@sha1:dde381ae59c419f817c765433d13371b651adf72

Two pods run, as the overlay's patch says:

kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
greeting-b7f6b6f75-fhvgq   1/1     Running   0          17s
greeting-b7f6b6f75-x8cgt   1/1     Running   0          17s

After the push, the Kustomization shows the new commit, and the pods run the new tag:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME    	REVISION          	SUSPENDED	READY	MESSAGE                              
greeting	main@sha1:fd092043	False    	True 	Applied revision: main@sha1:fd092043
kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME                        IMAGE
greeting-744b5b7bc4-lnq5g   gitlab.example.com:5050/practice/node-service:7d625fae
greeting-744b5b7bc4-wwtwm   gitlab.example.com:5050/practice/node-service:7d625fae
When you write it

For each Flux Kustomization you add, set prune: true, so that a file deleted from Git is deleted from the cluster. Add dependsOn when it needs another Kustomization's objects first, and wait: true when others depend on it. Keep its interval at a minute or more: that's Flux's minimum.

Spot the bugThe setting that waited#

A merge request adds a second ClusterSecretStore to infrastructure/config/eks. Twenty minutes after it was merged, the store still isn't on eks-prod. The add-ons Kustomization shows the External Secrets Operator's HelmRelease failing, since a chart upgrade that someone merged the day before.

megacorp/platform/gitops-configclusters/eks-prod/platform.yamlconfig
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: config
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  dependsOn:
    - name: add-ons
  interval: 10m
  path: ./infrastructure/config/eks
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: flux-system
QuestionWhy hasn't the new store appeared, and what do you fix first?
Show the answer

config depends on add-ons, and add-ons waits for the health of everything it applied. While the HelmRelease fails, add-ons isn't ready, so Flux never applies config, whatever it holds. Fix the failing HelmRelease first; config follows by itself (a Kustomization waiting for another).

Next46Argo CD5 min

Argo CD#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 46· 5 min read

Argo CD keeps applications in a cluster in step with Git, and shows them in a web UI. An Application names what to deploy, from which repositories, to which cluster and namespace. An ApplicationSet makes Applications from a template, such as one for each environment. Every Application has two statuses: sync, which compares the cluster with Git, and health, which says whether what runs works. MegaCorp's teams deploy with Argo CD: the payments team's ApplicationSet makes payments-api's Applications, for staging and production, on each cluster.

Argo CD's objects#

KindWhat it saysAt MegaCorp
AppProjectwhich repositories a team's Applications may use, where they may deploy, and which cluster-wide kinds they may createpayments: the charts and gitops-config, into payments-* namespaces, which it may create (a namespace the project doesn't allow)
Applicationone set of objects: its sources, its destination, and how to syncmade by the ApplicationSet, one for each environment
ApplicationSeta template, and a generator that fills it in to make Applicationspayments-api, with a list of two environments

All three are argoproj.io/v1alpha1 objects in the argocd namespace, where Argo CD runs.

payments-api's ApplicationSet#

megacorp/platform/gitops-configapps/eks-prod/applicationset.yamlproject
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  description: The payments team's services
  sourceRepos:
    - https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/charts.git
    - https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git
  destinations:
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: payments-*
  # CreateNamespace makes each environment's Namespace, which is cluster-wide, so the
  # project must allow that kind, and only with the team's names
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Namespace
      name: payments-*
megacorp/platform/gitops-configapps/eks-prod/applicationset.yamlapplicationset
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - env: staging
          - env: production
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "payments-api-{{ .env }}"
      annotations:
        notifications.argoproj.io/subscribe.on-deployed.grafana: "payments-api|{{ .env }}"
    spec:
      project: payments
      sources:
        - repoURL: https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/charts.git
          targetRevision: service-3.4.0
          path: service
          helm:
            releaseName: payments-api
            valueFiles:
              - "$values/envs/{{ .env }}/payments-api.yaml"
        - repoURL: https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git
          targetRevision: main
          ref: values
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "payments-{{ .env }}"
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true
  • The list generator gives two elements, staging and production. The template is filled in once for each, with {{ .env }} replaced.
  • There are two sources. The first is the shared chart, at the tag service-3.4.0. The second is gitops-config itself, named values, so that the chart's valueFiles can start with $values and read each environment's file from it.
  • The destination, https://kubernetes.default.svc, is the cluster Argo CD runs in, and the namespace is made if it's missing.
  • The sync policy is automated, with pruning and self-healing.

Sync and health#

StatusMeans
Syncedthe cluster matches Git, at the revision shown
OutOfSyncsomething in the cluster differs from Git: a new commit, or a change by hand
Healthyevery object works; a Deployment is healthy once all its pods are updated and ready
Progressingnot healthy yet, but still making progress
Degradedsomething has failed, such as a Deployment whose rollout missed its deadline
Suspendedwaiting for something outside to resume it
Missingthe object isn't in the cluster
UnknownArgo CD can't judge the object's health

The two are separate. An Application can be Synced and Degraded: Git and the cluster agree, and what they agree on doesn't work. An Application takes the worst health of its objects.

How it syncs#

Argo CD checks Git about every two minutes, with up to a minute's random delay added. With automated sync, it syncs any Application that is OutOfSync. Two options, both off by default, make it stricter: prune deletes objects that Git no longer holds, and selfHeal puts back a change made by hand, about five seconds after it happens.

Within a sync, objects can go in order. The annotation argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave gives an object a wave number, 0 by default; lower waves go first. argocd.argoproj.io/hook turns an object into a hook that runs at a phase of the sync, such as a Job that migrates a database before anything else changes:

metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync

Values, and what wins#

Argo CD renders a chart itself, with helm template, and applies the result, so no Helm release exists (no release in helm list). When the same value is set in several places, the order is: parameters, then inline valuesObject, then inline values, then value files, then the chart's own values.yaml. On aks-prod, the ApplicationSet sets the image's repository inline, so it beats the values file's:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configapps/aks-prod/applicationset.yamlazure-values
valuesObject:
  image:
    repository: megacorpprod.azurecr.io/payments-api
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      azure.workload.identity/client-id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  podLabels:
    azure.workload.identity/use: "true"

In the UI, and from the command line#

The UI shows each Application with its sync and health, and a tree of the objects it made, down to the pods. From there you can sync by hand, see what differs from Git, and run built-in actions such as restarting a Deployment. Argo CD's notifications can also mark each deploy on your dashboards (chapter 51).

argocd app get shows the same from the command line. This is payments-api in staging on the local cluster, with each object's sync and health:

argocdoutputcaptured at the baseline
Name:               argocd/payments-api-staging
Project:            payments
Server:             https://kubernetes.default.svc
Namespace:          payments-staging
URL:                https://argocd.example.com/applications/payments-api-staging
Sources:
- Repo:             https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/charts.git
  Target:           service-3.4.0
  Path:             service
  Helm Values:      $values/envs/staging/payments-api.yaml
- Repo:             https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/gitops-config.git
  Target:           main
  Ref:              values
SyncWindow:         Sync Allowed
Sync Policy:        Automated (Prune)
Sync Status:        Synced to service-3.4.0
Health Status:      Healthy

GROUP                KIND            NAMESPACE         NAME              STATUS   HEALTH   HOOK  MESSAGE
                     Namespace                         payments-staging  Running  Synced         namespace/payments-staging created

LabThe same service, with Argo CDabout 15 min#
You need

The cluster and the project from the Flux lab, and Argo CD on the cluster. Install it from the chart MegaCorp's platform team uses:

helm install argo-cd argo-cd --repo https://argoproj.github.io/argo-helm --version 10.9.0 \
  --namespace argocd --create-namespace

No cluster? Read the steps and the expected output: Argo CD applies the same overlay that kustomize build shows.

Steps
  1. Let Flux let go of greeting-service. With pruning on, deleting the Kustomization deletes what it applied: 
    flux delete kustomization greeting --silent
flux delete source git greeting --silent
  2. Use the argocd command through your kube context, without logging in to a server: 
    kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=argocd
argocd login --core
  3. Give Argo CD the repository's deploy token, then create the application: 
    argocd repo add https://<your GitLab>/<your group>/greeting-gitops.git \
  --username <token's username> --password <token>
argocd app create greeting --repo https://<your GitLab>/<your group>/greeting-gitops.git \
  --path kustomize/overlays/staging --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc \
  --dest-namespace greeting-staging --sync-policy automated --auto-prune --self-heal
    If your GitLab's certificate comes from a private authority, run argocd cert add-tls <its host name> --from <its certificate> first.
  4. Wait a minute, then run argocd app get greeting.
What you should see
argocdoutputcaptured at the baseline
application 'greeting' created

The application is Synced and Healthy, with the objects it made:

argocdoutputcaptured at the baseline

       Service     greeting-staging  greeting  Synced  Healthy        service/greeting created
