When you write it

For an Application you own, turn on automated sync with prune and selfHeal, so that Git stays the truth. Keep settings in value files, and use inline values only for what really differs between clusters, where reviewers will look for it.

Spot the bugSynced, and Degraded#

After a deploy, payments-api-staging shows Synced and Progressing for ten minutes. Then it shows Synced and Degraded. Nobody has changed anything since the deploy's commit.

QuestionWhat do the two statuses tell you, and where do you look next?
Show the answer

Synced means the cluster matches the deploy's commit: Argo CD did its part. Degraded means what it applied doesn't work. The Deployment was Progressing while its new pods weren't ready, and after its ten-minute deadline it counts as failed. Look at the new pods: their events and logs say why they never became ready (a rollout stuck half-way).

Next47OpenTofu and Terraform5 min

OpenTofu and Terraform#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 47· 5 min read

The clusters, registries and identities that delivery runs on are made from code, with OpenTofu or Terraform. The platform team writes modules; a root configuration calls them with inputs; plan shows what would change, and apply makes it so. The state records what exists, and a lock lets only one run write it at a time. You met plan-in-a-merge-request and apply-on-merge in Part II. This chapter adds what surrounds them: modules, reading a plan, the state's lock, and who changes what.

Two names, one language#

OpenTofu is a community fork of Terraform. It is open source, under the Mozilla Public License, and has been a CNCF Sandbox project since April 2025. Terraform is under the Business Source License. The two read the same language, HCL, and most configurations work in both. Where they differ, you will notice:

WhatOpenTofuTerraform
the commandtofuterraform
where hashicorp/aws comes fromregistry.opentofu.orgregistry.terraform.io
.tofu filesread; a .tofu file wins over a .tf file of the same namenot read
the licenceMozilla Public License 2.0Business Source License 1.1

OpenTofu can also encrypt state and plan files. The rest of this chapter says OpenTofu, and means both.

Modules, and the root configuration#

A module is a folder of .tf files with inputs, called variables, and outputs. MegaCorp's platform team keeps one for each cloud in infra-modules. This is what the AWS one asks for:

megacorp/platform/infra-modulesaws/main.tfinputs
variable "cluster_name" {
  type = string
}

variable "kubernetes_version" {
  type    = string
  default = "1.36"
}

variable "subnet_ids" {
  type = list(string)
}

variable "repositories" {
  description = "ECR repositories to create, such as payments-api"
  type        = set(string)
}

variable "workloads" {
  description = "Pods that get an AWS role, keyed by name, each with its namespace and service account"
  type = map(object({
    namespace       = string
    service_account = string
  }))
}

For each workload, it makes an IAM role that EKS Pod Identity hands to that namespace's service account:

megacorp/platform/infra-modulesaws/main.tfidentity
resource "aws_iam_role" "workload" {
  for_each = var.workloads
  name     = "${var.cluster_name}-${each.key}"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect    = "Allow"
      Principal = { Service = "pods.eks.amazonaws.com" }
      Action    = ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }]
  })
}

resource "aws_eks_pod_identity_association" "workload" {
  for_each        = var.workloads
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  namespace       = each.value.namespace
  service_account = each.value.service_account
  role_arn        = aws_iam_role.workload[each.key].arn
}

A module does nothing on its own. A root configuration, the folder where you run tofu plan, calls it with inputs. MegaCorp's is infra-live. It names each module's Git repository and a tag, so a module's new version reaches production only when someone changes the tag:

megacorp/platform/infra-livemain.tfeks
module "eks_prod" {
  source       = "git::https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/platform/infra-modules.git//aws?ref=aws-2.3.0"
  cluster_name = "eks-prod"
  subnet_ids   = ["subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718", "subnet-0b2c3d4e5f6071829"]

  repositories = ["payments-api", "web-portal"]
  workloads = {
    payments-api-staging    = { namespace = "payments-staging", service_account = "payments-api" }
    payments-api-production = { namespace = "payments-production", service_account = "payments-api" }
  }
}

Reading a plan in a merge request#

A plan starts each change with a symbol. + creates, - destroys, and ~ changes in place. -/+ destroys and creates again, because something that can't change in place did. Here is team-infra's plan from chapter 9:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ tofu plan -input=false -out=plan.cache
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
random_pet.queue: Refreshing state... [id=payments-helped-sunfish]
OpenTofu used the selected providers to generate the following execution
plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following symbols:
-/+ destroy and then create replacement
OpenTofu will perform the following actions:
  # random_pet.queue must be replaced
-/+ resource "random_pet" "queue" {
      ~ id        = "payments-helped-sunfish" -> (known after apply)
      ~ length    = 2 -> 3 # forces replacement
        # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
    }
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Changes to Outputs:
  ~ queue_name = "payments-helped-sunfish" -> (known after apply)
⋯ lines omitted
Saved the plan to: plan.cache
⋯ lines omitted
Releasing state lock. This may take a few moments...
⋯ lines omitted
plan.json: found 1 matching artifact files and directories
Uploading artifacts as "terraform" to coordinator... 201 Created  correlation_id=01M2DR15CECXP68NQ0SWZNPXZ2 id=303 status=201 token=[REDACTED]
⋯ lines omitted
Job succeeded

Read every must be replaced line before you merge. For a random name, a replacement costs nothing. For a database, a registry or a cluster, it can mean losing what it held. # forces replacement marks the line that caused it, and the counts at the end are what the merge request shows.

State, and its lock#

The state is OpenTofu's record of what it has made. A team's state lives remotely: in GitLab, as in Part II, or in cloud storage. While a run writes it, the backend locks it, so a second run can't write at the same time. That second run stops at once:

GitLab ranjob logcaptured from GitLab
⋯ lines omitted
$ tofu plan -input=false -out=plan.cache
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
╷
│ Error: Error acquiring the state lock
│
│ Error message: HTTP remote state already locked:
│ ID=5b0e8c3a-7d2f-4c1e-9a64-3f8b2d1c0e97
│ Lock Info:
│   ID:        5b0e8c3a-7d2f-4c1e-9a64-3f8b2d1c0e97
│   Path:
│   Operation: OperationTypePlan
│   Who:       root
│   Version:   1.12.6
│   Created:   2026-09-13 20:23:16.966 +0000 UTC
│   Info:
│
│
│ OpenTofu acquires a state lock to protect the state from being written
│ by multiple users at the same time. Please resolve the issue above and try
│ again. For most commands, you can disable locking with the "-lock=false"
│ flag, but this is not recommended.
╵
⋯ lines omitted
ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1

Only three lines describe the lock that's in the way: ID, Who and Created. With GitLab-managed state, Who is the GitLab user whose job took the lock. The other lines describe your own run: GitLab fills Operation and Version in from the request that failed, which is why this blocked plan says OperationTypePlan.

Usually the other run is still going, and waiting is the fix. A lock can outlive its run, though, when an apply is cancelled or its runner dies. Then:

  1. Make sure no job is still running against this state.
  2. Unlock it. In GitLab, open Operate › Terraform states, and use the state's Actions menu; this needs the Maintainer or Owner role. Or run tofu force-unlock <ID>, which removes the lock without changing any resources.
  3. Run the pipeline again, and read its plan: the interrupted apply may have done part of its work.

Don't reach for -lock=false. It lets two runs write the same state, and the second overwrites what the first recorded.

What your team changes, and what the platform team owns#

You wantWhere the change goesWho applies it
a registry repository for a new servicean entry in infra-live's repositoriesthe platform team, after reviewing your merge request
a cloud identity for your podsan entry in infra-live's workloadsthe platform team, likewise
a queue, bucket or database of your ownyour team's root configuration, if your organisation has one, calling the platform's modulesyour team's pipeline, as in the Build part
the cluster, its nodes, its networknowhere you can changethe platform team

So a team's usual change is a small merge request to someone else's repository. Read the plan in it as carefully as your own.

When you write it

Pin every module to a tag, never to a branch. Read every must be replaced line in a plan before merging. Never edit a state file by hand, and never apply with -lock=false: unlock a stale lock deliberately instead.

Spot the bugLocked for forty minutes#

team-infra's plan job fails with the lock error above. Its Created time was forty minutes ago. The project's pipelines show an apply job that was cancelled forty minutes ago, and nothing running now.

QuestionWhat happened, and what do you do, in which order?
Show the answer

The cancelled apply took the lock and never released it, so the lock outlived its run. With nothing running, unlock the state: Operate › Terraform states, the state's Actions menu, Unlock, or tofu force-unlock with the lock's ID. Then run the pipeline again, and read the new plan before anything applies: the cancelled apply may have made some of its changes. Don't use -lock=false to get past it.

See state locked.

Next48AWS and Azure for delivery4 min

AWS and Azure for delivery#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 48· 4 min read

EKS and AKS are Kubernetes run for you by AWS and by Azure. For a pipeline owner, what differs between them is identity: how a pod gets the right to read a secret or a bucket, and how a pipeline signs in when it must. Neither needs a stored password. A pod proves who it is with its service account's token, and a job with its GitLab ID token; the cloud checks that token against a trust set up once. MegaCorp runs the same service on both clouds, so this chapter shows each thing side by side.

The same service on two clouds#

WhatAWSAzure
the clusterEKSAKS
the registryECRACR
a job's identityan IAM role that trusts GitLab's ID tokensan Entra app with a federated credential for GitLab
a pod's identityEKS Pod Identity, or IRSA on older setupsAKS workload identity
secretsSecrets ManagerKey Vault
logs and metricsCloudWatchAzure Monitor

How a pod gets a cloud identity#

On both clouds, the identity belongs to a Kubernetes service account, in its namespace. Every pod that runs as that service account gets it.

With EKS Pod Identity, the link is made in AWS, not in the cluster: an association says that one namespace's service account gets one IAM role. MegaCorp's AWS module makes a role and an association for each workload:

megacorp/platform/infra-modulesaws/main.tfidentity
resource "aws_iam_role" "workload" {
  for_each = var.workloads
  name     = "${var.cluster_name}-${each.key}"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect    = "Allow"
      Principal = { Service = "pods.eks.amazonaws.com" }
      Action    = ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
    }]
  })
}

resource "aws_eks_pod_identity_association" "workload" {
  for_each        = var.workloads
  cluster_name    = aws_eks_cluster.this.name
  namespace       = each.value.namespace
  service_account = each.value.service_account
  role_arn        = aws_iam_role.workload[each.key].arn
}

The role trusts pods.eks.amazonaws.com, and an agent on each node hands its credentials to the pods. Nothing in the chart changes. Older setups use IRSA instead. You can tell by an eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation on the service account, and a role that trusts the cluster's own OIDC provider, checking system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

AKS workload identity needs three things to line up:

  • the service account's azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation, naming the managed identity;
  • the pod's label azure.workload.identity/use: "true", without which AKS doesn't give the pod its token;
  • a federated credential on that identity, with the cluster's issuer, the subject system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, and the audience api://AzureADTokenExchange.
megacorp/platform/infra-modulesazure/main.tfidentity
resource "azurerm_user_assigned_identity" "workload" {
  for_each            = var.workloads
  name                = "${var.cluster_name}-${each.key}"
  resource_group_name = var.resource_group_name
  location            = var.location
}

resource "azurerm_federated_identity_credential" "workload" {
  for_each  = var.workloads
  name      = each.key
  parent_id = azurerm_user_assigned_identity.workload[each.key].id
  issuer    = azurerm_kubernetes_cluster.this.oidc_issuer_url
  subject   = "system:serviceaccount:${each.value.namespace}:${each.value.service_account}"
  audience  = ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]
}

In MegaCorp's chart, aks-prod's ApplicationSet sets the first two, through its inline values (values: the defaults, then yours).

So payments-api in payments-staging and in payments-production get different identities, even from the same chart: the namespace is part of the match.

How a pipeline signs in#

A job presents its GitLab ID token, and assumes a role whose trust policy checks the token's audience and subject. Chapter 37 covers it, with the five things that must match (five things that must match).

The job declares an ID token and hands it to the Azure CLI:

id_tokens:
  GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN:
    aud: https://gitlab.example.com
script:
  - az login --service-principal -u "$AZURE_CLIENT_ID" -t "$AZURE_TENANT_ID" --federated-token "$GITLAB_OIDC_TOKEN"

Entra ID accepts the token when one of the app's federated credentials matches its issuer, subject and audience:

azureentra.ymlapp-registration
# The identity that image jobs sign in as. Each federated credential names one kind of
# pipeline that may use it.
acr_push_app:
  display_name: gitlab-acr-push
  client_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  tenant_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  federated_credentials:
    - name: payments-api-main
      issuer: https://gitlab.example.com
      subject: project_path:megacorp/payments/payments-api:ref_type:branch:ref:main
      audiences: [https://gitlab.example.com]

The match is exact: Entra allows no wildcards in a credential. So each kind of pipeline that signs in needs a credential of its own, one for main, another for each tag or environment, and an app can have at most 20. A token that matches none fails with AADSTS70021: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion. So does one that arrives just after its credential was added, before the credential has spread through Entra.

When a pipeline reaches a cluster#

With GitOps, a pipeline never touches the cluster. When a job must, for a push deploy or to run kubectl, it needs three things:

StepAWSAzure
sign inassume the job's roleaz login with the ID token
get a kubeconfigaws eks update-kubeconfig --name <cluster>az aks get-credentials, then kubelogin convert-kubeconfig -l azurecli
permissions in the clusteran EKS access entry for the role, with an access policy or a Kubernetes groupKubernetes roles, or Azure roles if the cluster uses them, for the identity

GitLab's agent for Kubernetes is the other way in: its ci_access gives jobs a kubeconfig without any cloud credentials for the cluster (GitLab's agent for Kubernetes).

When you write it

Give each environment's service account its own identity, and keep the namespace in every trust. On Azure, add a federated credential for each branch, tag or environment that signs in, and remember the limit of 20. Use an ID token instead of cloud keys in CI/CD variables whenever the cloud accepts one.

Spot the bugKey Vault works on one cluster only#

ExternalSecrets sync on eks-prod, but none sync on aks-prod: the External Secrets Operator there can't sign in to Key Vault. Its HelmRelease comes from aks-prod's add-ons overlay.

QuestionWhich things must line up for the Operator to get its Azure identity, and where is each one set?
Show the answer

Three things, from the Operator's side, and one more in Azure:

  • the service account's azure.workload.identity/client-id annotation, and
  • the pods' azure.workload.identity/use: "true" label, both set by the overlay's patch (a patch as part of an object);
  • a federated credential on the managed identity for system:serviceaccount:external-secrets:external-secrets, with the audience api://AzureADTokenExchange, made with the platform team's OpenTofu;
  • and a role on the vault, such as Key Vault Secrets User, for that identity.

Check them in that order. A missing label is the quietest: the pod starts, but gets no token.

See a pod without its Azure identity.

Next49Secrets and config after the pipeline4 min

Secrets and config after the pipeline#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 49· 4 min read

A pipeline's secrets live in CI/CD variables. A running service's secrets can't: they must reach its pods without ever being written into Git in plain text. There are three common ways. An operator copies them from the cloud's vault into the cluster, which is MegaCorp's way. The environment repository holds them encrypted. Or the service reads the vault itself. Settings that aren't secret go in the environment's values file. Either way, a running pod keeps the values it started with: a new value needs new pods.

How a secret reaches a pod#

WayGit holdsWho fetches or decryptsYou'll see
copied from the cloud's vaultan ExternalSecret: which keys, from which storethe External Secrets Operator, with its own cloud identityExternalSecret and ClusterSecretStore objects
encrypted with SOPSthe Secret, with its values encryptedFlux, with a key it holdsENC[AES256_GCM,… values and a sops: block
sealed with Sealed Secretsa SealedSecretthe Sealed Secrets controller in the clusterkind: SealedSecret, from bitnami.com/v1alpha1
read by the service itselfnothingthe service, with its own cloud identitythe vault's address in the service's settings

Whichever way it arrives, a Kubernetes Secret is not encrypted by default. It is stored base64-encoded, and anyone who may read Secrets in the namespace can read it. So who may read Secrets there matters as much as how they got there.

The External Secrets Operator#

Each MegaCorp cluster has one store, called cloud-secrets on both, so a service's values don't change between clouds:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/config/eks/secret-store.yamlstore
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: cloud-secrets
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: eu-west-2
megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/config/aks/secret-store.yamlstore
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: cloud-secrets
spec:
  provider:
    azurekv:
      authType: WorkloadIdentity
      vaultUrl: https://megacorp-prod-kv.vault.azure.net
      serviceAccountRef:
        name: external-secrets
        namespace: external-secrets

A service's values file names the keys it needs, and the shared chart turns them into an ExternalSecret:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/externalsecret.yamlexternalsecret
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "service.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: {{ required "secrets.store names the ClusterSecretStore" .Values.secrets.store }}
  target:
    name: {{ include "service.name" . }}
  data:
    {{- range .Values.secrets.keys }}
    - secretKey: {{ .name }}
      remoteRef:
        key: {{ .remote }}
    {{- end }}

The Operator reads each key from the vault, and writes a Secret with the service's name in its namespace. It reads again every refreshInterval, an hour here. The Deployment reads that Secret as environment variables, through envFrom.

On the local cluster, a Fake store stands in for the vault, under the same name, cloud-secrets. The ExternalSecret reports that it synced, and the Secret it made holds one key:

kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME           STORETYPE            STORE           REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS         READY   LAST SYNC
payments-api   ClusterSecretStore   cloud-secrets   1h                 SecretSynced   True    14m
kubectloutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME           TYPE     DATA   AGE
payments-api   Opaque   1      14m

Secrets encrypted in Git#

Some teams keep secrets in the environment repository, encrypted, so that Git holds everything the cluster needs.

  • SOPS encrypts the values in a file and leaves the keys readable, with a key from age, OpenPGP or a cloud's key service. A .sops.yaml file says which files and fields to encrypt, and with which key. Flux decrypts them when a Kustomization has decryption: provider: sops.
  • Sealed Secrets encrypts a whole Secret with the public key of a controller running in the cluster, using kubeseal. Only that controller can decrypt it. By default, a SealedSecret works only under the name and namespace it was sealed for, so it can't be copied into another namespace and read there.

Config for each environment#

Settings that aren't secret belong in the environment's values file, where reviewers can read them:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configenvs/staging/payments-api.yamlsettings
env:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: staging
  PAYMENTS_PROVIDER_URL: https://sandbox.pay.example.com
secrets:
  store: cloud-secrets
  keys:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      remote: payments-api/staging/db-password
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: payments.staging.example.com

MegaCorp's chart writes env into the Deployment's pod template. So a changed setting changes the template, and Kubernetes rolls out new pods with it. A ConfigMap works differently. A pod that reads one as environment variables keeps the old values until it restarts. Mounted as files, a ConfigMap is refreshed after a while. Secrets behave the same way: a rotated secret reaches a running pod's variables only when the pod restarts.

When you write it

Name secrets in an ExternalSecret, and keep their values out of Git. Give the store the same name on every cluster. Keep settings out of Secrets and secrets out of ConfigMaps. After a secret is rotated, make sure the pods restart, or read it from a mounted file that the service reads again.

Spot the bugThe old password, an hour later#

At 09:00, payments-api's database password is rotated in Key Vault. At 09:40, and again at 10:15, payments-api's staging pods on aks-prod still use the old password. Nobody has restarted anything.

QuestionWhy, and what gets the new password to the pods?
Show the answer

Two waits add up. The ExternalSecret reads the vault once an hour, so the Secret in the namespace can change up to an hour after the rotation. Then the pods read that Secret as environment variables, which never change in a running pod: they keep the old value until they restart. Once the Secret holds the new password, new pods get it. They start on the next deploy that changes the pod template, or when someone restarts the Deployment. With Argo CD, use its built-in restart action on the Deployment, from the UI or with argocd app actions run (config for each environment).

See old values in running pods.

Next50Releasing safely3 min

Releasing safely#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 50· 3 min read

A release is the moment new pods start taking real traffic. Kubernetes' default is a rolling update: it swaps pods a few at a time, and only counts a new pod once its readiness probe passes, so a broken version stalls instead of taking everything down. Blue-green starts a whole copy of the new version and switches traffic at once. Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and grows it while checks pass. Both need a tool such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger. Approvals come before a release, and going back is a revert in Git.

Rolling, the default#

MegaCorp's shared chart doesn't name a strategy, so every Deployment rolls. Kubernetes starts new pods and stops old ones in steps. By default it runs at most a quarter more pods than it should, and keeps at least three quarters of them available. A new pod counts only when its readiness probe passes:

megacorp/platform/chartsservice/templates/deployment.yamlprobes
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
    port: http
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
    port: http
  initialDelaySeconds: 20
resources:
  {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}

So a version whose pods never become ready doesn't replace the old one: the old pods keep serving, and the rollout waits. After ten minutes without progress, the Deployment reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. It does not roll back by itself. With GitOps, you go back by reverting the deploy's commit (drift, and going back).

A readiness probe that checks too little, such as one that always answers, takes that safety away. A pod then counts as ready while it can't serve anyone.

Blue-green and canary#

Kubernetes has no blue-green or canary of its own. Two tools add them, one from each side of GitOps:

ToolYou'll seeWhere the canary's share is set
Argo Rollouts, from the Argo projecta Rollout object in place of the DeploymentsetWeight in its steps
Flagger, from the Flux projecta Canary object beside the DeploymentstepWeight, up to maxWeight, in its analysis

A canary in Argo Rollouts is a list of steps: send some traffic, wait, check, send more.

strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
      - setWeight: 20
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - analysis:
          templates:
            - templateName: success-rate
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause: {}
  • setWeight: 20 sends a fifth of the traffic to the new version. With a traffic router, such as a service mesh or an ingress controller, that share is exact. Without one, Argo Rollouts gets close by running a fifth of the pods on the new version.
  • analysis runs the checks an AnalysisTemplate describes, such as a success rate from Prometheus. If they fail, the rollout aborts, and all traffic goes back to the stable version.
  • pause: {} waits for a person, who continues with kubectl argo rollouts promote.

Blue-green in Argo Rollouts uses two Services: activeService for real traffic, and previewService, which points at the new version while it is tested. The switch happens on promotion. Flagger does the same with a Canary object, and needs a traffic router for its weights.

Approvals, and going back#

GateWhere
merging production's merge request in the environment repositorythe environment repository's branch protection (promotion by merge request)
promoting a paused canary or blue-greenkubectl argo rollouts promote
approving a GitLab deployment jobGitLab environments, where approvals are Premium (environments and deployments)

Going back depends on how far the release got. A canary that fails its checks goes back by itself. Anything already released goes back by reverting its commit in the environment repository, so the controller deploys the old version again, and the history says so. kubectl rollout undo would be undone by the controller.

When you write it

Give every service a readiness probe that checks what the service needs to serve, not just that the process is up. Keep the default rolling update unless your team runs Argo Rollouts or Flagger. When a release goes wrong, revert the commit in the environment repository.

Spot the bugHalf a release#

payments-api's new version reaches staging with 4 replicas. Ten minutes later, 3 pods run the old version and 1 runs the new one, which restarts again and again. The service still answers.

QuestionWhat is Kubernetes doing, why does the service still work, and what do you do?
Show the answer

A rolling update is stuck. The new pod never passes its readiness probe, so Kubernetes won't count it or stop more old pods, and the old pods keep serving. After ten minutes the Deployment reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded, but it doesn't roll back by itself. Find out why the new pod restarts from its events and logs, then revert the deploy's commit in the environment repository, or fix forward with a new commit (rolling, the default).

See a rollout stuck half-way.

Next51Observability9 min

Observability#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 51· 9 min read

Once a deploy is out, its signals say whether it works. Logs record what happened, one event at a time. Metrics count things over time, such as requests, errors and restarts. Traces follow one request through every service it touches. OpenTelemetry is the common way to produce all three, and a collector sends them to the backends that keep them. In the open, those are Prometheus, Loki and Tempo. On AWS, they're CloudWatch and X-Ray; on Azure, Azure Monitor and Application Insights. You read them on dashboards, where each deploy is marked. A controller that says "synced and healthy" only means the new pods started. The signals say whether they work.

Three signals#

SignalWhat it isIt answersYou'll see
logslines a service writes as things happen, one event eachwhat happened to this request, and why it failedlines on standard output, often as JSON
metricsnumbers counted over time, each with labelshow often, how fast, how manya /metrics page for Prometheus to read, or numbers sent over OTLP
tracesone request's path through the services: a span for each step, all sharing a trace IDwhere the time went, and which service faileda waterfall of spans, one bar per step

A pod's logs are what its containers write to standard output and standard error. Kubernetes keeps them on the node for a while, and kubectl logs reads them from there. To keep them longer and search them, an agent on each node sends them to a backend. Metrics and traces need the service to produce them, usually through a library.

OpenTelemetry and the collector#

OpenTelemetry is a project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. It gives most languages one standard set of APIs, SDKs and tools for producing traces, metrics and logs. It isn't a backend, and stores nothing. Its protocol, OTLP, carries signals to whatever does, on port 4317 over gRPC or 4318 over HTTP.

The OpenTelemetry Collector sits between services and backends. It receives signals, processes them, for example by adding the pod's name, and exports them to one or more backends. So each service sends everything to one address, and the platform team decides where it goes. Each cloud's own agent does a similar job for that cloud's backends.

An OpenTelemetry SDK reads its settings from environment variables, so these are the ones you'll see in a service's values:

VariableWhat it sets
OTEL_SERVICE_NAMEthe service's name, on every signal it sends
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTESmore names and values, such as service.version=3f9c2e1a,deployment.environment.name=staging
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINTwhere to send signals, usually the collector

The open example: Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Tempo#

  • Prometheus keeps metrics. It pulls them: every so often, it reads each service's metrics page over HTTP, which is called scraping. It stores each number with its time and labels, and its query language, PromQL, reads them back. Its rules raise alerts, and Alertmanager sends them to people. A cluster that runs the Prometheus Operator has ServiceMonitor objects, from monitoring.coreos.com/v1. Each one tells Prometheus which Services to scrape, and on which port. A service's chart may include one.
  • Loki keeps logs. It indexes only each stream's labels, such as the namespace and pod, not the text of the lines, which keeps it cheap. Its query language is LogQL.
  • Tempo keeps traces.
  • Grafana shows all three on dashboards, side by side, and can alert on them.

Where each signal lives on AWS and Azure#

SignalOpen exampleAWSAzure
metricsPrometheusCloudWatch, through Container Insights; or Amazon Managed Service for PrometheusAzure Monitor managed service for Prometheus
logsLokiCloudWatch Logsa Log Analytics workspace, through Container insights
tracesTempoX-Ray, sent with OpenTelemetryApplication Insights
dashboardsGrafanaCloudWatch dashboards, or Amazon Managed Grafanathe Azure portal, or Azure Managed Grafana

On EKS, the amazon-cloudwatch-observability add-on installs Container Insights, which collects the cluster's metrics and logs. On AKS, Container insights collects the containers' logs, and managed Prometheus collects metrics. Both clouds point you to OpenTelemetry for traces. AWS put X-Ray's own SDKs and daemon into maintenance mode in February 2026, and recommends OpenTelemetry instead; X-Ray still keeps and shows the traces. Application Insights accepts OpenTelemetry too.

MegaCorp's platform team runs one Grafana, at grafana.example.com, that reads the signals from both clouds, and teams build their dashboards there. GitLab also has tracing, metrics and logs of its own, as an experiment since GitLab 18.1. This book doesn't use them.

Marking each deploy#

A graph that jumps is easier to read when you can see what changed just before. So MegaCorp marks each deploy on Grafana's graphs, as what Grafana calls an annotation. The pipeline can't do this well. With GitOps, it only commits to the environment repository, and never learns when the new pods are ready. The controller does. So Argo CD sends the mark, through its notifications controller, which the platform team sets up in Argo CD's chart values:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/add-ons/base/add-ons.yamlnotifications
notifications:
  secret:
    create: false
  notifiers:
    service.grafana: |
      apiUrl: https://grafana.example.com/api
      apiKey: $grafana-api-key
  triggers:
    trigger.on-deployed: |
      - description: Application is synced and healthy.
        send: [app-deployed]
        oncePer: app.status.operationState?.syncResult?.revision
        when: >-
          app.status.operationState != nil
          and app.status.operationState.phase in ['Succeeded']
          and app.status.health.status == 'Healthy'
          and (!time.Parse(app.status.health.lastTransitionTime).Add(1 * time.Minute).Before(time.Parse(app.status.operationState.finishedAt))
          or time.Parse(app.status.health.lastTransitionTime).Before(time.Parse(app.status.operationState.startedAt)))
  templates:
    template.app-deployed: |
      message: "{{ .app.metadata.name }} is synced and healthy"
  • service.grafana says where to send marks. $grafana-api-key names a key in the notifications Secret, which an ExternalSecret copies from the cloud's vault. That's why secret.create is false: the chart mustn't make the Secret too.
  • trigger.on-deployed is copied from Argo CD's catalog of triggers. It fires once a sync has succeeded and the Application is healthy.
  • template.app-deployed is the mark's text.

Nothing is sent until an Application subscribes. MegaCorp's ApplicationSet subscribes each payments-api Application, with two tags for dashboards to pick marks by:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configapps/eks-prod/applicationset.yamldeploy-marker
annotations:
  notifications.argoproj.io/subscribe.on-deployed.grafana: "payments-api|{{ .env }}"

The key comes from the same store as every other secret:

megacorp/platform/gitops-configinfrastructure/config/eks/secret-store.yamlnotifications-secret
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: argocd-notifications-secret
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: cloud-secrets
  target:
    name: argocd-notifications-secret
  data:
    - secretKey: grafana-api-key
      remoteRef:
        key: platform-grafana-api-key

A dashboard shows the marks by asking for annotations with those tags. Flux can send the same marks, through a Provider of type grafana and an Alert that picks which events to send.

Did my deploy work?#

Go through these in order. Each step needs the one before it, so the first one that fails is where to look.

  1. The change is in the environment repository. For staging, the deploy job's commit is on main. For production, its merge request is merged (promotion by merge request). No commit means the pipeline didn't deploy: read the deploy job's log.
  2. The controller applied that commit. Argo CD shows the Application as Synced to that commit, and Healthy. With Flux, the Kustomization is Ready, and its last applied revision is that commit. If not, the controller's message says why.
  3. The rollout finished. kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api -n payments-staging exits with 0 once every new pod is ready. If the rollout stalls, it ends with error: deployment "payments-api" exceeded its progress deadline, and exits with 1. Then the pods' events and logs say why (rolling, the default).
  4. The pods run the new version. The Deployment's image tag is the one the deploy wrote.
  5. The signals agree. After the deploy's mark, compare the error rate and the response times with before it. Look for restarts, and for new errors in the logs. With service.version set, you can split metrics and traces by version.

Step 2 looks different with each controller. This is greeting-service from the cluster labs, once each controller had applied the pushed commit:

fluxoutputcaptured at the baseline
NAME    	REVISION          	SUSPENDED	READY	MESSAGE                              
greeting	main@sha1:fd092043	False    	True 	Applied revision: main@sha1:fd092043

READY is True, and the revision is the commit that was pushed. While Flux is still applying it, or waiting for what it applied to become healthy, READY is Unknown, with Reconciliation in progress.

argocdoutputcaptured at the baseline
Name:               argocd/greeting
Project:            default
Server:             https://kubernetes.default.svc
Namespace:          greeting-staging
URL:                https://argocd.example.com/applications/greeting
Source:
- Repo:             https://gitlab.example.com/practice/greeting-gitops.git
  Target:           
  Path:             kustomize/overlays/staging
SyncWindow:         Sync Allowed
Sync Policy:        Automated (Prune)
Sync Status:        Synced to  (fd09204)
Health Status:      Healthy

GROUP  KIND        NAMESPACE         NAME      STATUS  HEALTH   HOOK  MESSAGE
       Service     greeting-staging  greeting  Synced  Healthy        service/greeting created
apps   Deployment  greeting-staging  greeting  Synced  Healthy        deployment.apps/greeting created

Sync Status is Synced, to the commit in brackets, and Health Status is Healthy. Each object has its own row, with its own sync and health.

If only the last step fails, the deploy didn't work, even though the controller calls it healthy. Healthy means the pods pass their probes, not that users' requests succeed. Revert the deploy's commit in the environment repository (drift, and going back), or fix forward with a new one.

LabBreak a deploy three waysabout 20 min#
You need

The application from the Argo CD lab, synced and healthy. No cluster? Make each change, run kustomize build kustomize/overlays/staging to see what the cluster would get, and read the signs below, which are what the cluster showed.

Steps
  1. An image that can't be pulled. Set newTag to does-not-exist, then commit and push. Once Argo CD has synced, run kubectl get pods -n greeting-staging, then kubectl describe pod on the new pod. Revert the commit, and push.
  2. A value that makes the pod crash. Add this to the overlay's patches, then commit and push: 
    - target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: greeting
  patch: |-
    - op: add
      path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env
      value:
        - name: PORT
          value: eight-thousand
    Run kubectl get pods -n greeting-staging, then kubectl logs on the new pod with --previous. Revert the commit, and push.
  3. A change made by hand. Run kubectl scale deployment greeting -n greeting-staging --replicas=5. Run kubectl get deployment greeting -n greeting-staging at once, and again 30 seconds later.
What you should see

An image that can't be pulled. The new pod never starts, and the old ones keep serving: a rolling update removes old pods only once new ones are ready.

When you write it

Ask for your Applications to be subscribed to on-deployed, so each deploy is marked on your dashboards. Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, and set service.version to the image tag, so every signal says which version sent it. Write logs to standard output, one event per line. After each deploy, go through the checklist, all the way to the signals.

Spot the bugHealthy, and failing#

At 14:02, payments-api 1c7d4b09 reaches production. Argo CD shows payments-api-production as Synced and Healthy, and all its pods are ready. On the service's Grafana dashboard, a mark tagged payments-api and production appears at 14:03. Just after it, the share of failed requests rises from 0.1% to 4%, and stays there.

QuestionDid the deploy work? What do you check, and what do you do?
Show the answer

No. Healthy means the new pods pass their readiness probes, not that they serve every request. The mark shows the failures started with this deploy. Check the logs and traces of failed requests, split by service.version, to confirm they come from 1c7d4b09. Then revert the deploy's commit in the environment repository, so Argo CD deploys the old version again, or fix forward with a new commit (did my deploy work?). A canary with an analysis step would have stopped this at a small share of the traffic (blue-green and canary).

Next52Around your service5 min

Around your service#

Part IX · After the pipeline · Chapter 52· 5 min read

Some tools shape how your service runs without being in its code or its pipeline. A service mesh puts a proxy in the path of every request between services. It encrypts that traffic, retries failed requests, and can split traffic between two versions. Feature flags turn code on for some users without a deploy: GitLab has its own, and OpenFeature is a standard way to read any tool's flags. A developer portal such as Backstage lists every service, and its templates create new repositories with a pipeline already in them. Each of these leaves fingerprints you can learn to spot.

A service mesh, as you see it#

A service mesh adds a proxy between your service and every service it calls. Your code still calls the other service by its usual address. The proxy adds what the platform team configured: mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splits and metrics. Istio and Linkerd are the common meshes.

You seeWhat it means
a second container in your pod, istio-proxy or linkerd-proxy, so the pod shows 2/2 readythe mesh runs as a sidecar: a proxy container added to each pod
the namespace label istio-injection=enabled, or the annotation linkerd.io/inject: enabledpods created in that namespace get the sidecar
the label istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient, and no extra containerIstio's ambient mode: a proxy on each node handles mutual TLS, and a separate waypoint proxy handles HTTP features
a VirtualService, from networking.istio.io/v1Istio's routes, retries and timeouts for a service
an HTTPRoute, from gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1the Kubernetes Gateway API's routes, a standard that many meshes and ingress controllers read

A sidecar is added when a pod is created, so pods that were already running need a restart to get one. To read your service's own logs in a pod with a sidecar, name its container: kubectl logs with -c.

Mutual TLS means both ends of a connection prove who they are with certificates, and the traffic between them is encrypted. The mesh does it for you. Linkerd, for example, turns it on for all TCP traffic between meshed pods. Each certificate is tied to the pod's service account, and is replaced every day. Your service still speaks plain HTTP to its own proxy.

Retries and timeouts are set in the mesh's routes. By default, Istio retries a failed HTTP request twice, and sets no timeout. A retry is only safe for a request that can be repeated. For a service that takes payments, find out how the mesh retries, and make a repeated request harmless, for example with an idempotency key.

Where a canary's share is set#

Splitting traffic between two versions is a job for the mesh or the ingress controller. The share is a pair of weights on a route. In the Gateway API, a route that sends a tenth of payments-api's traffic to a canary looks like this:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: shop
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: payments-api-stable
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: payments-api-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10

Weights are shares, not percentages: each backend gets its weight divided by the total. Who changes them depends on the setup:

SetupWhere the share is setWho changes it
by handweight in the route, in the environment repositorya person, through a merge request
Argo RolloutssetWeight in the Rollout's stepsArgo Rollouts, which edits the route as each step runs (blue-green and canary)
FlaggerstepWeight and maxWeight in the Canary's analysisFlagger, which edits the route while the checks pass
a feature flag's percent rolloutthe flag's strategy, in GitLabwhoever owns the flag, with no deploy

The last row is different. It splits users, not requests between two versions: both code paths are in the same deploy, and the flag picks one.

Feature flags#

A feature flag lets a deploy carry code that stays off until someone turns it on, for everyone or for some users. So releasing a feature no longer has to happen at the moment you deploy it.

GitLab has feature flags in every tier, under Deploy › Feature flags. Each flag has one or more strategies, and each strategy applies to some environments:

StrategyTurns the flag on for
All userseveryone
Percent rollouta share of page views; you choose whether a user or session keeps the same answer
Percent of usersa share of signed-in users; the application must pass each user's ID
User IDsthe users you list in the strategy
User lista named list of users, kept in GitLab and shared between flags

Your application reads its flags with an Unleash client library, because GitLab's flag API is compatible with Unleash, a feature-flag tool. The client needs the connection details that the Feature flags page shows. It also needs an application name, which must be the environment's name, such as production, not the service's. A self-managed GitLab allows 200 flags per project; GitLab.com allows 50, 150 or 200, by tier.

OpenFeature, an incubating project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, is a standard API for reading flags from any flag tool. Your code calls OpenFeature, and a provider translates each call for the tool in use. So changing tools doesn't change your code.

Old flags are debt. Once a feature is on for everyone, remove its flag and the code path it turned off.

Developer portals, and where a pipeline came from#

A developer portal is a website that lists every service and who owns it, with links to its repository, pipelines and dashboards. Backstage is the common one. Spotify created it, and it is now an incubating project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. MegaCorp's portal knows payments-api from this file at the root of its repository:

megacorp/payments/payments-apicatalog-info.yamlcatalog
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  description: Takes card payments for MegaCorp's shop
  annotations:
    backstage.io/source-template: template:default/java-service
    backstage.io/source-location: url:https://gitlab.example.com/megacorp/payments/payments-api/
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:default/payments

The portal's software templates create new repositories. A template copies a skeleton of files and fills in the names you type. Its publish:gitlab step pushes the new repository to GitLab, and its catalog:register step adds the new catalog-info.yaml to the portal. The skeleton usually includes a .gitlab-ci.yml, so a new service has a pipeline from its first commit.

A template copies files once. It isn't an include: when the platform team improves a template, repositories made from it earlier don't change. That's why MegaCorp's templates write a .gitlab-ci.yml that includes the golden pipeline, instead of copying its jobs (include: pulling in files). A pipeline that came from a template has these fingerprints:

  • a catalog-info.yaml at the root, with a backstage.io/source-template annotation that names the template
  • a first commit called initial commit, by the author Scaffolder, unless the template changed those defaults
  • a pipeline file that matches other services' files, comments and all
When you write it

If a portal template made your repository, change its pipeline in your repository. If the fix belongs in the template too, tell the platform team. Turn a new flag on in staging before production, and remove it once its feature is fully on. Before you rely on the mesh's retries, check that your requests can be repeated safely.

Spot the bugThe fix that never arrived#

billing-api's .gitlab-ci.yml has a sonar job written out in full. Last month, the platform team fixed a bug in that job in the portal's "Java service" template. billing-api's pipeline still runs the old job. Its repository has a catalog-info.yaml with backstage.io/source-template: template:default/java-service.

QuestionWhy didn't the fix reach billing-api, and where do you fix it?
Show the answer

The annotation shows that the portal's template created billing-api. A template copies its files once, so billing-api's .gitlab-ci.yml has been its own copy since then, and later changes to the template don't reach it. Fix the job in billing-api's own file. Better still, have the job come from the golden pipeline or a component that the file includes, so later fixes arrive with a version bump (developer portals, and where a pipeline came from).

The words a platform team uses, one row each: what the thing is, why you care as a developer, and where you'll meet it. Where a chapter covers a word, the last column links there. Search finds every row.

Next · Part X54The decoding method3 min

The decoding method#

Part X · Decode and debug · Chapter 54· 3 min read

Everything about a pipeline job comes down to five questions: where it is defined, when it runs, where it runs, what it executes, and what goes in and out. Chapter 1 named them. This chapter turns them into a procedure you can follow on any job in any organisation, and shows it on one of MegaCorp's jobs from start to finish. A deploy gets the same five questions, asked of the cluster instead of the pipeline.

When something is already wrong, start from the symptom instead. The decision tree at the end sends you to the right chapter of symptom cards.

The five questions, in order#

QuestionLook first atThenChapters
Where is it defined?the job's name in the pipeline graph, then Full configurationits extends chain, !reference tags and includes; if it's in no file, policies and settings11–19
When does it run?workflow:rules, then the job's own final rulesneeds and stages; compare pipeline types in a truth table20–24
Where does it run?the job's page: the runner's name and tagsthe runner's executor, and the job's image28–29
What does it execute?before_script, script and after_script in Full configurationthe scripts, functions and tools those lines call inside the image18 and 28
What goes in and out?the variables and secrets it needs, from YAML and from settingsits artifacts, caches, reports, and what it pushes or deploys25–31

Answer them in this order, because each answer narrows the next. You can't read a job's rules until you know where they come from. You can't judge its inputs until you know which runner and image it had.

Each question has one trap that catches most people:

  • Defined: a policy's job is in no file at all (chapter 19).
  • When: a job's own rules replace a template's list completely (chapter 13).
  • Where: the runner's configuration changes jobs, and no project can see it (chapter 28).
  • What: the script calls a tool or function from the image, whose code is somewhere else (chapter 18).
  • In and out: a settings variable beats anything in the YAML (chapter 25).

One job, decoded#

Here is payments-api's image-build, decoded using nothing but the specimen:

QuestionThe answer for image-buildFound in
Where is it defined?image-build in java-service.yml extends .image-build in container.yml, which extends .megacorp-base in base.ymlthe Full configuration view, and chapter 19's steps
When does it run?.megacorp-base's rules: merge requests, main and release tags, never schedules; it needs maven-buildthe .rules library, and chapter 24's truth table
Where does it run?on the megacorp-shared runner, in a Kubernetes pod, from the buildah imagedefault: tags, the runner's configuration, and the job's image
What does it execute?the ci-tools functions and the AWS login from the snippets, then Buildah's login, build and push, and on main a second push, to Azurethe !reference lines in before_script, and ci-lib.sh
What goes in and out?in: an ID token, AWS_ROLE_ARN, ECR_REGISTRY, AWS_REGION and the jar from maven-build; out: an image in ECR, on main in ACR too, and IMAGE_REF in a dotenv reportits variables and needs, and its artifacts

After five short answers, the job holds no more surprises.

A deployment, decoded#

A deploy has the same five questions, with different places to look (five questions for a deployment). Here they are for payments-api 1c7d4b09, deployed to production on eks-prod:

QuestionThe answer for payments-api in productionFound in
Where is it defined?the shared chart service at service-3.4.0, with the values in envs/production/payments-api.yaml, through Argo CD's ApplicationSetthe ApplicationSet's sources, then the values file (chapter 44)
When does it deploy?when the deploy's merge request is merged in the environment repository, and Argo CD next syncsthe merge request, then the Application's sync status
Where does it run?eks-prod, in the payments-production namespacethe ApplicationSet's destination
What does it run?123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1c7d4b09, in the Deployment that the chart rendershelm template with the same values (chapter 42)
What goes in and out?in: settings from the values file, and secrets that the External Secrets Operator copies from Secrets Manager; out: logs, metrics and traces, and a mark on the dashboardsthe ExternalSecret, and the service's dashboards (chapter 51)

When a deploy is missing or wrong, answer them in the same order. The first answer that surprises you is where to look (chapter 51).

Starting from a symptom#

Each symptom card names a symptom, then its cause, how to confirm it, and how to fix it. The cards come in four chapters, one per group, with the most common causes first: didn't run, failed, wrong result, and stuck or drifting. For your own pipelines, the worksheet is a printable form of the five questions.

Spot the bugDecode publish-docs#

payments-api defines one job of its own. Answer the five questions for it:

megacorp/payments/payments-api.gitlab-ci.ymlinherit
publish-docs:
  stage: deploy
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/docs:1.4
  inherit:
    default: [tags, retry]
    variables: false
  script:
    - mkdocs build --strict
  rules:
    - !reference [.rules, default-branch]
QuestionWhere is it defined, when does it run, where does it run, what does it execute, and what goes in and out? Which answer should worry its owners?
Show the answer
  • Defined in payments-api's own file. Nothing extends it, and inherit takes only tags and retry from default:.
  • When: in pipelines for main only, through the default-branch rule.
  • Where: on the megacorp-shared runner, because it inherits tags, in the docs:1.4 image.
  • What: mkdocs build --strict.
  • In and out: no YAML variables, because variables: false, but settings variables still arrive. Out: nothing at all.

The last answer is the worry. The job builds the documentation site and then ends. With no artifacts and no deploy step, the site is thrown away with the job's pod. Its name promises a publication that never happens. See the five questions.

Next55Field guide to enterprise setups3 min

Field guide to enterprise setups#

Part X · Decode and debug · Chapter 55· 3 min read

Large organisations build their pipelines in a handful of recognisable ways. Each leaves fingerprints: signs in a repository, a pipeline graph or a job log that tell you which setup you are looking at. Recognise the setup first, and you know where the answers live before you start reading YAML. This chapter lists ten pipeline setups and eight delivery setups, with their fingerprints and where to confirm each one.

Ten setups and their fingerprints#

SetupFingerprintsConfirm itChapters
The golden pipelinea .gitlab-ci.yml of a few lines: one include: project: of a central file at a tag, a few variablesFull configuration shows dozens of jobs that the file never names13–14
Componentsinclude: component: lines ending in @1.2.0, with inputs:the component's project, and its spec: inputs15
The generated monorepoa job that writes YAML, then a trigger that runs it; child pipelines to the right of the graphthe generator script, and the trigger's include: artifact:16
The central deployerdeploy jobs that are trigger: project: jobs; environments that live in another projectthe deployer project's pipeline and environments16, 39
GitOps deliverydeploy jobs that only commit to a configuration repositorythat repository's history, and the controller's sync status44
Policy-injected jobsjobs named like secret-detection-1, or in .pipeline-policy-pre and .pipeline-policy-post stages**Secure › Policies**17, 35
The invisible runner layerbehaviour that differs by runner; environment variables nobody set in YAMLthe runner's name in the job log, and the runner's configuration18, 28
The toolbox imagescripts calling commands such as mc or shell functions that the repository doesn't containthe job's image, and the image's own repository18
Cloud access by identityid_tokens: in templates, a login snippet, and no cloud keys in settingsthe role's trust policy, and aws sts get-caller-identity27, 37
The 2019 legacy fileanchors and <<: merge keys, only: and except:, include: remote:, trigger tokensthe parse phase: anchors are resolved in Full configuration12, 14, 22

MegaCorp shows all ten: payments-api is a golden pipeline with a component, mono is a generated monorepo, the deployer is central and GitOps-based, and billing-batch is the 2019 legacy file.

Eight delivery setups and their fingerprints#

After the pipeline, deploys follow a handful of setups of their own. These are the ones you'll meet, with where to confirm each:

SetupFingerprintsConfirm itChapters
Push deploysa deploy job runs kubectl apply, helm upgrade --install or a cloud's CLI, and holds the cluster's credentialsthe job's script, and where its kubeconfig or cloud identity comes from40, 37
GitOps with Argo CDan environment repository with Application or ApplicationSet files; deploy jobs that only committhe Application's sync status and revision, in Argo CD's UI46
GitOps with Fluxa clusters/<name>/flux-system/ folder in a repository, with Kustomization and HelmRelease objectsthe Kustomization's Ready condition, and the revision it last applied45
GitLab's agent for Kubernetesa .gitlab/agents/<name>/config.yaml file in some project; jobs whose $KUBECONFIG has contexts for agent connections**Operate › Kubernetes clusters**, and the agent's configuration file45
Image automationcommits in the environment repository by a bot, changing only image tagsImagePolicy and ImageUpdateAutomation objects, or an Argo CD ImageUpdater44
Infrastructure from modules.tf or .tofu files that call modules at ?ref= tags; plans in merge requests; backend "http"**Operate › Terraform states**, and the plan job's output47
Progressive deliveryRollout objects where Deployments would be, or Canary objects beside them; AnalysisTemplatesthe Rollout's or the Canary's status, step by step50
A repository from a portal templatea catalog-info.yaml with a backstage.io/source-template annotation; a first commit called initial commit, by Scaffolderthe portal's template, and whether the pipeline file copies jobs or includes a central file52

MegaCorp shows five of them. Flux installs its platform add-ons, Argo CD deploys its services, the platform team's OpenTofu builds both clusters from modules, and payments-api's repository came from the portal's template. Its deploy marks come from Argo CD too (chapter 51).

No .gitlab-ci.yml, but pipelines run#

This is the most disorienting fingerprint of all. Five mechanisms can produce it, and each has a place to confirm it:

MegaCorp's web-portal is the first case. Its settings point at pipelines/web.yml in ci-templates, so its repository needs no pipeline file (chapter 17):

megacorp/web/web-portalSETTINGS.ymlconfig-path
ci_cd_configuration_file: pipelines/web.yml@megacorp/devops/ci-templates
Spot the bugWhich setup is this?#

You join a team and open their newest pipeline. You notice three things:

  • the project's .gitlab-ci.yml is nine lines long, and includes one file from platform/ci-library at ref: v7.1.0
  • one job, deploy-prod, is a trigger job pointing at platform/release
  • two jobs are called sast-1 and secret-detection-1
QuestionWhich three setups are in play, and where would you look first for each?
Show the answer
  • A golden pipeline: read platform/ci-library at v7.1.0, starting from Full configuration.
  • A central deployer: the real deploy happens in platform/release's pipeline and environments.
  • Policy-injected jobs: the numbered scanners come from a scan execution policy, so check Secure › Policies.

See ten setups and their fingerprints.

Next56Idioms2 min

Idioms#

Part X · Decode and debug · Chapter 56· 2 min read

Central teams repeat a small number of patterns, called idioms, in every organisation. Each one solves a real problem for the team that writes the templates. Each also hides something from the people who read the pipelines. Learn to spot them, and an unfamiliar pipeline stops looking unfamiliar. For each idiom, this chapter shows what it looks like, why central teams use it, and how it confuses a reader.

A rules library, pulled in with !reference#

This is the idiom that confuses most readers, so here it is in full. MegaCorp keeps its conditions in one hidden job:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/rules.ymlrules-library
.rules:
  mr:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
  default-branch:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  release-tag:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/
  never-on-schedule:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
      when: never

Jobs assemble their rules from it: - !reference [.rules, mr].

  • Why central teams use it: "which pipelines does this job run in" is decided once, with one name for each condition. Every template agrees on what a release tag looks like.
  • What it hides: the conditions live in another file, so a job's rules read like a list of names. The names say nothing about the order, and in rules the order decides the outcome, because the first match wins. If you replace the job's rules:, every referenced rule disappears with them (chapter 13).

The catalogue#

IdiomLooks likeWhy central teams use itHow it confuses youChapters
The hidden base jobextends: .megacorp-baseshared rules, variables and expiry in one placesettings arrive from files you never opened; its variables beat your top-level ones13
Script snippets- !reference [.snippets, aws_login]the same few script lines in every templatea job's own before_script drops them; the functions they call live in the image13, 18
Variables as parametersimage: maven:3.9-jdk${JAVA_VERSION}one template serves many projectsthe default is in the template; a settings variable beats your YAML13, 25
Togglesif: $SKIP_SONAR == "true" then when: neveran escape hatch without editing the templatea toggle set in settings is invisible; policy jobs ignore toggles33, 35
The pinned includeinclude: project: … ref: v4.2.0projects upgrade when they choose towhat runs is that tag's content, not the central repo's current version; a tag can be moved14
Components with inputscomponent: …/sonar-scan@2.1.0 with inputs:typed, versioned settingsinputs are filled in before anything else, even into job names15
The dotenv hand-offecho "IMAGE_REF=…" >> build.envpasses a build's result to later jobsno file shows the value; needs and dependencies can block it; rules can't see it30
The trigger to a deployertrigger: project: …/deployer with strategy: dependone team controls every environmentthe deploy happens in another project's pipeline16, 39
Never on schedulethe first rule excludes schedulenightly pipelines run only what they shouldjobs are silently absent from scheduled pipelines22, 24
Opting out with inheritinherit: default: [tags, retry]a job that shouldn't get the shared image or scriptswhich defaults still apply is easy to misread13
No duplicate pipelinesa workflow rule with $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTSone pipeline per push, not twoonce a merge request opens, branch pipelines stop appearing21
Build once, deploy by referencethe image tagged with $CI_COMMIT_SHA, then passed onwhat is tested is what shipsa pipeline that rebuilds breaks the promise quietly38

Most real pipelines combine several idioms in a single job. Recognising each one tells you which file to open next.

Spot the bugCount the idioms#

This is the template behind payments-api's image-build:

megacorp/devops/ci-templatestemplates/container.ymlimage-build
.image-build:
  extends: .megacorp-base
  stage: package
  image: registry.example.com/megacorp/devops/ci-tools/buildah:1.37
  id_tokens:
    MC_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-ecr-push
    ECR_REGISTRY: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com
    IMAGE: $ECR_REGISTRY/$CI_PROJECT_NAME
  before_script:
    - !reference [.snippets, functions]
    - !reference [.snippets, aws_login]
  script:
    - mc_retry aws ecr get-login-password | buildah login --username AWS --password-stdin "$ECR_REGISTRY"
    - buildah bud -t "$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" .
    - buildah push "$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
    - !reference [.snippets, acr_push]
    - echo "IMAGE_REF=$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" >> build.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: build.env
QuestionWhich idioms from this chapter can you find, directly or through what the job extends?
Show the answer
  • The hidden base job: extends: .megacorp-base, which also brings in the rules library and never on schedule.
  • Script snippets: the three !reference [.snippets, …] lines, two before the script and one in it.
  • Variables as parameters: AWS_ROLE_ARN and ECR_REGISTRY, which a project could override.
  • The dotenv hand-off: IMAGE_REF written to build.env.
  • Build once, deploy by reference: the image tagged with $CI_COMMIT_SHA.

The job reaches payments-api through a pinned include as well: java-service.yml includes it at v4.2.0. See the catalogue.

Next57Worksheet: decode your own pipeline2 min

Worksheet: decode your own pipeline#

Part X · Decode and debug · Chapter 57· 2 min read

Print this page, or copy it into a private note, and fill it in for one of your own projects. It is the five questions, for a job and for a deployment, plus the few facts about your organisation that make every answer easier. Keep your answers private, because they describe your organisation's systems.

Once for your organisation#

Most of these answers are the same for every project, so you only find them once:

QuestionWhere to find the answerYour answer
Where do the central templates and components live?the include: lines of any project, and the platform team's group…
Which versions do projects pin, and who moves them?the ref: of each include, and the templates' release notes…
Which runners run your jobs, and which tags do they need?Settings › CI/CD › Runners, and default: tags…
Which executor do those runners use?the first lines of any job log…
Which CI/CD variables do your groups and the instance set?each group's Settings › CI/CD › Variables, if you can see it…
Which security policies apply?Secure › Policies…
How do jobs reach the cloud?id_tokens: in the templates, and the login script…
Where do deployments really happen?trigger jobs, environments, and any GitOps repository…

For each job you need to understand#

QuestionWhere to lookYour answer
Where is it defined?Full configuration; its extends chain; if it's in no file, policies…
When does it run?workflow:rules, its final rules, needs; compare pipeline types…
Where does it run?the job page's runner and tags; the job's image…
What does it execute?its scripts, and the tools and functions they call…
What goes in and out?variables, secrets, artifacts, caches, reports, images, deployments…

For each deployment you need to understand#

The same five questions, asked after the pipeline (a deployment, decoded):

QuestionWhere to lookYour answer
Where is it defined?the environment repository; the chart and its version; values files, overlays and inline values…
When does it deploy?the commit or merge request that changed it; the controller and its sync policy…
Where does it run?the cluster and namespace, in the controller's Application or Kustomization…
What does it run?the image reference, as rendered; whether that tag is in the cluster's registry…
What goes in and out?settings and secrets, and where each comes from; its logs, metrics and traces, and where they're kept…

When something goes wrong#

Write down, in this order:

  1. The symptom, in one sentence, and its group: didn't run, failed, wrong result, or stuck or drifting (chapter 54).
  2. The pipeline and job, with links, and what changed since the last good run: a commit, a setting, a template version, a runner, a date.
  3. The cards you tried, and what each confirmation showed.
  4. The fix, and who had to make it: you, the platform team, the security team or the cloud team.

Questions for your platform team#

Some answers aren't visible from a project at all. These are worth asking once:

  • What do the runners add to every job: environment variables, a pre_build_script, limits?
  • Which of the group's CI/CD variables are protected, and why?
  • Which stored tokens do the pipelines depend on, who owns them, and when do they expire?
  • How are template versions released, and can a tag ever move?
  • Which security policies are enforced, and on which projects?
  • Which controller deploys each environment, how often does it sync, and who may merge into the environment repository?
  • Where do the services' logs, metrics and traces go, and is each deploy marked on the dashboards?
Next58Cards: didn't run8 min

Cards: didn't run#

Part X · Decode and debug · Chapter 58· 8 min read

Use these cards when a job is missing from a pipeline, when the pipeline wasn't created, or when a job ran somewhere it shouldn't have. The most common causes come first. Each card gives the symptom, the cause, how to confirm it, and the fix. One more card for this group is in chapter 13: your rules replaced the template's. The last cards cover what happens after the pipeline.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
A job runs in branch pipelines but is missing from merge request pipelines, or the other way round.
Cause

Merge request pipelines and branch pipelines are different pipelines, with different variables. CI_COMMIT_BRANCH, for example, isn't set in merge request pipelines, so a rule that tests it is false there. The job has no rule for $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event".

Confirm

Open both pipelines and compare their job lists. Each pipeline's page shows its source. Then read the job's final rules in Build › Pipeline editor › Full configuration.

Fix

Add a rule for merge request pipelines, or reuse your organisation's rule from its rules library with !reference. See merge request pipelines.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
A push creates no pipeline at all, or Run pipeline refuses to start one.
Cause

workflow:rules decide whether a pipeline exists. None of them matched this push, or the one that matched said when: never.

Confirm

Run pipeline and the API answer with:

The pipeline did not run. Review the workflow:rules configuration for the pipeline.

Read workflow: in Full configuration.

Fix

Add the missing pipeline source or branch to the workflow rules, or push where the workflow allows. See the first matching rule.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
The workflow allows the pipeline, yet it isn't created, because no job would have been in it.
Cause

Every job's rules excluded it for this source and branch. MegaCorp's deployer does this deliberately: all its jobs need IMAGE_REF, which only a trigger supplies.

Confirm

GitLab says:

The resulting pipeline would have been empty. Review the rules configuration.

The Validate tab, run for the same branch, shows no jobs.

Fix

Provide what the rules expect, such as the variable a trigger would send, or change the rules. See when a pipeline is missing.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
Pushing a tag such as v1.5.0-rc1 creates no pipeline, and shows no error anywhere.
Cause

The workflow allows tag pipelines, but no job's rules match this tag. MegaCorp's release rule accepts only tags shaped like v1.5.0, exactly ^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$. A pipeline with no jobs isn't created, and on a push GitLab doesn't say why.

Confirm

Run Validate for the tag: it shows no jobs. Starting a pipeline for the tag by hand gives The resulting pipeline would have been empty. Review the rules configuration.

Fix

Name tags the way the rules expect, or widen the rule if release candidates should build. See what the truth table says.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tScanners and policies#
GitLab's scanner jobs, such as secret_detection, appear in branch pipelines but never in merge request pipelines.
Cause

GitLab's scanner templates run their jobs in merge request pipelines only when AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES is "true". Otherwise the jobs run in branch pipelines only.

Confirm

In Full configuration, the job's rules contain the AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES conditions. The branch pipeline for the same commit has the job.

Fix

Set AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES: "true", in the YAML or in settings. The job then moves to the merge request pipeline. Or redefine the job's rules. See the merge request gap.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
A job runs on every push, but never in scheduled pipelines.
Cause

Its rules start with a rule that excludes schedules. MegaCorp's .megacorp-base begins with !reference [.rules, never-on-schedule], so every job that extends it skips scheduled pipelines.

Confirm

The job's final rules in Full configuration start with the schedule rule, and the pipeline's source is schedule.

Fix

If the job should run on a schedule, give it rules without that line, or ask the template's owners to change the base. See each job's final rules.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
A job shows a play button and never starts. The stages after it may wait too.
Cause

The job is manual, through when: manual on the job or in the rule that matched. Manual jobs run only when someone starts them. A manual job added by a rule blocks the later stages, unless it has allow_failure: true.

Confirm

The job page offers Run, and its rules or when in Full configuration say manual.

Fix

Run it. If nothing should wait for it, add allow_failure: true to that rule. See manual jobs.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
A job with rules: changes runs on the first push of a new branch, or on a tag, although none of its files changed.
Cause

For new branches, for tags, and for pipelines without a push event, rules: changes is always true. There is nothing to compare with. On the local GitLab, mono's first push ran its docs job although there was no docs/ folder.

Confirm

The pipeline is a tag pipeline, or the branch's first pipeline.

Fix

Compare against a fixed branch with changes: compare_to:, or add a rule that excludes tags. See rules about files.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
Every push to a merge request's branch creates two pipelines, and every job runs twice.
Cause

The workflow allows both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline for the same push.

Confirm

The pipelines list shows two pipelines for the same commit, one of them marked as a merge request pipeline.

Fix

Add a workflow rule that skips branch pipelines while a merge request is open, using $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS. See duplicate pipelines.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tScanners and policies#
A scanner job has vanished from every pipeline, and nobody changed the YAML.
Cause

Someone set its toggle, such as CONTAINER_SCANNING_DISABLED, in the project's or a group's CI/CD settings. The template's first rule removes the job. MegaCorp's own container scanning rule accepts only "true".

Confirm

Look for the variable in the project's and each group's CI/CD settings. Its rule is the job's first.

Fix

Remove the setting if the scan should run. A scan execution policy's jobs are never affected by toggles. See toggles against policies.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tScanners and policies#
The SAST template is included, but no SAST job appears.
Cause

Each SAST analyzer's job exists only when files that it reads are in the repository, such as *.java or *.py for semgrep-sast.

Confirm

In Full configuration, compare the analyzer's exists patterns with the repository's files.

Fix

None is needed if the repository has no code in those languages. Otherwise check that the source files are where the patterns look. See what the templates add.

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tScanners and policies#
The dependency scanning template is included, but its jobs never appear.
Cause

Those jobs' rules require the dependency_scanning feature, which comes with Ultimate. On Free and Premium, the template adds nothing, without an error.

Confirm

The jobs' rules in Full configuration test $GITLAB_FEATURES.

Fix

Use Ultimate, or run another dependency scanner as an ordinary job (chapter 34).

Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tRules and conditions#
The pipeline isn't created, and the error names a job that another job needs.
Cause

The needed job's rules left it out of this pipeline, while the job that needs it is still in.

Confirm

GitLab's message, captured here with other job names, says:

'unit-tests' job needs 'compile' job, but 'compile' does not exist in the pipeline.
