Next69One-page card2 min

One-page card#

Appendix · Appendices · Chapter 69· 2 min read

The book on one page, to print and keep next to your screen.

Five questions for any job#

Ask them in this order (chapter 54):

QuestionLook at
Where is it defined?Full configuration, then its extends chain and includes; if it's in no file, policies
When does it run?workflow:rules, the job's final rules, and needs
Where does it run?the job page's runner and tags, and the job's image
What does it execute?its scripts, and the tools and functions those call
What goes in and out?variables and secrets; artifacts, caches, reports, images and deploys

Five questions for a deployment#

The same five, asked after the pipeline (chapter 54):

QuestionLook at
Where is it defined?the environment repository: the chart, its values, overlays and inline values
When does it deploy?the commit or merge request, then the controller's sync
Where does it run?the cluster and namespace, in the Application or Kustomization
What does it run?the rendered image reference, and whether that tag is in the cluster's registry
What goes in and out?settings and secrets in; logs, metrics and traces out

Four kinds of symptom#

SymptomCheck firstCards
Didn't run, or ran when it shouldn'tthe pipeline exists; the rules matched; everything it needs existsdidn't run
Failedthe log's first error; the image and runner; what went infailed
Passed, but did the wrong thingwhich value won; which image or artifact; what was deployedwrong result
Stuck, slow, or broke with no commitrunners online; tokens expired; central files or images changedstuck or drifting

Writing your team's pipeline#

  1. Start with a workflow: merge request pipelines while a merge request is open, branch pipelines otherwise (chapter 6).
  2. Pin every image, include and component to a version.
  3. Keep what later jobs need as artifacts; use the cache only for speed.
  4. Put secrets in settings, masked and protected, and expect them to be empty on branches.
  5. Tag each image with its commit, and deploy that one tag everywhere.
  6. Give every deploy job an environment, and make production manual.

Which variable value wins, highest first#

Security policies, then values given when the pipeline started, then the project's settings, then the groups', closest first, then the instance's. Below those come dotenv reports, then the job's own YAML, then top-level YAML, then deployment and predefined variables (chapter 25).

Where to look in GitLab#

PlaceShows
Build › Pipeline editor, Full configurationevery file and template, merged
Build › Pipeline editor, Validatethe jobs a pipeline would get, and problems with them
The pipeline graphwhich jobs exist, and any downstream pipelines
The job pagethe runner, the image, the timeout, and the log
Settings › CI/CD › Variables, Runners, General pipelinessettings variables, runners, clone depth and the pipeline file's location
Settings › CI/CD › Job token permissionswhich projects may use your job tokens
Secure › Policiesthe security policies that apply
Operate › Environmentsdeployments, approvals and rollback
Operate › Kubernetes clusters, Terraform statesthe agents that connect clusters; OpenTofu's states and their locks

Where to look after the pipeline#

PlaceShows
The environment repository's history and merge requestswhat should run where, and what waits for a merge
Argo CD's Application, or Flux's Kustomizationwhat the controller applied, and whether it's healthy
kubectl describe pod, and its eventswhy a pod won't pull, start or become ready
The service's dashboardswhether the deploy worked, after its mark

Commands worth remembering#

aws sts get-caller-identity                              # which AWS role is really in use
echo "$MC_ID_TOKEN" | cut -d '.' -f2 | base64 -d | jq .  # an ID token's claims, not the token
env | cut -d= -f1 | sort                                 # which variables exist: names only
git fetch --unshallow                                    # full history, for scripts that need it
az account show                                          # who the Azure CLI is signed in as
helm template payments-api ./service -f values.yaml      # what a chart renders
kustomize build overlays/staging                         # what an overlay builds
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments-api -n payments-staging   # did the rollout finish?
kubectl logs <pod> --previous                            # a crashed container's last output

Ten traps#

  1. A job's own rules, before_script, tags or services replace the inherited list completely.
  2. A settings variable beats anything in the YAML.
  3. A job's variables, including those from extends, beat top-level ones.
  4. Toggles never stop a security policy's jobs.
  5. GitLab's scanners skip merge request pipelines unless AST_ENABLE_MR_PIPELINES is "true".
  6. Protected values reach only protected branches and tags.
  7. A cache can miss at any time; only artifacts are guaranteed.
  8. Jobs get a shallow clone of their own ref only.
  9. With GitOps, green means written to Git, not running.
  10. A pipeline that rebuilds an image ships something nobody tested.

Four traps after the pipeline#

  1. Healthy means the pods pass their probes, not that requests succeed.
  2. A running pod keeps the settings and secrets it started with.
  3. Entra ID matches a federated credential's subject exactly, with no wildcards.
  4. In Argo CD, inline values beat value files.

End of the book
